INTRODUCTION
 
  
            I, the Chairman of the Departme nt-related Parliamentary Stan ding Committee on Science & 
Technology, Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on
its behalf, present this One H undred-twenty fourth Report on the Action Taken by the Department o f 
Science & Technology on the recommendations c ontained in the One Hundr ed-seventeenth Report o f 
the Committee on Demands for Grants (2003-2004) of the Department of Science & Technology. 
      2.   The Report of the Committee deals wi th the Action Taken by the Department of Science &
Technology on the recommendations contained in  the One Hundred-seventeenth Report of the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Co mmittee on Science & T echnology, Environment &
Forests on the Demands for Grants (2003-2004) of the Department of Science & Technology which was
presented to the Rajya Sabha on 2nd May, 2003.   
      3.   There were eleven recommendations c ontained in the One Hundred-s eventeenth Report of the 
Committee.  Action Taken Notes on the recommendations of the Co mmittee were r eceived from the
Department  on 5th September, 2003. 
            4.         In the meeting held on 23 rd January, 2004, the Committee c onsidered the draft Action
Taken Report and adopted the same.

The Committee’s recommendations, act ion taken thereon and comments of the             
Committee on the action taken by the Department of Science & Technology are set out in the
succeeding paragraphs: - 
FUND FOR THE IMPROVEMENT OF S&T IN FRASTRUCTURE IN UNIVERSITIES AND
OTHER HIGHER EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS (FIST) 
Recommendation 
            The Committee notes with constr aint that the quality of in frastructure available in ou r
Universities and research laborator ies for pursuing scientific resear ch is not upto the mark. Lack o f
interest on the part of students to go for science education is indeed alarming.  The Department is taking
steps to encourage young scientists  to pursue serious sc ientific work.  The Committee notes with
concern the decline of the quality of  our research papers.  There is an  urgent need to take concerted
efforts to arrest this trend to give new dynamism and momentum to Indian science. 
(Para 10)
Action taken by the Department 
            The Scheme ‘Fund for Improvement of S&T In frastructure in Univ ersities and Highe r
Educational Institutions’ was initiated in the year 2000 to address these concerns.  The scheme has so far
identified and supported about 460 Departments at various universitie s and related higher educational
institutions in the country.  The supports are mainly provided for st rengthening of infrastructure and
equipments, acquisition of comput ation networking facilities, mode rnisation of library, providing good
quality teaching material, enha ncement of research facili ties in this departments.   While majority of the
Departments supported so far are now  in the process of acquiring thes e facilities, a few departments
have already acquired the same.   Towards monitoring and reviewing of  the progress, these departments
have now submitted the Technical Progress Report, which are being evaluated along with the visit of the
sites by the area Experts. 
In 2003-04, the fresh proposals re ceived from the prospective Departments/Centres of the 
Universities and related acad emic institutions are be ing processed for consideration of support in the
current financial year. 
Comments 
The Committee feels that the Department shoul d monitor and supervise the Technical Progress
Report to evaluate the performanc e of the schemes being implemente d to prevent the misuse of the
funds made available under the schemes. 
 SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY FOR WOMEN 
Recommendation 
            The Committee appreciates the Department fo r launching a new  Schemes for women and hopes
that with the intr oduction of the Scholarships, the contri bution of women to science and technology
would increase. The Committee recommends that the Department may specially focus on rural women. 
The aim should also be to tap the pot ential of women in smaller towns who because of lack of financial
support of infrastructure do not pursue science studies.   
(Para 16)
Action taken by the Department 
            The response to the Women Scientists Sche me has been overwhelming. The screening o f 
applications by high-level  Expert Committee is currently in progr ess. Special consideration is being
given to women who have faced women-s pecific and location-s pecific problems in pursuing science

studies. 
            In the first year there has been a very encouraging response from  women scientists from rural
areas and small towns.  This focus will be maintained in future also.  
Comments 
The Committee notes the position a nd would like the Department to take steps to provide current
information on careers, training, scie nce and scientific policies to wo men through universities, colleges
etc. Apart from this there is a need to take initiatives to increase the men to women ratio in science and
engineering fields.  The Committee al so suggests that the special cons ideration which is being given to
women scientists should be given wide publicity in print and audio-visual media. 
SPECIAL COMPONENT PLAN FOR SCHEDULED CASTES 
Recommendation 
            The Committee hopes that this pr ogramme would aim at  providing alternate vocation as well as
additional income to these communities.  The pr ogrammes should also aim at uplifting their social
status.  These communities mostly are not aware of these programmes.  By giving due publicity to such
programmes the Department can reac h out the lowest rungs of thes e communities and sensitise them
about the benefits of such schemes for improving their living conditions and for their empowerment. 
The I & B Ministry is willing to cooperate in the direction and it should be tapped without delay. 
(Para 20)
Action taken by the Department 
The recommendation is noted. Provi ding alternate vocations as we ll as additional income are
being attempted through various innovative programmes with sciences and technology intervention such
as functional capability development, skill upgradation training, etc.  Regarding publicity a dialogue has
already been initiated with Pr asar Bharati although th is is a not a major bottleneck since the
interventions are designed and implemented by scient ists and technologists in  academic and research
institutions.  
Comments 
The Committee would like the Department to evol ve an effective monitoring mechanism to see that
the benefits of the programme reach the targeted community. 
PATENT FACILITATION CENTRE 
Recommendation 
            The Committee notes that patent  literacy will promote grea ter awareness and knowledge among
people and enable them to make informed choices.  To safeguard  our germplasm and traditional
knowledge and to assert our ri ght to own our genetic divers ity knowledge about patenting is
indispensable.  Patenting of Haldee and Basmati abroad a nd our successful fight against those patents is
a clear pointer towards adopting greater vigilance for protecting our biodivers ity.  The Committee
recommends that the Department ma y augment its own efforts in this  regard and give due publicity to
such activities for the benefit of scientists, resear chers and the general public.   After all to save ou r
traditional knowledge we will not only depend on scie ntific community but also on women, rural fol k
and people and individuals. 
(Para 25)
Action taken by the Department 
            The Department will augment its efforts in creating awareness about Intellectual Property Rights
(IPR) among scientists and researcher s.  Attempts are also being ma de to create awareness in schools
and general public.

Comments 
        The Committee notes with satisf action that attempts are being made to create awareness in
schools and among general public about  intellectual property rights.  The committee would like the
Department to provide support to th e scientific community for protect ing their inventive work and take
steps to setup Patent Facilitation Centre (PFC) in all States and Union Territories. 
 JOINT TECHNOLOGY PROGRAMME 
Recommendation 
            While the Committee notes with sa tisfaction that the Department is engaged in producing and 
applying, technologies for the all ro und development of India it reco mmends that special focus may be
given on the issue of producing clean  and eco-friendly technologies fo r sustainable development of ou r
country.  Increasingly, we have to follow the path  of eco-friendly industrial revolution.  For ou r 
sustainable development eco-friendl y industrial revolution seems to be  a necessity.  Therefore, the
Committee recommends that the Department must  concentrate its attent ion towards producing such
technologies which will be consistent with ecology and industrial development. 
(Para 28)
Action taken by the Department 
The recommendation is noted and this Departme nt would give special focus on producing clean
and eco-friendly technologies for sustainable development. It may be pertinent to mention here that DST 
has already initiated activities in th e line of clean and eco-friendly tec hnologies in the area of alternate 
fuels for substitution of diesel by the non-edible oil from karanj seed s, promotion of pollution control
technologies for cupola, rice shelling and brick kiln  industry, clean disposal of arsenic and fluoride
sludge, plastic waste disposal using plasma pyrolysis technology, use of micro hydel for powe r
generation in hilly and plain terrain etc.. Concerted efforts are be ing made by the department to develop
technologies in the field of sensor s for detection of LPG and CNG leak ages and also for instrument and
systems development for eco-friendly industrial development. 
Comments 
The Committee feels that the technologies developed should be disseminated to industry and end
users at the earliest for the wider acceptance. 
TECHNOLOGY FOR BAMBOO PRODUCTS 
Recommendation 
            The committee was informed that while some of  the national centres of excellence in India
possess rich expertise in bamboo technology, the knowledge flow to the industry has not come up to the
desired level. As such it is high time to bring the technology sourcing avenues and industries fo r
technology development, transfer and commercialization. Thus the aim is to undertake a programme at
the national level which could impa rt a significant boost to the usage of bamboo, promote specialized
products for commercialization and would generate good employment opportunities. 
(Para 33)
Action taken by the Department 
To bring together technology sourcing avenues and industrie s for technology development,
transfer and commercialization, and to provide a si gnificant boost to the usage of bamboo and its value
added products, a major initiative has been ta ken in the form of Na tional Mission on Bamboo
Applications (NMBA). Th e task of implem enting the Mission has been en trusted to the TIFAC, an
autonomous organisation under Depa rtment of Science & Technolo gy. The Mission has been devolved
to provide a new impetus and direction to the bamboo sector by seeking to:

(i)               Develop and promote environment friendl y value added bamboo based products, 
practices, technology and processes, 
(ii)                Promote innovative design capabilities, fabricati on techniques & testing
methodologies 
(iii)               Improve industry-lab-user linkages and effect inter-institutional / industry interaction
(iv)              Provide financial assistance for risk mi nimization towards new product and market 
development 
(v)                Develop small and medium enterprises 
(vi)              Empower people at the gra ss root level encompassing fa rmers, artisans and othe r 
stakeholders for incremental employment  generation with improved remunerative
opportunities. 
Comments 
The Committee expresses its sa tisfaction with the progra mmes being conducted for the
promotion of bamboo and hopes that this would significantly increase usage of bamboo in diverse more
employment opportunities for people at the grass root level.  
Recommendation 
While the Committee appr eciates the Department for launchi ng the scheme for Technology fo r
Bamboo Products it observes that the benefits of research and development in this field have not reached
the people who are engaged in making bamboo products.  The Committee expressed concern that
imported instruments are not suitabl e for cutting bamboos which are ha rder than the ones in foreign
countries from where such instru ments are obtained.  The Committee,  therefore, strongly recommends
that the Departme nt should design instruments, as soon as possible, which would be useful for the
varieties of bamboos found in differe nt parts of our country.  The Co mmittee also recommends that the
Department should coordina te with the Indian Plyw ood Industries Research In stitute at Bangalore, an
autonomous body with the Ministry  of Environment & Forest, for conducting research and training
programmes on bamboo relate d activities.  The Committee also suggests that the Department may
explore the possibilities of  collaborating with China with a view  to exchanging and sharing ideas and
experiences related to making of bamboo products. 
(Para 39)
Action taken by the Department 
The National Mission on Bamboo A pplications (NMBA) is work ing closely with technical,
research and academic institutions, and with us er groups including producer s, entrepreneurs and
converters to bridge the laboratory industry-user gap.  The areas of focus include a) resins, adhesives 
and treatment of bamboo (b) machin ery, presses and tooling (c) packag es of practices for propagation
and cultivation (d) processing of edible bamboo shoots (e) development and commercialization of value
added products. 
The Mission has also taken up a programme of development of indigenous machinery fo r
complete lines of primary processing machinery for production of a) slivers for bamboo composites and
b) slivers for woven applications have been established and evalua ted, and are now available through
local manufacturers. 
The Mission, in collaboration with the Indian Plywood Industries Research and Training Institute
(IPIRTI), Bangalore has taken up an exercise to develop validat e and document process technology fo r
manufacture of bamboo composite boa rds, from sympodial bamboo of commercially significant species
available in India to be able to offer techno-economic packages of support to prospective entrepreneurs.

The Department of Scienc e and Technology (DST) and th e National Mission on Bamboo
Applications (NMBA) have initiated discussions with research and sector al institutions in China, with a
view to identifying areas for knowledge and technology exchange. 
Comments 
The Committee would like to be apprised of the pro gress of the National Mission on
Bamboo Applications (NMBA) during the consideration of Demands for Grants in 2004-2005. The 
Committee also suggests that there should be an effective monitoring system so that the benefits of
research and development in this field may reach the concerned people. 
THE PHARMACEUTICALS RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT SUPPORT FUND (PRDSF) 
Recommendation 
            The Committee commends the Department for re orienting its strategy to produce molecules fo r 
production of drugs so that it can meet the challenges of product patent arising out of the enforcement of
intellectual property rights from December, 2004.  Wh ile the Committee notes that the Department has
earmarked Rs.150 crores as corpus  fund for pharmaceutical research and development, it recommends
that the benefits derived from the funds provided by the Governme nt of India should be utilized
correctly.  The Committee was told that many multin ational corporations coul d help in pharmaceutical
research and development.  The Committee noted with anguish and pain that most of the pharmaceutical
formulation developed under the exemptions given by the Government of I ndia is taken by the
multinational corporations to their head offices abroad and patented th ere and marketed as international
brands and at international rates.  The Committee was agonized to know that such formulations are
produced by Indian scientists and with the help of Indian tax paye rs’ money and yet the benefits are 
reaped by the multinational drug companies who sell the products at a price wh ich most of the Indians
cannot afford.  The Committee, therefore, strongl y recommends that such technology or formulation
produced by Indian scientists must be patented in India before these are transferred or taken abroad.  The
Committee further recommends th at patenting of such formulat ions in India should be made
compulsory.  The Committee notes  the alarming trend of multina tional companies manufacturing even
Ayurvedic products, branding them and selling them with a high co mmercial pitch.  The Committee
recommends that all out efforts must be made to  reverse this trend and safeguard our traditional
knowledge from appropriation by foreign agencies. 
(Para 48)
Action taken by the Department 
“Drugs & Pharmaceuticals Research” (D&P Programme) was mounted by DST in 1994-1995 for 
promoting collaborative R&D in the Drugs and Pharmace utical sector between industry and institutions.
The programme supports rese arch in all systems of medicine, be it the trad itional Indian Medicinal
System (IMS) or the modern one . Till date the department (DST) has funded 45 Projects, 38
collaborative research projects alongwith 7 Nationa l Facilities. The overall commitment for these 45
programmes is of the or der of Rs.77.00 crores. (Government shar e of Rs. 32.00 crores and industry’s 
share of Rs.45.00 crores). Out of the various projects financially supported under the scheme 4 product
patents and 12 process patents have been filed so far by the institution and industry.

POPULARISATION OF SCIENCE 
Recommendation 
            The Committee was informed that the Department is making the children the real starting point 
for popularizing science and technol ogy.  However, the Committee notes with concern that there are no
laboratories and other infrastructure  for promoting science among childr en.  The Departme nt itself has
informed the Committee that ther e is marked decline of interest  among students to pursue science
courses in our educational institut ions.  To generate interest among students for scien ce and scientific
research, the Committee recommends  that science cafes and childr en’s scientific parks may be 
established in rural and ur ban areas with local as well as corpor ate assistance.  Apart from this the
Committee recommends that wides pread publicity must be given for the works done b y our scientists

Action taken by the Department 
The recommendation for setting up science cafes and corporate sponsored science parks fo r
generating interest in science am ong youth has been noted.  A projec t for giving these a proper shape
and determining their utility is under consideration.   
Widespread dissemination about the achievements and contributions of Indian scientists and
scientific institutions is very necessary.  Several initiatives have been launc hed to project them among
the masses and specially students under a programme called ‘Rise of M odern Indian Science’.  Public 
lectures, radio and video programmes, an interactiv e web site, wallpaper, et c., in a well-orchestrate d 
programme are creating a positive impact on the youth.  
Comments 
The Committee feels scie nce as a choice of car eer should be promoted and sincere efforts and
affirmative action from the Department and its scientis ts will surely witness a new renaissance in Indian
science.

 No.83).

Report
 
India is a land of one of the oldest civilizations of the world with rich cultural heritage, thriving economy and civic life. It has
 been a fountainhead of ancient knowledge and wisdom. The traditions of Science & technology in India are over 5000 years old. The
 resurgence of science in India came as an offshoot of the Nationalist Movement, towards the end of 19th century and the early decades of
 the 20 th century. Since 1947 a renaissance was witnessed with the emergence of India as a politically independent nation and as it
 pursued a programme of employing modern Science and Technology for national development. A few exceptionally talented and
 committed scientists and teachers of that period laid the solid foundation of Indian science by their zeal, dedication ad sacrifice. 
2.         Post independence, conscious efforts were made to enhance and modernize the scientific infrastructure in the country by
 establishing a series of national laboratories, institutes of advanced technical education, universities etc. Science & Technology inputs
 are made an intrinsic part of the planning process and development strategies. Many institutions were created soon after independence to
 promote basic research and technological progress.
3.         As a result of these pragmatic policies, India has turned from a largely agrarian society to a highly industrialized country today.
 Due to systematic exploitation of Science & Technology for socio-economic development and scientific innovations, the country has
 been successfully transformed from a food starving country at the time of independence to a food-surplus nation.
4.         To give direction to the promotion of Science & Technology in the country the Department of Science & Technology was
 established with the primary objective of promotion of new areas of Science and Technology and to play a role of a nodal Department

                        29.       The Committee was informed that the Department recognizing the profound influence of R&D on the prospects
 and opportunities for the growth of the Indian Drug Industry initiated the scheme on Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Research

 National facility.

 novel herbal ectoparasiticidal product ( a veterinary product), Study of safety and efficacy profile of “Kodiveli”-a siddha medicine in use
 for the management of rheumatoid arthritis and development of a novel controlled/sustained release formula for cardiovascular &

 Designer Polymers for Tailored Oral Drug Delivery systems, study of molecular mechanism of action of Cardoguard and its efficacy in
 the regression of ventricular hypertrophy, Efficacy and Safety evaluation of a Siddha medicine HIVS-2003 for HIV/AIDS, Development
 of herbo mineral and plant based disease oriented immuno-modulator formulations, increase efficacy of herbal medicines and
 standardization and modernization of ayurvedic/herbal formulations using modern techniques.
33.       The emerging economic, trade and intellectual property scenario, nationally and internationally, necessitates a qualitative change
 in the industry, to drive Indian pharmaceutical industry away from manufacturing only known drugs to discover and commercialize new
 molecules.  The availability of trained scientific manpower of high quality, S&T infrastructure, accumulated knowledge of traditional
 medicinal system and large bio-diversity of our country offer a great opportunity to our industry.  However, at present, most Indian drug
 firms, due to their small size compared to international operators and limited resources, are not in a position to invest in a viable new
 drug development programme.  At the same time, several Indian academic institutions and national laboratories have established
 impressive infrastructure and developed excellent expertise in selected areas of drug development. 
34. The Committee observes that most of the drugs developed or available in markets for diseases like malaria, tuberculosis etc. are no
 longer effective as the disease parasites has become resistance to drugs, and this poses a challenge to the scientific community to develop
 more effective drugs. The Committee recommends that Department to look at the repository our traditional medicine which may have
 answers to many of the challenges.

 institute aims at conducting R&D in observational studies and will  also embark upon conducting experiments on climate change using
 modern equipment.

 up climatology Centre with ST Radar facility at Devasthal.  And also to procure Two Modern IK x IK CCD Cameras for I meter optical
 telescope, two other CCD Cameras for solar observations, latest JHK-near IR Photometer, filters, gratings, Controllers, Computers, UPS,
 Batteries, EPABX etc.

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MEDIUM RANGE WEATHER FORECASTING (NCMRWF)
39.       The Department while giving an overview of the activities conducted by the Centre has stated that one of the major activities was
 the performance evaluation of the Global Data Assimilation-Forecast System (GDAFS) during successive summer monsoon seasons. 
 The task was pursued thoroughly as the successful prediction of various facets of the summer monsoon is the most challenging task for
 any forecasting system which is highly sensitive to various factors viz. model resolution, availability of good quality observational data;
 intra-seasonal variability; variability of various regional/global scale surface boundary fields etc.
40.       Besides, the centre issued temporal range of forecast to Agromet Advisory Service (AAS) units. They improved temporal ranges
 of forecasts of daily weather like cloud cover, maximum and minimum temperatures, wind speed and direction and rainfall were issued
 to 82 Agromet Advisory Units twice a week.  In addition, weekly cumulative rainfall forecast were also supplied to crop weather watch
 groups.
41.       They also augmented Agromet Advisory Science (AAS) network by opening one more site at Allahabad.  The total number of
 AAS units now stands at 82.

 take part in the mountain meteorology programme and field experiments under ICRP for this purpose a  25 new Agromet Advisory
 Service Units are proposed to be opened. 
43.       The Committee was informed that the Department envisages setting up 20 more meteorological centers in different agroclimatic
 zones for accurate weather forecast during current financial year.  In addition, the NCMRWF with its new campus established at Noida
 shall require some additional developmental expenditure. It was further informed that the supercomputer facility was established for
 providing medium range (4 to 10 days) forecast for farmers. At present 4-days forecast are being provided to farmers through 83 field
 centers established all over India. These forecasts are found very useful by farming community and concerned departments.

45.       The Committee was informed that Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) has undertaken implementation of new plan schemes

 informed that during the year the Department aims to install two

 for which action will be initiated for indigenous fabrication by ISRO.  Fourteen old and obsolete radio theodolites are to be replaced with
 State-of-art technology equipment. 2 Nos. Brewer Ozone Spectrophotometers are to be procured for installation at  Varanasi and Pune. 
 The Department proposes to establish a National Satellite Data Centre.  Digital Meteorological Data Dissemination (MDD) equipment
 will be procured for installation at field stations for reception of INSAT imagery and existing MDD workstation will also be replaced. 
 Old CWDS receivers will be replaced by digital Cyclone Warning Dissemination System  (CWDS) receivers in the coastal areas.  Action
 will also be initiated for replacement of old and obsolete INSAT-DCPs (AWS) at field stations alongwtih establishment of Earth Station
 at Pune.  Automatic Message Switching  System(AMSS) Chennai will be commissioned and action for replacement of AMSS GHT will
 be initiated.  Touring Standard Barometers – 100 Nos. and 2 dead weight testers will also be procured.  Equipment will also be procured
 for upgradation of Central Radiation Lab.  Remaining equipments vis. Sky radiometer, High volume sampler, Sunphotometers and gas
 analysers will be procured for modernization of Air Pollution Lab at Pune.  Delhi VSAT Seismic Telemetry System will be augmented. 
 Continuous action is in progress for augmentation and operationalisation of seismo network and data base for which MEQ-800 (5 Set),
 Handi GPs (4 Sets) and Reftek antenna (Portable) are being procured.  Specification for Earthquake Risk Evaluation Centre  (EREC) are
 being finalized.  Proposal for World Bank Aided Project on Hydrology-Phase-II is under process. Network of 500 automatic rain gauge
 stations will also be established.

 precision in our weather       forecasting system. The Department should consider enhancing the accuracy of the forecasts by constantly
 upgrading the techniques and models of prediction. The Committee observes that higher allocation should be made available to the
 Department for their new plans and programmes aimed at ensuring accurate predication of weather forecasts.
 
INSTRUMENTATION DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME (IDP)
47.       The Committee was informed that the Department under its Instrumentation Development Programme (IDP) has been funding
 projects on design and development of indigenous instruments /technologies for over two decades.  As a result several instruments have
 been developed such as IR Spectrometer, UV-VIS Spectrophotometers, Atomic Absorption Spectrometer, Soil Salinity Tester, Ion
 Selective Electrodes, Digital Tide Gauge etc. at various R&D institutions and know how of the   developed technologies have been
 transferred for commercial production to industry.
48.       It was also informed that during the 10
th Plan, the Department has initiated the Instrument Development programme in mission
 mode for capacity building & development of instruments in the country.  The National Instrument Development board set up for the
 purpose and the Expert Panels meet periodically to guide the Department in executing the programme. 
This programme has identified the following thrust areas namely;
            Analytical / Optical instrumentation;
            Medical Instrumentation;
            Industrial Instrumentation; and
            Imaging Techniques and Instrumentation.
Besides, a training programme on Repair and Maintenance of medical instruments has been supported at several places for
 hospital doctors at various parts of the country.
49.       It was further informed that some of the major instruments/systems under development are; Bio sensor with flow injection
 analysis system for the online monitoring of glucose and fructose; continuous infrared heating system for food processing, drying,
 baking and roasting; vascular micro endoscope; treatment applicator for treatment of carcinoma cervix  for high and medium dose rate
 radiation source; multidisciplinary microcomputer based student laboratory; PC based semi optical inspection system for printed circuit
 boards (PCBs) mounted with surface mounted devices (SMDs) and conventional components;  Setting up of National Facility for testing
 &calibration of sensors;  Development of Ammonia Sensor; Development of Electronic Nose; Development of Oxygen Sensor; 
 Development of prototype CO/Nox Sensor; Development of Portable Metal Oxide Sensor for the detection of Foul Odour; Development
 of laboratory type sensors for LPG using Nano technology; Development of electrochemical sensor for pollution control i.e. industrial
 and vehicular; Development of process technology for LPG &CNG Sensors; Development of LPG/Oxygen sensor based on Nano-
materials; Development of Fish Freshness Sensor; and Development of commercially viable Humidity sensor at IIT, New Delhi etc.
50.       Besides, the Department during the year has initiated steps to support the various instruments/systems like controlled atmospheric
 instrumentation for long shelf life of apples humidity meters, particle size analyzer; Isolation, purification ad immobilization of urea  for
 technical development of urea biosensor; Development of Zeolite-Modified electrodes for environmental monitoring; Design of
 Electrochemical Sensors for Co, SO
2 and Development of multi-zone optical fibre based perturbation sensing system.       
 
51.       TheCommittee feels that the instruments developed should be made cost effective especially ones for medical instrumentation as
 the major cost of setting up of specialized medical centers is of instruments and if they are reduced; rural areas can also afford trauma
 centers and operation theatres.

52.       The Committee was informed that to inculcate of scientific temper among youtha Science City is being erected at Allahabad, the

 especially among children and common people of the eastern parts of Uttar Pradesh. The project is likely to be completed during 3
 years.  one gallery to highlight work of DST related Research & Development is being established in the city.
53.       The Department has decided to observe the year 2004 as the Year of Scientific Awareness and efforts are being made to spread
 scientific awareness and scientific temper all around in the country. The primary objective is to empower people for informed decision
 making on issues of science and technology. Vigyan Jathas covering different geo-climatic regions, viz., coastal, Himalayan, desert and
 central regions are being organized. The focus is primarily on issues related to health and nutrition, water and sanitation, environment
 and biodiversity, disaster preparedness/ management and use of information technology.
54.       It was further informed that under the project technology popularization a project has been supported in five schools of Delhi to
 introduce carpentary, masonary, painting, electric repairs etc. by a science based voluntary organization, the skill training programme is
 being done as a part of ‘work experience’ in the schools.
55.       The Department has also conducted wide range of activities involving students/teachers and general public to help overcome
 superstitions and unscientific beliefs associated with rare celestial event of transit of Venus on June 8
th, 2004. Besides, new programmes
 for tribes, visually challenged, women and other less privileged sections of the society are to be taken up.
56.       The Committee appreciates the efforts taken by the Department in popularizing the various Scientific Programmes.  However
 there is a need to utilize vast potential work force which mainly rests among youth.  The Committee feels that there is need to generate
 interest among students for basic science and scientific research and would like the Department to establish science parks and science
 cafes in rural areas as lot of talent is lying untapped in rural areas. The voluntary organization should focus on rural areas to introduce
 work experience to improve skills of rural students.
 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY FOR WOMEN
 
  57.     The Committee was informed that keeping in view the socio economic reality of women and the need for design and adaptation of
 technology suited to their needs, the focus of this scheme will be on supporting and implementing need based projects.  Some of the
 technology areas identified are value addition to natural resources, occupational health hazards and hygiene products, low cost diagnostic
 kits, vector control with community involvement, drudgery reduction, tools and implements - ergonomically designed and user friendly,
 drinking water management, post harvest technology, soil fertility management. Coordinated programmes on Women’s’ health focusing
 on development of prevention and intervention strategies for nutrition related non – communicable disorders among post reproductive
 period women and Fodder and Feed focusing on transfer of improved fodder production technology to rural areas will also be launched
 in select locations of the country.
58.       Fellowship programme for Women Scientists to undertake research, design, and adaptation of technology for societal benefit will
 continue. Women Technology Parks for rural women will be set up in different agro-climatic regions of the country.   The Women
 Scientist Cell “Protoshayaki’ that has been set up at DST will continue to function as a single window to address the needs of women
 scientists.

REPORT
 
 
The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) is a part of the Ministry of Science and Technology
 with the mandate of indigenous technology promotion, development, utilization and transfer. Establishment of the Council
 of Scientific & Industrial Research in 1942 was a landmark event in our quest for using science and technology for national
 reconstruction.
 
2.         The primary endeavour of DSIR is to encourage industry to increase their share in country’s R&D expenditure,
 support a larger cross section of small and medium industrial units to develop state-of-the art globally competitive
 technologies of high commercial potential, catalyze faster commercialization of lab-scale R&D, enhance the share of
 technology intensive exports in overall exports, strengthen industrial consultancy & technology management capabilities
 and establish user friendly information network to facilitate scientific & industrial research in the country.  It also provides a
 link between scientific laboratories and industrial establishments for transfer of technologies through National Research
 Development Corporation (NRDC) and facilitate investment in R&D through Central Electronics Limited (CEL).
3.         The above objectives are sought to be achieved through the following during Tenth Plan:
(i)
                    Technology Promotion, Development and Utilization (TPDU) Programmes.
(ii)                  National Research Development Corporation (NRDC)
(iii)                 Central Electronics Limited (CEL)
(iv)                Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)
 
4.         Other activities assigned to the Department are:
(i)
                  Matters relating to International R&D collaboration involving industrial companies and industrial R&D
 centres.
(ii)                International Cooperation/Collaboration agreements with other countries relating to industrial R&D with the
 concurrence of the Ministry of External Affairs.
(iii)               Matters concerning domestic technology, particularly the promotion of ventures involving the
 commercialization of such technologies other than those under the Department of Science & Technology.
(iv)              Matters relating to Technology Trade including exports of Technology and Technical Consultancy Services,
 in close cooperation with the Ministry of Commerce.
(v)                Matters relating to technical, engineering and management consultancy organizations and services.
 
5.         The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research in the Ministry of Science and Technology provides the
 administrative link between the Government of India and the CSIR Society.
COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH
6.         The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), an autonomous organization with its 38 laboratories and
 fifty outreach, centers has recently completed sixty years of their existence. CSIR has emerged as a scientific institution
 which has been highly acclaimed inside and outside India.  It aims at achieving global excellence with local relevance; it
 symbolizes a culture that links science with society through technology, industrial manufacture, and dissemination of
 scientific temper among people.
7.         The detailed functions assigned to the Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR) are as follows:
(i)
                  Promotion, guidance and coordination of scientific and industrial research in India, including the institution and
 financing of specific researches;
(ii)                Establishment or development and assistance to special institutions or departments of existing institutions for
 scientific study of problems affecting particular industries and trade;
(iii)               Establishment and award of research studentships and fellowships;
(iv)              Utilization of the results of the researches conducted under the auspices of the Council towards the development
 of industries in the country and the payment of a share of royalties arising out of the development of the results
 of researches to those who are considered as having contributed towards the pursuits of such research;
(v)                Establishment, maintenance and management of laboratories, workshops, institutes and organizations to further
 scientific and industrial research and to utilize and exploit for purposes of experiment or otherwise any discovery
 or invention likely to be of use to Indian industries;
(vi)
              Collection and dissemination of information in regard not only to research but also to industrial matters
 generally;
(vii)             Publication of scientific papers and journals; and

8.         CSIR has been striving to perform these functions in accordance with the priorities laid down in Five Year Plans and
 perceived needs of the nation from time to time.
9.         The Committee was informed that during the Ninth Five Year Plan, CSIR had effected wide spread changes to meet
 the challenges of economic reform, introduction of new industrial and trade policies and liberalization of economy. It also
 effected a reorientation of its programmes with the aim to make CSIR more responsive and move towards a self sustaining
 R&D institution. The cardinal feature of the Ninth Five Year Plan was the White Paper on CSIR focusing on its Vision and
 Strategy. Some of the reform process effected relate to re-engineering of the organizational structure; linking research to
 market place; mobilizing and optimizing the resources base; creating conducive and workable infrastructure and investing
 in high quality science that would be a harbinger of future technologies.
10.       As a result, CSIR stands today amongst the finest publicly funded scientific and industrial research establishments of
 the whole world. As the nation’s strongest holder of intellectual property rights (IPR), it leads the way in protecting
 traditional knowledge strength while adding to the new IPR capital.    CSIR today ranks second amongst the major PCT
 applicants from developing countries at USPTO.
11.       CSIR has also promoted excellence in science and is the only S&T organization which had nurtured and supported
 human-tech from 16 to 65 years of age through numerous schemes on human resource for scientific research.   CSIR’s
 mission is to provide scientific and industrial R&D that maximizes the economic, environmental & societal benefits for the
 people of India.
12.       The Committee was informed that the guiding principle for CSIR during the Tenth Five Year Plan would be to
 provide scientific industrial R&D that maximizes the economic, environmental and societal benefits for the people of India
 and accordingly, the Tenth Five Year Plan of CSIR and the Annual Plans have been formulated keeping in mind 8% growth
 rate envisaged by the Planning Commission and Government policy to invest 2% of GDP on Science & Technology. 
13.       CSIR seeks to foster the organizational values of: Excellence in science; Global competitiveness in technology based
 on high science; Local relevance in tune with socio-cultural and economic ethos of the people; and Innovation ranging in all
 the spheres of activities from science to technology and from management to financing.   These principles coupled with
 detailed analysis on strength, weakness, opportunities and threats carried out by CSIR laboratories were taken into
 consideration in deriving the opportunities for CSIR in the market place as well as for socio-economic development.
14.       The other factors which have a bearing on CSIR programmes for the Annual Plans are responsibilities on CSIR
 arising out of International Intellectual Property Rights arena, continuous training and re-training of CSIR staff,
 advancement of knowledge through enlarging the scope of fellowships to trans-disciplinary areas and supporting basic
 research that dovetails with its own requirement and expansion of S&T to proliferate CSIR technologies to the masses.

17.       The Committee was informed that in the Tenth Plan CSIR has endeavoured to create major and innovative
 knowledge networks across and beyond CSIR laboratories.   In persuing this, some well focused programmes/projects were
 identified and formulated with a view to synergise the competencies developed in laboratories and get them implemented in
 a network mode.  The enhanced allocation of Rs. 163.59 crore (Rs. 130 crore Plan and Rs. 33.59 crore Non Plan) is
 essentially to provide appropriate support to the projects approved by the Planning Commission, in the last quarter of the
 previous financial year, under “National Laboratories” Scheme.  Further, the increase in the Non-plan allocation would help
 to meet partly, shortfall in grant for payment of research fellowship etc. It would also meet the increased pensionary
 requirement of CSIR pensioners.
18.       It was also informed that during the current year, under Technology Promotion, Development and Utilization
 (TPDU) Programmes it is proposed to provide support to: consortium projects for technology development; setting up of
 technology and innovation management centres, technology trade facilitation centres, consultancy clinics & design
 engineering centres; and development of IT based modern tools for optimum utilization of resources available in the
 country and promoting collaborative research among industries and institutions.
NATIONAL LABORATORIES      
19.       CSIR has a network of 38 Laboratories and 47 field stations/extension centres/regional centres located all over the
 country that undertake R&D in various S&T areas and disciplines.   The extension and regional centres have been
 established to reach the diverse users and disseminate knowledge and information of R&D capabilities, techniques and
 technologies developed by the National laboratories of CSIR.
 20.      Under the National Laboratories, three types of activities are carried out, namely:
·
                    Continually building and refurbishing competence at globally competitive level, skills and
 competency in all scientific areas;
·                    Taking up in-house projects with well defined objectives, deliverables, time frame; and
·                    Performing contract R&D for industry and other users to deal with problems through expertise gained
 over the years.
 
21.       A key feature of CSIR’s programmes during the Tenth Plan is the creation of major and innovative knowledge
 networks across and beyond CSIR laboratories.The focus of the programmes thus evolved have been to synergise the vast
 competence developed in CSIR Laboratories and to implement the programmes/projects in network mode.  The emphasis is
 also on deriving maximum output from less input.  Accordingly, categorisation of programmes under National Laboratories
 have been carried out keeping in view the requirement at the national level, at CSIR level and at the laboratory level.   Some
 of the projects would be implemented in a mission mode while others would be to further develop core competence.
 22.       In Tenth Five year Plan period, CSIR will undertake programmes that promote:
·
                    excellence in science-science that will lead and not follow;
·                    global competitiveness-technology based on high science rooted wherever feasible in India’s rich
 heritage of knowledge;
·                    local relevance-finding holistic and optimal solutions to the pressing problems of the people; and
·                    innovation in all spheres of activities ranging from science to technology management to financing.
 
23.       Projects of the Tenth Five Year Plan have been evolved over a period of one year, through interactive and repetitive
 consultations with the Steering Committee on S&T, Working Group for Tenth Five Year Plan, Sectoral Subgroup of the
 Working Group, and Research Councils of the respective National Laboratories.  The evolution of the Projects, thus, have
 gone through a great deal of churning of vast S&T expertise available in the country and also in the concerned
 departments/agencies of the Government.
24.       The Committee was informed that the major chunk of financial allocation (Approx. 72%) is incurred to meet
 requirements of National laboratories, thirty eight in number and its forty seven outreach centres which undertake scientific
 and industrial R&D to maximize economic, environmental & societal benefits for the people of India.  While doing so CSIR
 continuously seeks to foster the organizational value of Excellence in Science.  Global Comptitivencess in technology based
 on high science, local relevance in tune with socio-cultural and economic ethos of the people; and innovation in all spheres
 of activity ranging from Science & Technology to management to financing.  The emphasis is placed on deriving maximum
 output from minimal input.

25.       Some of the areas identified for networking are aerospace S&T, genomics & proteomics, integrative biology, herbal
 preparations, bioinformatics, green technologies, neutraceuticals & neutrogenomics, speciality materials, waste
 minimization, new building & road construction technologies, new advanced manufacturing technologies, etc.
26.       In reply to a question regarding the details of projects, the Committee was informed that CSIR under the scheme of
 National laboratories during the Tenth Plan is implementing 57 new projects in network mode, besides programmes for
 enhancing core competencies in various areas, residential and laboratory buildings and other establishment expenses.  Out
 of the 57 new networked projects 12 projects were approved during the last quarter of the previous financial year costing
 around Rs.188 crore.  The allocation of Rs.927 crore under the National Laboratories is to meet the requirement of these
 projects as well as projects approved earlier and other programmes and establishment expenses. The short fall between the
 sanctioned grant and anticipated expenditure under the scheme on National S&T Human Resource Development is of the
 order of Rs.35 crore.
27.       The Committee appreciates the Department for carrying out research in many frontier areas of science and
 technology.  It is true that science is one of the areas, which can bring leadership and meet the kind of objectives that India
 has set for itself.   However, the Committee is of the opinion that the Department should make efforts for transfer of
 technologies to industry and also strive for wider dissemination of technologies to raise funds from Industry by having a
 greater interface between Industry & R&D laboratories.   
 
RESEARCH SCHEMES, SCHOLARSHIPS AND FELLOWSHIPS
28.       Over the years CSIR has evolved a broad based portfolio of highly versatile and well targeted schemes aimed at
 developing and retaining S&T manpower; nurturing young talent and promoting and facilitating basic research, and put in
 place mechanism for their smooth operation and implementation.   CSIR provides financial assistance in the form of
 junior/senior research fellowships and research associateships for pursuing doctoral and postdoctoral research. Research
 grants are given to universities/institutes for overall promotion of scientific research in the country.
29.       It was informed that keeping in view the declining trend in the brightest of youth taking to science education and
 R&D as a career, CSIR has already operationalised CSIR Programme on Youth for Leadership in Science (CPYLS) and
 Shyama Prasad Mukherjee (SPM) fellowship.  In the Tenth Five Year Plan period, the ongoing programmes would aim to
 rectify this situation further and take up training and motivation pogramme for selected science teachers and adopt at least
 one school and college; inculcate a spirit of entrepreneurship in research scholars; and establish fellowships in trans-
disciplinary areas.        
30.       The Committee was further informed that the scheme on National S&T Human Resource Development comprising
 Research Scheme, scholarships & fellowships and Scientists Pool has been provided with a budgetary allocations of Rs. 70
 crore (Rs. 8 crore  Plan and Rs. 62 crore Non-Plan) during 2004-05 which is higher by Rs. 9 crore against BE (2003-04). 
 This marginal increase in outlay does permit CSIR to initiate new schemes under Plan.  However, it is not adequate to meet
 the committed liability of the existing level of scholarships and fellowships being provided under Non-Plan allocation.
 During 2003-04, the gap between commitments & government grant of Rs. 25 crore was met by providing the funds from
 the internal resources of CSIR.  This gap would further increase to the extent of Rs. 35 crore during the current year if full
 support is not provided.
31.       In reply to a question regarding the details of fellowships and scholarships, the Committee was informed that the
 total number of Pool Scientist (SRAs) as on April, 2002, April, 2003 and April, 2004 were 210, 202 and 206 respectively.  
 They were provided temporary employment to work in Chemical Sciences, Earth Sciences, Engineering & Technology,
 Life Sciences, Mathematical Sciences, Medical sciences, Physical Sciences and Social Science and Humanities. About 125
 to 150 Pool Scientists (SRAs) are expected to be selected during the current year.  The existing level of Scholarships and
 Fellowships is 7272 for which budgetary support of Rs.58 crore has been provided for 2004-05.  The committed liability
 during the current year would be Rs.93 crore.  Thus a gap of Rs.35 crore exists.
32. The Committee notes with satisfaction the efforts made by Department for stimulating interest and awareness among
 students for science. The Committee recommends that the fellowships be given for basic sciences as fewer students are
 showing interest in them.  It is hoped that individual record of progress of scholarship holders is being maintained. 
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY AND TECHNOLOGY MANAGEMENT
33.       The scheme basically seeks to capture, secure, enhance and realize the value from the Intellectual Property of CSIR. 
 This would be done by developing mastery over management of Intellectual Property by forming homogenous patent
 portfolios, valuing and valorizing these through leveraging and forging strategic alliances, bartering and licensing and even
 outright sale.  In the Tenth Five Year Plan period the emphasis will be on exploiting this portfolio internationally and
 expanding it rather selectively based on commercial potential, strategic reasons or for pioneering and positioning CSIR in
 new direction.
34.       CSIR has truly made Intellectual Property its business, and it continued to be the number 1 Indian entity securing
 patents in India and abroad.  In 2002-03, CSIR was granted a record 146 patents in USA, a feat unmatched by any other
 Indian firm or organization.  During the year 2003-2004, CSIR has filed 896 patents of which 490 patents were filed abroad

NEW MILLENIUM INDIAN TECHNOLOGY LEADERSHIP INITIATVE (NMITLI)
39.       The New Millennium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative  (NMITLI) scheme envisages to catalyze innovation
 centered scientific and technological developments as a vehicle to attain for Indian economy a global leadership position in
 selected niche areas in a ‘Team India’ partnership.   NMITLI therefore looks beyond present day technologies and seeks to
 build, capture and retain for India a leadership position in the global arena based on technology by synergising the best
 competence of publicly funded R&D institutions, academia and private industry.
40.       During the financial year 2003-2004, a next generation bioinformatics software, “ Bio-Suite” has been soft
 launched.   It is comprehensive, portable, modular and scalable software, which has more features than any existing
 commercial product.  The project, which symbiotically and synergistically networks over 20 partners from academic, R&D
 institutions and industry, was conceptualized and developed under NMITLI.  A new herbal formulation for the treatment of
 psoriasis has been developed.  Industrial partner intend to file IND application to US-FDA by December 2003.
41.       It was informed that NMITLI looks beyond present day technologies and seeks to build, capture and retain for India
 a leadership position in the global arena based on technology by synergising the best competencies of publicly funded R&D
 institutions, academia and private industry, Thus, it is based on the premise of consciously & deliberately identifying,
 selecting and supporting potential winners.  With over 50 private sector companies and over 150 institutes & laboratories
 networked together, NMITLI is the largest public private partnership in India today.
42.       The Committee was informed that the New Millennium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative (NMTLI) being a
 proactive scheme, the endeavour is to select and support, through churning of best of the minds, the projects which are in
 potential niche areas to achieve technology leadership for the country.   The projects supported so far are in the following
 areas: advanced nano-materials and composities; nano-material catalysts; decentralized power packs; fictionalization of
 alkane; defunctionalisation of carbohydrates; biodegradable plastics; value added polymeric materials; environmentally
 secure rare earth based colorants for surface coatings; hydrogen based fuel cells; novel office computing platform;
 mesoscale modeling; low cost horizontal axis wind turbine; microbiological conversions; biotech molecules; new targets
 and markers for cancer; therapeutics for latent M. tuberculosis; herbal therapeutics for degenerative disorders; advanced
 drug delivery systems; oral delivery of insulin; gene expression modulation; oral herbal therapeutics for psoriasis;
 diagnostics for eye diseases and low vision enhancement devices; software for bioinformatics; pharmacological and
 genomic investigations on withania somnifera; improvement of plant species with special reference to pulp and paper and
 novel fungicides.  The scheme operates on the premise of consciously & deliberately identifying, selecting and supporting
 potential winners. Thus the partners in the projects scheme are the identified “Winners”   It may be further emphasized that
 in each project – after the concept proving stage, the commercialization will be taken up by the concerned industrial
 partners on their own or by seeking further development funding.  For example, in the case of Biosuit, a unique
 bioinformatics software created by the partnership of Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) & nineteen institutional partners, the
 commercialization is now being done internationally by TCS.  Similarly in the case of the new Psoriasis drug, Lupin
 laboratory have moved from IND filing to phase I clinical trials and will complete the rest o the Phase II & phase III trials

INFRASTRUTURE RENOVATION AND REFURBISHMENT
44.       The infrastructure for most of the CSIR laboratories was built or acquired over four decades ago, some are even of
 older vintage.  Thus, the infrastructure is not suited for modern day globally competitive R&D especially in terms of Good
 Library Practice (GLP), International Organization for Standardization (ISO), National Accredition Board for Testing and
 Calibration Laboratories (NABL) requirements for accreditation and certification.   These are proposed to be refurbished
 through a new scheme of infrastructure renovation.
45.       Under Information Technology Infrastructure, in 1997 CSIR was amongst the first to plan for V-SAT connectivity to
 all its laboratories.  To some limited extent this could be established, however, the delays in implementation and the radical
 changes in communication set-up since then have made it imperative that it be upgraded into an efficient internet.  CSIR has
 been advising and assisting other organizations to take up computerization and the use of information technology but it has
 not benefited fully from the revolution, except in isolated pockets.  Thus the organizational benefits of the radical gains in
 productivity brought about by IT have not yet been realized.   The IT Task Force has also enjoined that every organization
 devote 2% of its outlay on IT.  In order to inculcate an IT culture in the system, it would be assigned a driving role. For the
 last year, the Department had targets to initiate minimum IT infrastructure and to study and proliferate the best practices by
 imparting training of over 1000 man weeks. Besides, for the current financial year, IT infrastructure will be created fully in
 all the laboratories and connectivity provided to establish online management of resources.
46.       The Committee was informed that the infrastructure Renovation & Refurbishing scheme is a new scheme of CSIR
 for the Tenth Plan with the emphasis on renovation and refurbishment of infrastructure facilities of CSIR laboratories which
 are few decades old.  It originally had two components: (i) IT infrastructure & (ii) Building infrastructure.   Subsequently,
 with the approval of the Planning Commission, Building Infrastructure Renovation component was made part of National
 Laboratories scheme and an outlay of Rs. 20 crore was provided under it.  The IT infrastructure scheme component is to
 provide on real time basis internet connectivity to all the laboratories.   The schema could not be initiated during 2003-2004
 due to non-availability of approval.  An outlay of Rs. 10 crore has been provided during 2004-2005 to initiate the Scheme.
47.       The Committee was informed that as per the requirement, the proposal on Infrastructure Renovation &
 Refurbishment was sent to the Planning Commission for in principle approval.   After obtaining the in principle approval,
 detailed project report and the Expenditure Finance Committee proposal has been sent to the Planning Commission and
 other appraising agencies.  The response from the Planning Commission & other agencies are awaited.   The renovation and
 refurbishment of infrastructure on selective basis would be taken up in the current year.
48.       The Committee feels that to face the challenges coming from research initiatives from developed countries, India
 needs the state-of-art infrastructure and laboratories. The infrastructure should be seen as a strategic national resource and
 funding should be given on a long-term basis so that the modernization becomes a continued process for effectiveness,
 improvement in our scientific growth.  The Committee is of the view that the university laboratories need to be upgraded so
 that a world-class infrastructure is provided for research in under-graduate and post-graduate level so that the interest for
 further research is sustained in young students. This in the long term would facilitate advances in the scientific research.

69.       Apart from this, the Committee is of the opinion that since bacteria have the ability to degrade biological wastes, it
 enables pollution control and waste management.   This process can act as energy source.  Hence, the emphasis of the work
 of this Institute should be on anaerobic digestion of vegetable and fruit wastes which is also known as municipal market

70.       The Committee is pleased to know that Institutes programme in Environmental Bio-Technology also includes
 projects for development of know how for monitoring and treatment of effluents and biological wastes by anaerobic
 digestion.   The Committee is given to understand that the know how for monitoring the pollution load i.e. Biological and
 Chemical Oxygen Demands i.e. BOD and COD in wastewater has also been developed at IGIB.  The know how has been
 named as BODSEED and has been validated by Central Pollution Control Board after receiving cross validation by seven
 states in the country.
71.       Yamuna River is constantly polluted by domestic and industrial wastes.  About 2,700 million Liters of Domestic
 Sewage per day (mld), are discharged, of which more than 60% goes untreated in the river Yamuna.  The problem is
 complicated by the 300 mld of untreated industrial sewage discharge in the river.
72.       The Committee therefore, feels that an Anaerobic digestion method for treatment of sewage waste water is
 undoubtedly a good alternative application of anaerobic   digestion theory. The Committee is of the opinion that with this
 simple,  rapid and cheap technology, it will be possible to treat 3000 (cu.m)   of sewage waste water per day and bring the
 pollution load BoD and CoD within  permissible limits.
73.       The Committee is also given to understand that presently, research is underway at IGIB to develop pollution
 sensitive BoD Biosensor for rapid estimation of BoD i.e. in 10 minutes as against 5 days by conventional methods for BoD
 estimation.  Hence, the know how developed is a refinement of the existing method in order to monitor the pollution load
 precisely, accurately and rapidly.  The Institute has also undertaken research of Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) reduction, a
 major unsolved problem of wastewater management by making a breakthrough in reducing TDS to 10 per cent by using
 biotechnological approach.
74.       The Committee is strongly convinced that environmental biotechnological research of the institute can prove to be a
 boon particularly for environmental management and control and disposal of municipal market waste, wastewater treatment
 and management, treatment and monitoring of Effluents, for TDS reduction and BoD and CoD estimation for monitoring
 pollution load in waste water.
75.       The Committee would therefore, like to recommend the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research to explore
 the possibilities of working jointly with the Ministry of Environment & Forests to develop a comprehensive waste
 management programme including both municipal market waste, management of waste water and control of bio-pollutants
 concentration in ambient air in the country so that the entire issue of waste management and control could be given a new
 dimension.

 friendly plastic particularly biodegradable plastic like bacterial plastic. Since plastic are non-degradable, they have become
 a serious environmental threat.   Developing expertise and state-of-the-art know how for environment friendly plastic i.e.
 bacterial plastic production has been identified as a major challenge before environment friendly researchers.  In the post
 genomic era, where more than 100 bacterial genome have been sequenced, the Committee is, happy to know that IGIB has
 combined the power of bio-informatics tools to the genetic engineering tools to show that soil bacteria can degrade many
 biological fibers/polymers.  The plastic is also a sheet of synthetic fibers.  In fact, strategy has been applied at IGIB to
 search novel hydrogen producing microbes through bio-informatics tools using genomic databases; novel metabolic
 pathways have been identified by IGIB for developing know how to produce environment friendly plastics from cheap raw
 materials like bio-wastes. IGIB is also trying to train bacteria to take up the wastes from environment and clean the
 atmosphere.

 undertaken for production of such plastics by IGIB so that new areas of knowledge for production of environment friendly

      I, the Chairman of the Department-rel ated Parliamentary Standi ng Committee on Science &
Technology, Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on
its behalf, present this One Hundred -Twenty Seventh Report of the Commi ttee.  This Report deals with 
the detailed Demands for Grants (2004-2005) of the Department of Biotechnology (Ministry of Science
and Technology) (Demand No.85). 
  
2.  In the meetin g of the Committee held on 9 th August, 2004 the Secretar y and other Officers of the

R E P O R T 
  
            The field of biotechnology world over, as in India, has moved with spectacular speed towards 
developing a better understanding and insight into  life processes and addressing many problems
concerning humankind.  Its impact in the domain of health, ag riculture, environment and industrial 
sectors has given a new dimension to  our development process.  Ther e is a paradigm shift in basic 
research in modern biology; scien tists are moving closer to the f undamental secrets of life and the
application of the knowledge generated.   
2.         The Department of Biotechnology (DBT), under the Ministry of Science and Technology was set 
up in February 1986 to give an imp etus to the development of bi otechnology in the country.  The 
objectives of Department of Bi otechnology include the developmen t of products, processes and
technologies whose large-scale appl ications would result in societal and economic benefits.  The 
biotechnology programmes are implemented thr ough a number of autonomous and statutory
institution/universities by giving  them grants-in-aid. 
3.         Work on transgenic, coupled with pros pecting for new genes from our rich biodiversity, is 
poised to pay rich dividends in terms of new products and technologies for improved production and
enhanced nutritive quality of food, fruit and vegetable crops and reduce post-harvest losses.  Application 
of biotechnology to animal health and productivity  including our marine bi oresources will yield
attractive dividends.  India bei ng a global mega biodiversity hub, c onservation, characterization and 
sustainable utilization this natural wealth through the application of biotechnology assumes priority.   
4.         New generation of vaccines, diagnostic kits and therapeutics, are likely to lead to a major shift in
the healthcare strategy for preventi on, early detection and treatment of  diseases that impose the highest
burden.  Stem cell research has emer ged as a cutting edge area of enormous potenti al for application in 
cancer, autoimmune deficiencies, cardio-vascular and neurological disease and other disorders.  
5.         India is likely to require high quality human resource in the biotechnology sector, as industry and
public sector-driven R&D expands to propel the country into a global power in this sector.  The creation 
of infrastructural facilities, promotion of biotech parks and incubators are some of the programmes taken
up during the year, which have contributed significa ntly to the speedy progress.  The importance o f 
bioinformatics has also increased manifold and the best-performing centres are being upscaled as centres 
of excellence.  
6.         Biotechnolo gy-based programmes for societ y es pecially women, weaker sections and rural

GREEN COWS 
59.       The Committee would like to suggest that a section of resear ch in Biotechnology should 
concentrate on the br eeding of special cows that naturally produce low-fat milk that boost immune 
system which may be termed as ‘g reen cow’ and which are specifi cally engineered to produce less 
methane to help stem global warming.  Green cows  generally deliver low fa t milk that boosts immune
system, improve lactose utilization a nd relive diarrhoea.  Recent adva nces in Biotechnology as what the 
Committee has been given to understa nd have identified gene for milk  fat synthesis th at may one day
allow scientists to selectively breed cows that naturally produce low fat milk.  This will also 
considerably improve the efficiency of the milk production of the cows.  Si nce the green cows are
environmentally cleaner cows they produce less si gnificant amount of methane, which is a majo r
contributor to green house effect, in the atmosphere, second, only to CO2 which generally contributes to
global warming.  Green cow can alter cattle digest ion either by removing microorganisms from thei r 
stomachs that produce methane or by creating microor ganisms that can pr oduce metabolic products
other than methane.  The Committee also feels that  if DBT makes a concentr ation on such type o f
research, the emphasis on food safety  will increase and by increasing the body’s defence mechanism, a 
great section of population could be saved from constant attacks of common incurable diseases.  
  
BIO-TERRORISM 
60.       The Committee recommends  that the Department of Bio-technology should take steps to ensure 
bio-security without  hampering legitimate re search or free flow of information in the field 
biotechnology, first, there must be an increased awareness of risk of Bio-Terrorism among scientists and 
scientific leaders.  In order to  augment awareness about security, the committee woul d like to suggest
for arrangement of training and accr editation programmes that would in crease considerable awareness
and stimulate better communications between scient ific and national security communities.  The 
Committee feels that any Bio-secu rity policies must take a ‘botto m up’ approach by including direct 
involvement of working scientists.  The security provisions should wo rk hand in hand with the progress 
in biological research.  It is th e categorized opinion of the Committee th at the strategies that block the 
publication of certain research mate rials would deter the free flow of  information, impede careers o f
scientists in the field of bio-t echnology and discourage new incumbents  in entering the field of research
in Bio-Technology. 
            The guidelines should, therefore, be developed to allow researches to publish their work without 
providing information that would be useful to Bio-Terrorists.  Universities and other scientific 
institutions as what the Committee feels should deve lop the procedures to monitor scientific activities
and design full proof action plan to prevent any strategic inform ation leakage relating to Bio-
Technology to bio terrorists who w ould in turn adversely utilize th ese information for creating Bio-
Terrorism thereby throwing considerable threat on the very existen ce of human communities by waging
biological warfare. 
            Biological weapons pose a strategic threat mirrored by no other form of attack other than nuclear
weapons.  The Committee feels that as there is no simple solution to bio s ecurity, the Department o f
Bio-Technology must construct a syst em of checks and balances need ed to assure that the growing
power of life sciences is only used to protect life and not to destroy it.

knowledge based manpower though training course; a P.G. di ploma on biotechnology and IP R
publications on WTO negotiations and Patent Act and rules, as modified from time to time, pertaining to

(Para 58)
15.       The Committee would like to suggest that a section of resear ch in Biotechnology should 
concentrate on the br eeding of special cows that naturally produce low-fat milk that boost immune 
system which may be termed as ‘g reen cow’ and which are specifi cally engineered to produce less 
methane to help stem global warming.  Green cows  generally deliver low fa t milk that boosts immune
system, improve lactose utilization a nd relive diarrhoea.  Recent adva nces in Biotechnology as what the 
Committee has been given to understa nd have identified gene for milk  fat synthesis th at may one day
allow scientists to selectively breed cows that naturally produce low fat milk.  This will also 
considerably improve the efficiency of the milk production of the cows.  Si nce the green cows are
environmentally cleaner cows they produce less si gnificant amount of methane, which is a majo r
contributor to green house effect, in the atmosphere, second, only to CO2 which generally contributes to
global warming.  Green cow can alter cattle digest ion either by removing microorganisms from thei r 
stomachs that produce methane or by creating microor ganisms that can pr oduce metabolic products
other than methane.  The Committee also feels that  if DBT makes a concentr ation on such type o f
research, the emphasis on food safety  will increase and by increasing the body’s defence mechanism, a 
great section of population could be saved from constant attacks of common incurable diseases.  
(Para 59)
16.       The Committee recommends  that the Department of Bio-technology should take steps to ensure 
bio-security without  hampering legitimate re search or free flow of information in the field 
biotechnology. First, there must be an increased awareness of risk of Bio-Terrorism among scientists 
and scientific leaders.  In order to augment awareness about security, the committee would like to
suggest for arrangement of trai ning and accreditation programmes that would increase considerable
awareness and stimulate better communications betw een scientific and nationa l security communities.  
The Committee feels that any Bio-security policies must take a ‘bottom up’ approach by including direct 
involvement of working scientists.  The security provisions should wo rk hand in hand with the progress 
in biological research.  It is th e categorized opinion of the Committee th at the strategies that block the 
publication of certain research mate rials would deter the free flow of  information, impede careers o f
scientists in the field of bio-t echnology and discourage new incumbents  in entering the field of research
in Bio-Technology. 
            The guidelines should, therefore, be developed to allow researches to publish their work without 
providing information that would be useful to Bio-Terrorists.  Universities and other scientific 
institutions as what the Committee feels should deve lop the procedures to monitor scientific activities
and design full proof action plan to prevent any strategic inform ation leakage relating to Bio-
Technology to bio terrorists who w ould in turn adversely utilize th ese information for creating Bio-
Terrorism thereby throwing considerable threat on the very existen ce of human communities by waging
biological warfare.  
            Biological weapons pose a strategic threat mirrored by no other form of attack other than nuclear
weapons.  The Committee feels that as there is no simple solution to bio s ecurity, the Department o f
Bio-Technology must construct a syst em of checks and balances need ed to assure that the growing
power of life sciences is only used to protect life and not to destroy it.
