R  E  P  O  R  T 
  
            Oceans have always influenced the life and history of mankind. From time immemorial, man has
been using oceans in several ways. According to our mythology, the Gods and Demons churned the
ocean and extracted amrita, the elixir of life. Even in the presen t ages, we get mineral, food and energy 
resources from the oceans. 
            The oceanic part of the world has an area of about 361 million sq km  (that is 71% of the globe),
an average depth of about 3,730 m, and a total volume of about  1,347,000 million cubic km.  The 
deepest part of the oceans is the Mariana Trench (11,516 m) in the Pacific Ocea n.  Compare this with 
the 8,849 m above sea level of the highest peak, the Mt.Everest.  Because of its vastness and interplay of 
processes, oceans control the atmosphere and global climate besides being a vast storehouse of resources
necessary for sustenance of life on  earth. Appreciating the importance of the subject, Government o f
India established Department of  Ocean Development in 1981 with  an aim to create a deepe r
understanding of the oceanic regime of the northern and central Indi an Ocean and also to develop
technology and technological aids  for harnessing of resources a nd understanding of various physical,
chemical and biological processes.  The Ocean policy statement was also enunciated in 1982. 
2.         The Department of Ocean Developmen t is the nodal Department for organising, coordinating 
and promoting development activitie s relating to ocean development in  the country.  The national level 
R&D laboratories, educational institutions and industries assist the Department in carrying out its multi-
disciplinary plans and programmes of national importa nce.  Further, marine research and capacity 
building is one of the key areas of the Department to promot e basic research in marine science for self-
reliance. Hence, the activities of the Department are targeted toward s scientific research and technology
development with orientation towa rds its applications and harnessing ocean resources. The Department
has also the mandate towards inte rnational programmes arising out of  international obligations and
bilateral and multilateral coopera tive ventures to create a technol ogical capacity building and human
resource development for self-reliance.

11.       The objectives of the Antarctic Research Programme are to identify and initiate programmes o f

monitor global phenomena, such as th e atmospheric patterns and ocean circulations.  Glaciological and 
geophysical research provide s a clue to the geologica l history and evolution of  the earth.  In addition, 
Antarctica provides a singular platform for conducting studies on so lar terrestrial interaction, adaptation

Antarctic expedition is proposed to be launched.  This expedition will ca rry out research in the fields o f 
atmospheric, geological, biologica l, environmental, medical and engineering sciences and global
change.

22.       Although the Committee is happy with the contents and perf ormance of projects under Poly 
Metallic Nodules programme of Department, it is, however, scep tical about the Department’s 
assessment about the preservation of environmental norms for optimal sea ecology at the mining site.   
            The Committee is of the opinion that  before a comprehensive pla nning is undertaken for on-site 
mining of nodule, the Department should prepare an experimental chart about the precise disturbance of
the sea floor at the mining area to  assess its geological and ecologi cal conditions.  The Committee feels 
that while organisms would be de stroyed in the mined area undisturbe d areas would remain because o f
the complex terrain of sea bed which could serve as  biological reservoir for recolonizing the destroyed
section.  
23.       The Committee is of the opinion that dangers arising from the release of underlying heavy metals
when the upper sediment layer is removed, could change or disrupt geochemical systems that has been
stabilized over geological time, possibly creating zones of reduce d oxygen where life would become
impossible. 
            The Committee, therefore, feels that  before mining is initiated, Department must examine the
effect of mining on local animals at the site caused by dragging of plough across the bottom to stimulate
the effects of nodule mining on the se a bed, including the rates at whic h animals of the same species
returned to the disturbed area.  The study should be  done in this respect on mega fauna animals large 
enough to be seen at the ocean botto m.  The Committee is of the opinion  that the effects of mining will 
be greatest on the sea sponges that liv ed directly on the nodules because their habitat will be completely
destroyed.  Other free swim ming species will suffer a considerable  reduction in numbers due to serious 
disruption in food supply.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view that from emerging picture above 
the evaluation of bio-threat exposed by sea bed mi ning is indispensable to  be addressed thoroughly 
before venturing into mining operation and the Commit tee feels that any such evaluation is difficult
without better knowledge of the orga nisms living at the mining site a nd the eco-system in which they 
function.  It is quite appa rent that animals at the site area woul d be killed by the im pact of the mining
vehicle and by resettlement of the se diment cloud that impact of the mining vehicle will raise from the
sea floor.  
            Another potential effect of mining on the ocean floor is the bri nging up of unwanted materials 
during a mining operation i.e. sedi ments, trace metals from nodule waste and cold and nutrient rich
bottom water into the upper ocean. Owing to this probl em, the Committee feels that deep or mid ocean
level will be most desirable area for discharging of  miners waste as it would not be harmful to the
environment.  
24.       The Committee further feels that burial sens itivity of sea bed organism s i.e. the consequences o f
dumping a layer of sediment on t op of them as a direct reperc ussion of mining should be studied
thoroughly by Department as lesson for Environmental Impact Assessm ent of sea-bed mining.  The 
Committee feels such studies c ould be undertaken by the Depart ment through Remotely Operated
Vehicle (ROV). 
            The Committee, therefore recommends  that Department should undert ake critical assessment o f 
different mining technique s and their subsequent effects on Geochemistry  and Ocean Biology and
Department should generate relia ble data for determining the optimal mining techniques i.e. ideal
extractive metallurgy to minimize environmental impacts.  
            The Committee, therefore strongly recommends for constant assessment of environmental 
impact of deep sea-mining by Depa rtment before venturing into ac tual mining operation keeping the 
following into consideration for a meaningful assessment of the impact:-

biogeochemical pump, which are micr oorganisms at the sea surface and which take Co2 from the
atmosphere and convert it via phot osynthesis into the organic carbon of  their cells should be studied in
minute details.  When these Microor ganisms die subsequently or cons umed and excreted, some portion 
of that carbon sinks to these floors where it is buried.  As the entire world is confronting the threat of the 
global warming, understanding this concept of biogeochemical pump is essential because it could extract
huge amount of excess heat trapping Co2 from our atmosphere.  A key clue lies in the tiny interface 
where sea water meets se a floor and this critical chemical  reaction determines how much carbon
dissolves back into the water and how much remains in the sediments.  This is known as carbon flux.

atmospheric Co2 content and also the quantum of sink of Co2 and other gr een house gases on the sea
floor.

is needed by Department which is  an unmanned vehicle equipped with  latest advanced technology and
which can easily undertake researches beyond a dept h of 6 thousand metres.   The most striking 
advantage for using the ATV for underwater research is that it is extremely helpful to make researches at

the vast majority of the ocean depths are bone chilling cold, completely dark and have ambient pressures
equivalent to the weight of the hundreds of atmosphe res. The exploration of th e deep sea is, therefore,
impossible without a subs tantial investment on la test technology.  The Comm ittee therefore strongly 
recommends that the Department may use Advanced Tethered Vehi cle (ATV) for the purpose of deep
sea research in view of its deep sea advantages and cost effective a pplications.  This vehicle will be 
extremely helpful for researches at  ocean benthos where gr eater variety of biotic  and abiotic elements
are available and a study of which could add consid erably to the store house of human knowledge about
ocean depth.

PRESISTENT ORGANIC POLLUTANTS 
64.       The Committee feels that Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) are the most common sea 
pollutants which are consta ntly affecting the Ocea n environment and optimal  marine ecology.  The 
POPs usually gets generated in th e deep sea environment from the d ead biotic organisms. When the
particles of this organisms get sink in the sea bed, a degradation of organic matr ix occurs and
consequently POPs get released in the surr ounding water.  Under anoxi c conditions, sediments 
containing organic carbon releases contaminants into the surrounding water.  POPs not only affect 
microbial food chain but also coas tal environments which are the most productive areas of the sea.
POPs  are also ubiquitous.  Accord ingly, it is an extreme threat towards maintenance of optimal sea 
ecology and it has high exposure to  humans also.  Keepi ng the gravity of the situation into active 
consideration, the Committee feels that Sagar Purvi and Sagar Pasc himi two ocean research vessels,
which are monitoring research on ocean pollution may also direct a major chunks of their study towards
the understanding of POPs behavior and subsequent control of  the same from spreading on the sea
benthos so that the entire biotic community of ocean flora and fauna could be effectively preserved from
environmental pollution.  
            The Committee also feels that two of the main POP group namely dioxin and furans which are
the principal threat to humanity s hould also be studied as a part of  the pollution control programme by
the Department.

damages done to such coral surroundings should be reduced to the minimum so that scientific researches
in the field may not stand on the way of preserva tion of holistic sea-ecol ogy with a preposterous 
consequences. 
          (Para 29) 
10.       The Committee observes that the efforts of  the Department to monitor pollution in the coastal 
areas need to be continued vigorously. The Depa rtment should identify locations for periodical
monitoring alongwith stipulated para meters for diffusion and dispersi on characteristics.  Besides, the
stations for collection of near-shore samples must be  planned with a view to reflect the pollution load 
that was occurring there and the da ta collected should be processed and forwarded to State Pollution
Control Boards for taking remedial measures. 
          (Para 32) 
11.       The Committee also observes that the land- based pollutants effect the marine and coastal 
environment, including estuaries and inshore coas tal waters, which are th e most productive areas.
Therefore, it recommends that  a well-planned and we ll-managed marine wate r quality monitoring 
system is required to predict change s of trends in the qua lity of a particular marine water body so that
curative or preventive measures can be taken to restore and mainta in ecological balance in the wate r
body. Monitoring is needed to ensure that standards and criteria set by the regulatory agencies are met
for the protection of marine water quality. 
          (Para 33) 
12.       The Committee feels that for strengthening o cean research centers, the Department should focus
its efforts in assistin g Universities to cr eate infrastructure f acilities and buildin g u p a skilled human

resource base in marine sciences. Moreover, marine  science teaching on the su stainability of ocean
space and its resources should be strengthened at all levels, from primary to adult education; in curricula
at university level; in adult e ducation programmes for ocean users (fishermen, seamen, workers in oil
industry, coastal engineers) and for managers of ocean affairs. 
          (Para 36) 
13.       The Committee would like to define th e term Bio Technology as reference to a range o f
techniques for identifying, developing and using the propertie s of living  things  to make products o r 
services, it selects natural strains of organisms that carry desirabl e traits makes hybr ids by fusing cells
from different parental sources, us es chemicals and radiation to creat e mutant strains or genetically
engineered plants, animals and microorganisms to produce specific phenotypic characteristics. 
            The Committee by keeping in light the crux of the above comprehensive definition of Bio-
Technology, is of the firm opinion th at any oceanographic research remains incomplete unless emphasis
is given for a deep study in Mari ne Bio Technology for better aqua  culture and improved sea food
supply and increased potential for commercial and Industrial productio ns of Marine substances through
Marine Scientific Research ha ving potential market value. Th e Committee also advocates fo r
encouragement of advanced studies in the field of Marine Scientific  Research through indepth emphasis
on Marine Bio-Technology Research. 
          (Para 37) 
14.       The Committee is also happy to note that two ot her ocean coastal research vessels namely Saga r 
Purvi and Sagar Pashimi are main ly being used by the Department  of Ocean Development for the
assessment of sea pollution within the Exclusive Economic Zone of India.  
            The Committee would like to s uggest that since the assessm ent of the sea pollution and 
subsequent action plan for dealing with the density of pollution is extremely important from the point of
view of maintaining an optimal sea ecology, it is necessary that indepth re search through these two
vessels should be undertaken for a complete monitoring of the ocean pollution and initiating subsequent
steps to control them.  The Co mmittee accordingly, would like to  advise the Department that 
biogeochemical pump, which are micr oorganisms at the sea surface and which take Co2 from the
atmosphere and convert it via phot osynthesis into the organic carbon of  their cells should be studied in
minute details.  When these Microor ganisms die subsequently or cons umed and excreted, some portion 
of that carbon sinks to these floors where it is buried.  As the entire world is confronting the threat of the 
global warming, understanding this concept of biogeochemical pump is essential because it could extract
huge amount of excess heat trapping Co2 from our atmosphere.  A key clue lies in the tiny interface 
where sea water meets se a floor and this critical chemical  reaction determines how much carbon
dissolves back into the water and how much remains in the sediments.  This is known as carbon flux.  
          (Para 41) 
15.       The Committee feels that if Department undertakes a detailed study on this phenomena of carbon 
flux, particularly within the Ex clusive Economic Zone of the I ndian Ocean, comprehensive knowledge
and essential data could be made  available in establishing the role of the oceans in governing
atmospheric Co2 content and also the quantum of sink of Co2 and other gr een house gases on the sea
floor.  
            Accordingly, the Committee feels th at the aforesaid entire progr amme could be made a success 
only if the following primary objectives are kept before it by the Department:- 
1.      Applying the knowledge and e xperience gained through oc ean research to develop
technology in specific fields  like studies in carbon flux through biogeochemical pump, sea
bed mining, ocean energy etc; 
2.      To assist the ocean scientists in the develo pment of suitable engineering and instrumentation

3.      To develop technology for emerging concept of coastal zone management; 
4.      To effectively coordinate with various technical  institutes and other R&D institutes in the
country for monitoring the entire concep t of ocean pollution through an effective
technological programme;  
5.      And to utilize energy from the ocean waves for producing electricity through power plants as 
an alternative to the conventional sources. 
The Committee therefore strongly advocates the Department to initiate comprehensive
programme to fulfill these objectives as a part of their ocean pollution studies and control.  
          (Para 42) 
16.       The Committee is of the view that th e collection and analysis of primary and secondary
data/information for the locations identified along the coast for zona tion of coastal waters should be
carried out as zonation of coastal waters will be useful in sust ainable management and effective
planning for future developmental activities without jeopardizing coastal habitats.

expositions so that our scientists get exposure to the developments and innovations taking place in other
countries.  It will also help in exchanging knowledge about the scientific developments of other nations. 
          (Para 48) 
18.       The Committee commends the activities be ing pursued by the Indian National Centre for Ocean
Information Services (INCOIS) in the field of Ocean information and observations.  However, being the 
nodal agency for providing coastal and ocean data  and value added products to the users, the
Department should monitor the performance a nd work-mechanism of the INCOIS to process an d 
disseminate ocean data and data pr oducts to user communities like fi sheries, weather, climate, ports,
shipping etc. on a regular basis so that ocean weather forecasting is precise. 
          (Para 54) 
19.       The Committee is pleased to note that the Department is mainly using two Ocean Research 
Vessels, namely Sagar Sampada a nd Sagar Kanya for deep sea rese arch.  These vessels are using 
remotely operated vehicle (ROV) and Autonomous Underwater vehicl e (AUV) to study about deep sea
life forms at considerable depth.  However, the Committee feels that scope of deep sea research could be
more challenging and informative if machineries could dive be yond a depth of 6000 meters.  The 
Committee is therefore of the opinion that for a r eal deep sea study Advanced  Tethered Vehicle (ATV)
is needed by Department which is  an unmanned vehicle equipped with  latest advanced technology and
which can easily undertake researches beyond a dept h of 6 thousand metres.   The most striking 
advantage for using the ATV for underwater research is that it is extremely helpful to make researches at
extreme depth where it is dangerous  for divers to venture.  The Co mmittee is given to understand that 
such vehicles are cost affective and can be used in oc ean abyss with much flexibility.  It is observed that 
the vast majority of the ocean depths are bone chilling cold, completely dark and have ambient pressures
equivalent to the weight of the hundreds of atmosphe res. The exploration of th e deep sea is, therefore,
impossible without a subs tantial investment on la test technology.  The Comm ittee therefore strongly 
recommends that the Department may use Advanced Tethered Vehi cle (ATV) for the purpose of deep
sea research in view of its deep sea advantages and cost effective a pplications.  This vehicle will be 
extremely helpful for researches at  ocean benthos where gr eater variety of biotic  and abiotic elements
are available and a study of which could add consid erably to the store house of human knowledge about
ocean depth.

22.       The Committee feels that Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs)  are the most common sea 
pollutants which are consta ntly affecting the Ocea n environment and optimal  marine ecology.  The 
POPs usually gets generated in th e deep sea environment from the d ead biotic organisms. When the
particles of this organisms get sink in the sea bed, a degradation of organic matr ix occurs and
consequently POPs get released in the surr ounding water.  Under anoxi c conditions, sediments 
containing organic carbon releases contaminants into the surrounding water.  POPs not only affect 
microbial food chain but also coas tal environments which are the most productive areas of the sea.
POPs  are also ubiquitous.  Accord ingly, it is an extreme threat towards maintenance of optimal sea 
ecology and it has high exposure to  humans also.  Keepi ng the gravity of the situation into active 
consideration, the Committee feels that Sagar Purvi and Sagar Pasc himi two ocean research vessels,
which are monitoring research on ocean pollution may also direct a major chunks of their study towards
the understanding of POPs behavior and subsequent control of  the same from spreading on the sea
benthos so that the entire biotic community of ocean flora and fauna could be effectively preserved from
environmental pollution.  
             
The Committee also feels that two of the main POP group namely dioxin and furans which are 
the principal threat to humanity should also be studied as a part of the pollution control programme by 
the Department.

INTRODUCTION 
  
      I, the Chairman of the Department-rel ated Parliamentary Standi ng Committee on Science &
Technology, Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on
its behalf, present this One Hundred Twenty-Ninth Report of the Committee.  This Report deals with the 
detailed Demands for Grants (2004-2005) of the Department of Space (Demand No.89). 
  
2.  In the meeting of the Committee held on the 9th  August, 2004 the Secretary and other Officers of the 
Department of Space gave an overv iew of the various activities of  the Department and the Members
sought clarifications on va rious aspects of the perfor mance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise
the Demands for Grants. 
  
3.  The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers  of the Department for re plying to the clarificati o
sought by the Members and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scruti n
the Demands for Grants of the Department of Space. 
  
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 24th August, 2004. 
  
  
REPORT 
  
 India has an impressive array of achievements in the scientif ic and technological fields afte r 
independence. Nowhere is this more apparent than in the arena of Space. India has effectively developed
space technology, applied it successfully for its rapid developments and is presently offering a variety of
space services globally. The Space Technology has allowe d the nation to move into the world of high
technology, a place previously occupied only by more developed nations.  
2.         The Indian space efforts started in th e sixties with the establis hment of Thumba Equatorial
Rocket Launching Station near Th iruvananthapuram for the scientific  investigation of the ionosphere
over the earth’s magnetic equator that passes over Thumba. During the formative decade of 1960’s 
space research was conducted by Indi a mainly with the help of s ounding rockets. The Indian Space
Research Organisation (ISRO) was formed in 1969. Space resear ch activities were provided an
additional fillip with the form ation of the Space Commission and the Department of Space by the
Government in 1972. In th e 70’s satellite programmes like Arya bhatta, Bhaskara, Rohini and APPLE
were conducted. The success of those programmes led to the era of operational satellite programmes like
INSAT and IRS came into being. In dia has come a long way in devel oping a multi fa ceted and multi-
dimensional space programme-which is indigenous, self-reliant and a pplications driven. India is now 
capable of building its own state of the art satellites. Now INSAT and IRS are the major programmes o f
ISRO.

3.         The Indian space programme has th e primary objective of deve loping space technology and 
application programmes to  meet the developmental needs of  the country. Towards meeting this
objective, two major operational spac e systems have been established — the Indian National Satellite 
(INSAT) for telecommunication, tele vision broadcasting and meteorolog ical services and the Indian
Remote Sensing Satellite (IRS) for resources monitoring and management . Two satellite launch
vehicles, the Polar Satellite Launc h Vehicle (PSLV) for launching remo te sensing satellites into the
required polar orbits and the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) for launching
communication and meteorological satellites in to 36,000 km high Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit
(GTO) have been operationalised.  
4.         The application programmes cover te lecommunications, television broadcasting, tele-education, 
telemedicine, meteorology, disaster  management, resources survey and management. A new initiative
for the exploration of the solar system has been  taken up with the announcem ent of Chandrayaan-1, a 
scientific mission to moon.

following action plans: 
a)   Launch and Operationlisat ion of GSAT-3 (Edusat) on board th e third flight of India’s GSLV. 
Edusat is a satellite dedicated for the spreading education at all levels covering a large part of the
country including North Eastern region. 
b)   Launch and Operationlisation of IRS-P5  (Cartosat) on board India’s PSLV for mapping 
applications. 
c)   Launch and Operationalisat ion of INSAT-4A, the first satellite in f ourth generation INSAT 
services, to augment the INSAT system with additional C and Ku band transponders 
d)   Initiate work on ASTROSAT, INSAT-4D/GA|SAT-5 & Oceansat-2 satellite. 
e)   Progress in other ongoing pr ojects, viz., Cartosat-2, RISA T, CUSP, GSLV Mk-III, Space 
Capsule Recovery Experiment (SRE), GSAT-4, INSAT-4 and Chandrayaan-1.

INDIAN LUNAR MISSION-CHANDRAYAN-1 
10.       India has vast experience in developing and launching operational spacecrafts systems for survey 
and management of natural resour ces, meteorological services a nd satellite comm unication.  The 
technologies developed and availabl e now at ISRO can be fully expl oited for embarking on planetary
missions with well thought out scientific objec tives.  The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is 
capable of undertaking missions to moon and other terrestrial planets. 
11.       Chandrayaan-1, India’s first scientific mission to Moon is slated for launch during 2007.  The 
primary objectives of the mission are to expand the sc ientific knowledge about th e origin and evolution
of moon, upgrade India’s technologi cal capabilities and provide ch allenging opportunities to the young
scientists working in planetary sciences.

Lunar Mission Task Force was consti tuted by ISRO with leading scient ists and technologists from all

astronomy and cosmology and after detailed discussion, the participants unanimously recommended that
India should undertake the Moon Mission.

talents to the arena of fundamental research.

further refinement to include  other innovative ideas from a broader scientific communit y

RAJIV GANDHI NATIONAL DRINKING WATER MISSION (RGNDWM) 
63.       The Committee was informed that Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission (RGNDWM)
is funded by the Department of Drinking Water Supply (DDWS) of the Ministry of Rural Development; 
the first phase of Groundwater Prospects Mappi ng was launched for six States (Andhra Pradesh,
Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Chhatisgarh and Rajasthan). It involved preparation of maps on
1:50,000 scale and generation of the digital database and so far about 1650 maps have been prepared. 
64.       The feedback received by the Department  in fi rst week of December 2003, the utility of these 
maps, a total of about 24,300 wells have been drilled using these ma ps, in Chhattisgarh, Karnataka,
Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Kerala out of which 22,000 wells have been
successful with a (success rate of around 90%). Thes e maps have also been  used to construct 3,450
recharge structures in Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala.  
65.       The Department further informed the Comm ittee that under Phase-II of  the project, four more 
States - Jharkhand, Orissa, Gujarat and Himachal Pradesh are being c overed. All the maps of Jharkhand 
have been prepared. Work is in progress for other States. 
66.       The Committee appreciates the clai m of the Department that util ity of digital database has
resulted in wells having a success rate of around 90% in Rajasthan and sugge sts that such type o f
mapping may be carried out in all drought prone
areas.

67.       The Committee was informed that this pr ogramme is funded by the De partment of Agriculture
and Co-operation; an integrated remote sensing based study has been taken up towards the generation of

TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER 
71.       During the year, a significant number of tec hnologies were licensed to Indian industries, taking 
the total number of transfers to 261 covering the industries in small, medium and large- scale sectors. 
These technologies span a wide spectrum of areas ranging from electro-mechanical, chemical and optics 
hardware to specialised software in representing a range of applications for industrial and societal
purposes including several spin-offs. Prominent am ong the technologies licensed during the year are
know-how for 11 m diameter earth st ation antenna with mono-pulse tr acking feed and sub reflectors, 
Infrared antireflection coatings on Germanium base d optics, band pass optical filters, precision opto-
mechanical multi element refract ive optics lens assembly, rubber based adhesives and an emerging
technology for Molybdenum disulphide- based dry lubricant. The t echnology of a coaxial resonato r
oscillator developed for in-house applications has attracted further demand and has been licensed to
industry. Technology for a special type of polyurethane foot, which can be used as an artificial limb, was
transferred to a small-scale enterp rise that manufactures and markets various pros thetic devices. DOS 
also licenced, during the year, two of its manufacturing technologies to meet its demands.  
72.       Amongst Department’s earlier license s, the spin-off technol ogy of OLFEX, the fire 
extinguishing powder has been effective in wide ning its market. ISRO ’s Parallel Aerodynamic 
Simulator software is well accepted in the Computational Fluid Dynamics area.  
73.       In the space applications area, the Digital Sound and Data Broadcast (DSDB) Receivers, licensed
by Deapartment has been successful ly productionised by a private pa rty at Mumbai. More than 100
Mobile Satellite Service (MSS) Reporting Terminals were delivered by the industry to the users. 
74.       There are quite a few technologies that  are in the advanced st age of licensing. Technology 
transfer of a special high temperat ure resin, Angular Motion Simulator,  Samarium Cobalt Magnet, etc.,
are slated for immediate licensi ng. Besides these, the know-how of Erasable Programmable Logic 
Device (EPLD) based Scrambler an d Descrambler, Differential Encoder and Convolutional Encoder,
Instrumented Coin-Tap debond detect ion system, Ultrasonic  level sensor, Spacecr aft load simulator,
pressure transducers, etc., are in th e pipeline for transfer to suitable industries. It is also planned to
vigorously pursue licensing of a variety of software devel oped by ISRO. KSHAMTA (Reservoi r
Capacity Estimation Software) is licenced to private industry. Packages such as Finite Element Analysis
Software (FEAST), CAPE WORKS (Crop Acreage and Production Es timation), OCM Data Processing
(OCM DP), SAPHIRE (Stereo and DEM generati on for IRS) and PARIKRAMA (AM/FM software
package) have been offered for licensing.  
75.       The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department  in the field of technology
transfer especially the spin off technologies. The Committee reiterates that the technologies before being
transferred be patented so that commercial interests are taken care of.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the
 Committee to submit the report on its behalf, present the thirteenth report on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of
 Scientific and Industrial Research (Ministry of Science and Technology) for the year 1994-95 (Demand No.72)
 
2.     In its, meeting held on April 11, 1994, the Committee considered the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific and
 Industrial Research on the basis of the documents made available to it and the submission made before it by the Secretary and the
 other representatives of the Department.
 
3.     The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the Hon'ble
 Members and for placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the
 Department of Scientific and Industrial Research.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the report at its meeting held on April 21, 1994.
 
NEW DELHI
April 21, 1994.
SYED SIBTEY RAZI
Chairman,
  Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
REPORT
 
            The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research forms part of the Ministry of Science and Technology. DSIR is
 concerned mainly with the activities of tile Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) - an autonomous body registered
 under the Registration of Societies Act. It also supports two public sector undertakings viz. the National Research and Development
 Corporation (NRDC) and the Central Electronics Limited (CEL). DSIR also undertakes various schemes in specific areas like
 Research and Development by industry, Programme Aimed at Technological Self Reliance (PATSER), Scheme to Enhance the
 Efficiency of Transfer of Technology (SEETOT) and National Information System for Science and Technology (NISSAT), and
 international scientific institutions such as Asia and Pacific Centre  for Transfer of Technology. The Committee was told that the
 CSIR constitutes the largest component of DSIR activities. DSIR, in fact, provides the administrative link between the Government
 on the one hand and the CSIR, NRDC and CEL on the other.
 
2.     While giving a brief account of the activities of CSIR, the Secretary DSIR informed the Committee that the CSIR has a network
 of 40 National laboratories and 81 Field Stations/Extension Centres, located all over the country, which undertake R&D activities in
 various areas and disciplines of science & technology. The involvement of CSIR in accelerating industrial development has been in
 terms of providing technical know how for up gradation of existing technologies as well as generating new indigenous technologies
 in response to emerging needs of the industry. Over the years, CSIR has made significant contributions to industrial and socio-
economic development and promoting the growth of S&T manpower in the country. Secretary, DSIR apprised the Committee of
 major achievements made by CSIR in the areas of drugs, catalysts, chemicals, biotechnology, equipment and machinery, etc. He also
 made a mention about the work done for prevention of environmental pollution, disaster mitigation, quality assessment and

13th Report of Committee on S & T
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/13threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:09:55]
 conservation of water. Regarding programmes oriented towards social welfare, Secretary, DSIR mentioned about improved devices
 of palm oil extraction and oil expeller developed by the CSIR, S&T services being provided by CSIR in the areas of primary
 standards, testing at international standards of transmission line towers, air quality trend analysis, wind tunnel testing, toxicological
 evaluation, etc. were also mentioned. The Committee was informed about the policy initiatives taken to reorient CSIR in the light of
 the changed environment of liberalised economic and industrial policies. Secretary, DSIR stated that the laboratories of the CSIR are
 becoming increasingly market-oriented and user-responsive, and the activities are being decided on the basis of the needs of the user
 industries and agencies. The clientele of CSIR has been enlarged by cultivating new client groups such as large industrial houses,
 PSU's., Government departments etc. and by globalizing its R&D in association with agencies abroad. Secretary, DSIR informed the
 Committee about the taking up  Mission Mode programmes in leather, clean coal technologies, drinking water and wood substitutes.
 Besides taking up the upgradation of existing technologies, CSIR is giving importance  to strategic area needs and societal needs in
 choosing its programmes.
 
3.    Budget Estimates of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) for the year 1994-95 have been placed at
 Rs.360.45 crores, of which Rs.161.00 crores constitute the plan
 
component and Rs.199.45 crores the non-plan component. Budget Estimate for the year 1994-95. is Rs. 17.51 crores more than the
 revised estimate for the year 1993-94.* While examining the Demands for Grants of the Department for the year 1994-95, the
 Committee noted that during the years 1991-92 and 1992-93 the approved budgetary plan outlay could not be utilised fully. The
 Committee was informed that this had happened because of economy measures and budgetary cuts proposed by the Government. It
 was further noted that economy cuts were applied in the case of plan component only which included R&D, and various other
 important initiatives. The Committee is happy to see that the Department was able to utilise the entire amount provided ill 1993-94
 under plan, and hopes that it would be able to do so in 1994-95 also. The Committee is of the view that scientific and technological
 researches by their nature are long term continuing processes which once started should not be stopped or delayed as it effects the
 morale, tempo and environment for producing results. A developing country like ours can ill-afford to allow its research and
 development activities, when the amounts involved are relatively small to suffer. The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that the
 economy measures and budgetary cuts applied by the Government from time to time should not affect scientific and technological
 researches per se that have been approved after careful consideration.
 
4.     The Committee further noted that in the case of CSIR, monies demanded and approved have consistently been morn lot the non-
plan component than for the plan-component. The rate of increase in the non-Plan expenditure is more than that in the case of plan
 expenditure. It is also noted that the utilisation of funds in the non-plan category has exceeded the approved amount during the last
 two years i.e. 1992-93 and 1993-94. When the Committee desired to know the reasons for such an unusual feature in the case of
 CS1R, Secretary DSIR (who is also the Director-General, CSIR) explained to the Committee that CSIR being an old established
 agency has a lot of financial obligations relating to salary, allowances and pensions to its employees, Council contribution and
 interest payment on GPF/CPF, contingency and maintenance expenditure, etc. Besides, CSIR has also to maintain its infrastructure
 created over the last 50 years. The expenditure under non-plan has also been increasing due to payment of higher rates of DA,
 increased pay and allowances on account of promotions and normal increments. These facts arc mainly responsible for demands
 being more under non-plan. These are also the reasons for utilisation being more than the approved amount under non-plan,
 particularly since the financing provided by Government in this category has been at a lower growth rate than the actual.
 
5.     The Committee drew the attention of the Secretary towards another unusual situation, where CSIR has been diverting funds from
 plan to meet the expenditure under non-plan. Secretary, DSIR explained to the Committee that the budgetary support given by the
 Government in the non-plan category is generally not sufficient to take care of the increase in committed liabilities on sub-heads
 mentioned above and other committed non-plan expenditure on Extra Mural Research (EMR) and Scientist's Pool etc. He accepted
 that this gap between committed liabilities and non-plan budget allocations
________________________________________________________________________*

 over the years have been met by diverting plan fund to non-plan sector adversely affecting thereby the R&D activities. Secretary,
 DSIR observed that besides depletion of plan financial resources due to such diversion of funds, the increase in prices of scientific
 equipments chemicals, journals,etc., due to rise in general price-index and rupee devaluation have seriously hampered the capabilities
 to procure essential R&D inputs even at minimum sustenance level When the Committee asked him to provide the percentage of
 such expenses to the total outlay of CSIR vis-à-vis the percentage spent on R&D, Secretary DSIR informed that the expenditure on
 pay and allowances in 1992-93 was 46.35% of the total expenditure viz, RS.301.50 crores. The expenditure on R&D was 30.60% of

 Rs.353.50 crores. The expenditure on R&D was 31.84% of the total expenditure in that year. The Committee was informed that the
 expenditure on pay and allowances is expected to go up by 13% in 1994-95 primarily due to increase in DA and clearance of backlog
 in promotions of staff after Merit and Normal Assessment Scheme (MANAS) is finally approved. Secretary, DSIR submitted before
 the Committee that the new industrial and economic policies are expected to generate more demand for indigenous technologies
 which are internationally competitive. This scenario puts additional responsibility on CSIR, being the primary scientific and
 industrial research organisation in the country. CSIR, therefore, has to intensify its efforts to generate new and viable
 environmentally sound technologies especially in the areas of drug, leather, agro-chemicals, catalysts, coal, building materials, new
 biological, food, processing, hi-tech areas of aerospace materials and electronics and many others.
6.     After considering the explanation given, and the facts placed before the committee by Secretary, DSIR, the Committee notes that
 the funds provided to the CSIR under non-plan exceed those under plan, that the non-plan budgetary support is not sufficient to meet
 increases in committed liabilities of the CSIR; and that the gap between the non-plan budgetary support is not sufficient to meet
 increases in committed liabilities of the CSIR; and that the gap between the non-plan budget allocations and expenditure on

 committed liabilities over the years is being met by diverting plan funds which is meant primarily for R&D activities. The Committee
 agrees with the Secretary, DSIR that in the wake of globalisation of economy CSIR is certainly called upon to speed up its R&D
 efforts in important and critical areas and that it would need higher investments. In view of the fact that a large part of the CSIR
 budget is spent on paying salary, allowances, pension and other committed liabilities, the committee feels flint the expenditure on pay
 and allowances in the posts continuing from Seventh plan period is of recurring nature and should be met in entirety from the non-
plan allocations during the Eighth Plan period. The Committee, therefore, recommends that enough funds for meeting committed
 liabilities of CSIR should be provided under non-plan, so that the need for diverting plan allocations does not arise and the plan fund
 could be fully available for R&D activities.
 
7. The Committee notes further that the budget estimate of CSIR for the year 1994-95 under the non-plan sector is only Rs. 4.43
 crores more than what was allocated during the year 1993- 94. Secretary, DSIR told the Committee that he anticipates an increase of
 Rs.21.00 crores under pay and allowances and pension payments only. The Committee feels, if increase under other heads due to
 normal inflation is also taken into account, the additional allocation of Rs. 4.43 crores in non-plan in 1994-95 appears to be
 inadequate and this situation needs to be remedied at the appropriate stage.        
____________________________________
*          For details see Schedule
 
Modernisation
8.    The Committee was informed that most of the laboratories of CSIR are four decades old and while new equipment and facilities
 have been inducted over the years, by and large the equipment and facilities are fast becoming obsolete.  Some of the CSIR
 laboratories like Indian Insitute of Chemical technology ( IICT) are 50 years old.  The Committee is of the view that in the present
 context, developing internationally competitive technologies and providing high quality S&T services is absolutely necessary.
  Therefore, there is an urgent need to modernize these facilities as well as to acquire state-of-the-art-equipment so that CSIR is able
 to meet the challenges and become globally competitive.  This is particularly so considering the rapid change on the S&T scene in
 the world in terms of infrastructural capabilities and facilities.  With the present level of allocations, Committee feels that it is not
 possible for CSIR even to think of sparing any funds for the major procurement of modern equipment, apparatus and instruments. 
 When the Committee asked as to how much fund was required for this purpose, Secretary, DSIR pleaded that SCER would need a
 minimum additional amount of Rs. 200.00 crore towards removing obsolescence and modernization for the remaining period of the
 Eighth Plan.  He also informed the Committee that in December 1986, the Abid Hussain Committee has recommended a one-time
 grant of Rs. 100.00 crores for CSIR to remove obsolescence and for modernization.    
            In view of the above, the Committee feels that there is imperatives need to provide a suitable amount as one-time grant to tile
 CSIR for the removal of obsolescence and to modernise its laboratories. As the Abid Hussain Committee had recommended Rs.
 I00.00 crores for this purpose in the year 1986, the demand of Rs. 200.00 crores appears to be reasonable keeping in View tile overall
 inflation and escalation in tile cost of equipment, etc. since 1986. These funds can be administered on a highly selective basis with
 outside monitoring where necessary to ensure that we capitalize on our strengths and not distribute the funds on a uniform basis.
 
Manpower
 
9.     The Committee during the course of examination came to know that the existing staff strength of CSIR as on 1-3-94 is about
 23500 under different categories, against the sanctioned strength of 27768. The staff strength in  CSIR was determined in 1987. Since
 then there has been practically no increase in the staff strength. This is in line with the Government directive to reduce staff strength
 by 10%. As a consequence, the scientific and technical staff strength has declined over the years.  The strength would go further
 down due to the freeze on all new recruitments.  The Committee expresses its concern about the situation, which does not permit
 induction of young talent in the system.  No R&D system can remain competitive in the absence of induction of bright young
 scientists in it at all levels in the system.   The members of the Committee were apprehensive that if the situation is not corrected it
 could lead to decline of expertise and excellence in the national laboratories which our country needs most at this juncture.  The
 Committee, therefore, is of the view that in order to sustain the level of excellence of these excellence of these R&D institutions as
 well as to build up expertise in new and emerging areas, it is imperative that S&T institutions should be exempt from the blanket ban
 on the recruitment of scientists and technical personnel and cut, if any, should  applied on those posts which are not absolutely
 necessary for carrying out R&D activities.  This could be achieved by modernizing the administration and support structures.
 
Emeritus Scientists Scheme
 
10.    The Committee is of the view that the expertise and experience of retired scientists should be made use of appropriately. The
 Committee desired to know whether the talents of S&T Personnel after retirement are being utilized by CSIR. Secretary  DSIR
 informed that there is an Emeritus Scientists Scheme operating at CSIR. At present 100 scientists have been appointed under this
 scheme. A fixed grant of Rs.4000.00 for pursuing research work in the areas of their interest and in the institutes of their choice is
 provided. The Secretary submitted that it is not possible to increase the number unless more funds are made available for this
 purpose. The Committee feels that the Emeritus Scientists Scheme should be examined in detail from the viewpoint of funds
 available, effectiveness, desirability of enlargement, etc. and put up for consideration at -the time of mid-term appraisal of the Eighth
 Plan.
 
Internal Resources
 
11.    The Committee notes that the Department has many avenues for raising its resource by way of earnings from exports and from

13th Report of Committee on S & T

 sponsored research programmes consultancy, etc. Generating more extra budgetary resources has been mentioned as one of the
 policy initiatives of the CSIR in the year 1994-95.  The Committee wanted to know as to what the Department is doing in this area. 
 The committee was apprised that CSIR has already initiated efforts to raise resources from external sources arising out of the
 recommendations of Abid Hussain Committee.  Extra budgetary resources (FBR)  through R&D are being raised by contract R&D,
 consultancy, S&T Services, licensing of know how technology, business development from foreign clients and by providing
 specialized training
            Several initiatives have been taken to, raise extra budgetary resources which include inter alia, reorienting R&D
 programmes/activities to be user responsive  widening of clientele base, putting emphasis is on marketing of CSIR knowledge base,
 developing strong linkages with other constituents to offer value added packages, etc. The committee notes that devising a marketing
 set up for commercialising its research outputs and capabilities is one of the thrust areas of the DSIR. When, the Committee asked as
 to how the Department was going to achieve this, the Secretary, DSIR replied that the National Research Development Corporation
 (NRDS), a Public Sector enterprise under DSIR was created for licensing and commercialisation of indigenous technologies as well
 as export of technologies. In order to strengthen and enlarge the marketing set `up and provide specialized technical services, the
 CSIR has now decided that its laboratories can also license the technologies directly, if necessary.
 
N.R.D.C.
 
12.    Since NRDC has recently strengthened its activities in the area of export of technologies and executing turnkey projects abroad,
 the laboratories are taking advantage of NRDC's expertise for licensing their technologies wherever necessary. In addition, CSIR is
 strengthening its marketing set up to commercialise its research outputs and capabilities through establishing business development
 groups in each laboratory, creating a separate budget head for marketing in the laboratories, enlarging the marketing network through
 engagement of consultants for business development and through across the counter sale of simpler technologies. The committee
 noted that NRDC has performed reasonably well and its earnings from premia; royalty and exports have increased over the years.
 The committee, however, is of the opinion that NRDC needs to be strengthened and its role has to be expanded-with a view to
 increasing its earnings which are at a very small level at this stage. It has to play a more dynamic and aggressive role in the area of
 patents, venture and risk capital projects (with the collaborating financial institutions); etc.
 
Programmes Aimed at Technological Self-Reliance (PATSER)
 
13.    Under this programme, DSIR supports activities relating to technology absorption, adaptation and demonstration as also capital
 goods development. The committee noted that while the actual expenditure on the Programmes Aimed at Technological Self
 Reliance was Rs. 1.68 crores in 1992-93 and Rs. 2.94 crores in 1993-94, Budget estimate for the year 1994-95 are placed at Rs. 7.68
 crores for this purpose. When the Committee asked the Department to explain the reasons for this increase, the Secretary DSIR
 replied that earlier, DSIR support covered only those public sector units which under took Research, Development, Design and
 Engineering (RDDE) projects mainly for absorption and up gradation of imported technology. However, from April, 1993, DSIR
 support has been extended, to both public and private sector units. Further more, the scope of the programme has been expanded
 from absorption of foreign technology to development and demonstration of new or improved technologies including those of special
 purpose capital goods. DSIR is now actively involved in discussing and identifying priority RDDE projects with various Public
 Sector units, particularly those in important sectors. While the bulk of these projects would be supported by public Sector units
 themselves, DSIR support will be considered on a selective basis to some of the important projects having wide sector impact and
 requiring networking of R & D organisations to assist these industrial units. Besides, out of around 80 project proposals received
 from industrial units, in both the public and private sectors, 12 new projects have already been financed. Due to these initiatives,
 according to the Secretary, over 25 new R&D projects with a support of about Rs. 6.00 crores during 1994-95 are likely to be
 approved, in addition to a support of about Rs. 1.70 crores required for the on-going R&D projects and Technology Evaluation
 Studies which are in their final stages. This would amount to a total support of Rs. 7.7 crores during 1994-95 which explains the
 increase in budget provision for PATSER over 1992-93 during 1994-95.
 
Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of Technology (SEETOT):
 
14. The scheme run by DSIR essentially aims at facilitating acquisition of technologies, accelerating export of technologies and
 services, enhancing the consultancy capabilities and increasing awareness about the usefulness of consultancy services among its
 customers. Development and commercialisation of indigenous technologies is encouraged and mechanisms for technology transfer
 such as Asian and Pacific Centre for Transfer of Technology (APCTT) located at New Delhi are supported. The scheme has four
 major programmes. The Committee notes that the actual expenditure for SEETOT has comedown from Rs. 2.21 crores in 1992-93 to
 Rs. 1.93 crores in 1993-94. Budgets estimate for this scheme has further been reduced to Rs. 1.35 crores in 1994-95. When the
 Committee asked the reason for the decline in allocation for this scheme, the Secretary DS1R said the SEETOT is essentially a
 continuing scheme from the Seventh plan, envisaging activities mentioned above. In December 1992, the scheme was reviewed and
 it was decided that the emphasis should now be on identification and supporting of developmental projects with the participation of
 the national R & D system, industry and consultants, on a highly selective basis, particularly in the context of new policies. It was
 also decided that the funding of the projects Should be generally through one scheme only within the DSIR, and the capabilities and
 experience built up in the Department Should be fully utilised to implement the projects. In view of the changed priorities, no new
 studies have been taken up since December, 1992 except in special cases, and hence expenditure towards preparation of reports was
 substantially reduced. Besides, the Department is also providing support to Consultancy Development Centre (CDC) situated in New
 Delhi to meet recurring expenses and other capital requirements. There is no budgetary provision for the capital requirement of CDC
 from 1994-95 onwards. Thus the expenditure under SEETOT has declined mainly due to the change in emphasis from studies and
 other promotional activities to projects and reduced requirements of capital funds for CDC. The Committee appreciates the efforts

 made by the Department under this scheme and the fact that allocations for the CDC are coming down gradually. The Committee still
 feels that the CDC should be impressed upon to generate revenues on its own to reduce its continuing dependence on funds from
 DSIR.
 
Research and Development by Industry (RDI):-
 
15.  DSIR deals with all activities relating to recognition of In-house R&D units in Industry and non-commercial Scientific and
 Industrial Research Organisations, providing fiscal incentives and other mechanisms towards supporting and encouraging the R&D
 initiatives of industry. When the Committee asked as to how the Department has planned to make investment in R&D by industry
 morn attractive and productive; and how much are the industries public and private sector, contributing towards total industry related
 R&D efforts, Secretary DS1R replied that several fiscal incentives and support measures have been announced for encouraging R&D
 by industry and enhancing investments in R&D. These include relief from taxes, exception from government control measures,
 nation’s awards for outstanding R&D achievements, etc. Besides, DSIR is providing direct support to industry for undertaking R&D
 projects in the form of co-financing specific R&D projects undertaken in-house in industry either by a company alone or jointly
 between a company and a Government laboratory/ IIT/University. The DSIR share of the total project cost ranges typically from 20-
50% of the project cost and is provided in the from of a grant. Such direct R&D financing is undertaken by DSIR through its
 Programmes Aimed At Technological Self-Reliance and Research and Development by Industry programmes using budgetary
 resources. Resources from the Venture Capital Fund (VCF) of IDBI and IFCI and Technology Development and Information
 Company of India (TD1CI) of the ICICI are also facilitated for supporting technology development and commercialization
 programmes.
 
16.    As regards contribution by industry in total R&D efforts. The, Secretary informed that over 1200 in house R&D Centres have
 been recognised by DSIR.  Of these, around 135 are in public sector, 35 in joint sector and around 1075 in private sector.  R&D
 expenditure incurred by the recognised in-house R&D units is estimated to be Rs. 1100  crores during 1992-93 which is around 23%
 of the total R&D expenditure in the country. The share of the in-house R&D expenditure   by the Public and Joint sectors is 45% and
 by the Private sector is 55%. The average ratio of R&D expenditure to annual turnover for the 1200 units as a whole is 0.68% The
 committee finds that While he percentage share of Private Sector in in-house R&D activity is more than that of the public and joint
 sectors put together, the percentage share of private sector to the total R&D expenditure in the country, and the average ratio of R&D
 expenditure to the annual turnover for the 1200 Units as whole also is very low.  The Committee therefore, feels that in the wake of
 various incentives, and concessions given to the industry, the Government Should strive to strengthen in-house R&D ill Industry by
 encouraging more and more private sector industries to put more money into it.
  
Information Pool                                     
 
            17.    The Committee notes that R &D, activities  are being carried out in the country by Several Ministries, Departments.
 Industries and autonomous bodies.  The committee wanted to know whether any information pool exists in the DSIR  from where
 information can be obtained regarding R&D activities going on at various places.  DSIR explained that DSIR is the nodal
 Department for granting recognition to in-house  R&D units in industry.  DSIR also has a scheme of granting recognition to non-
commercial Scientific and Industrial Research Organisations (SIROs).  Some of these SIROs also undertake industrial R&D units in
 industry.  DSIR also has a scheme of granting recognition to non-commercial Scientific  and Industrial Research Organistaion
 (SIROS).  Some of these SIROs also undertake industrial R&D Centres. “Profile of Scientific and Industrial Research Organisations”
 and other related DSIR  publications.  Besides, industrial R&D is also being pursued in the laboratories of national R&D
 organizations such as DRDO, Department of Atomic Energy, Electronics and Space, R&D institutions attached to various economic
 Ministries (e.g. Central Power Research Institute attached to Department of power, Research, Designs and Standards Organisations
 attached to the Ministry of Railways), universities, IITs, cooperative industrial research association (e.g. Indian Plywood Industry
 Research Institute and the various Tetile Industry Research Institutes) and R&D institutions of State  Governments.  The Committee
 notes that the information pool available with CSIR covers only its recognized in-house R&D units and non-commercial SIROs and
 national laboratories run by it, It does not cover, however, works being done in the Government Departments, universities and other
 autonomous bodies.  The committee, therefore, emphasizes the need to extend the scope of existing information pool in DSIR to
 cover information about R&D works being done at other places also with a view to creating a national information pool in this area.
 
Societal Programmes
 
18.    CSIR is undertaking some societal programmes aimed at making the benefits of S&T available to the welfare of the
 economically weaker sections of the society and the people living in rural areas.  The Committee wanted to know the areas in which
 the benefits have already been provided to the weaker sections in the rural areas.  The Secretary, DSIR, informed that CSIR has been
 developing appropriate technologies for rural population and as a result, a basket of technology has been accumulated by now.  The
 appropriate technologies, relevant for rural areas, offered by CSIR are for meeting (a) minimum needs i.e. providing safe drinking
 water, building low-cost dwelling units, etc; (b) for employment generation/income enhancement; i.e. cultivation and processing of
 medicinal, aromatic and other economic plants, food processing and post harvest technologies, improved technologies for leather
 sector; alternate building materials ad housing, simple brick making etc., improved technology for leather flaying, tanning, carcass
 processing; and (c)           for improvement in quality of life i.e. energy efficient smokeless chullas. Improved latrines and sanitation
 systems water purification and treatment technologies etc.
 
19.    Members of the Committee evinced keen interest in society-related programmes, particularly those which aim at mitigating
 hardships faced by the poor people living in rural areas. The Committee appreciates the work being done by the Department in this

 regard. But in view of the magnitude and nature of the problems faced by people in different climatic and geographical regions,
 committee is of the opinion that the society-related programmes have to be gradually undertaken by adopting locale or region-
specific approach. Special emphasis has to be provided to develop appropriate technologies in such areas as rural development,

 The committee showed interest by the Central Building Research Institute and the Centre Road Research Institute. The Committee

The Atomic Energy Commission (AEC), created by a Governme nt of India Resolution on
August 10, 1948, is the apex body for formulation of pol icies and direction of the programmes relating
to peaceful uses of atomic energy in electricity generation, medicine, agriculture industry and research.
The Commission implements its polic ies and programmes that are mult idisciplinary in nature through
the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), wh ich was formed on August 3, 1954. This year the
organisation is celebrating its Golden Jubilee year. From the si ngle unit, namely, the Atomic Energy
Establishment, Trombay (AEET) in  1957, today DAE comprises five Re search Centres, five Public
Sector Undertakings, three Industria l Organisations and three service organisations and seven out of its
eight fully funded institutes are engaged in basic research. In addition, the Department ’s Board o f 
Research in Nuclear Sciences (BRNS) and the National Boar d for Higher Mathematics (NBHM)
promote research in nuclear and allied fields, and mathematics. 
  
2.         The programmes being pursued by DAE emanate from the following mandate: 
  
¾      Increasing share of nuclear power through deployment of indigenous and other proven
technologies, along with devel opment of fast breeder react ors and thorium reactors with
associated fuel cycle facilities; 
¾      Building and operation of res earch reactors for production of  radioisotopes and carrying
out radiation technology applications in the field of medicine, agriculture and industry; 
¾      Developing advanced technologies such as  accelerators, lasers, supercomputers, 
advanced materials and instrumentation, and encouraging transfer of technology to
industry; 
¾      Support to basic research in nuclear ener gy and related frontier areas of science; 
Interaction with universiti es and academic instituti ons; Support to research and
development projects having a bearing on DAE ’s programmes, and International 
cooperation in related advanced areas of research; and

the Department are provided by budge tary support. The public sector undertakings of the Department
provide Internal and Extra Budgetary Resources (I EBR) in addition to budgetary support to the capital

commercial power reactors with a ssociated safety in all its phase s.  This comprises building o f 
Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors  (PHWR) and development of Fa st Breeder Reactors (FBR) and
Thorium Reactors on commercial s cale.  Associated waste manage ment and environment monitoring
and technology development relating to operation and maintenance of the reactors also form part of the
programmes.

the R&D facilities and includes- pr ogrammes related to nuclear fuel cycle covering design, construction 
and operation of industrial plants for refining ores, fabrication of  fuel, production of heavy water,
instrumentation and control, etc. needed for sustai ned operation of the power reactors; and applications
of radioisotopes, radi ation, laser and accelerator  technology for developmen t in industry, medicine,
agriculture and food preservation. 
  
6.         Research & Development Sector pr ovides R & D support to the Nuclear Power Programme o f 
the Department.  The R & D effort s of DAE are in multidisciplinar y high technology areas.  Significant 
achievements have been made in building technical capabilities in the design, construction and operation
of Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHW R); exploration, mining ex traction, purification and
conversion of nuclear mate rials; production of fuel element for nuclear reactors; pr oduction of heavy
water; health and safety research; development and application of lasers and accelerators; development

management and production and use of  radioisotopes, besides basic re search in frontier areas of S&T,

Nuclear Waste Management and Disposal 
  
50.       The Committee has been given to unde rstand that there are two main options for the 
management of spent nuclear fuel. The first option is to use the fuel  in reactor only once.  After its 
removal from the reactor, the spent fuel is declar ed high level waste as such.  Another option is to 
recycle spent nuclear fuel by reproc essing.   Spent fuel contains Uran ium and Plutonium.   They can be 
reused in the manufacture of nuclear fuel.  In or der the separate Uranium and Plutonium from spent 
nuclear fuel, it is reprocessed at  reprocessing plants.  Reprocessi ng does not solve the waste problem 
because the remaining high level liquid waste generate d by reprocessing must be  disposed of in some
places.  The liquid is solidified in glass for final disposal. 
  
51.       There are five more or less possible alternativ es for final disposal of hi gh-level waste.  They are 
monitored long-term storage, final disposal deep in bedrock, embedding in th e bottom sediments of the
ocean, final disposal in deep bore holes and transmutation.  
  
52.       In monitored long-term storage, wastes are stored temporar ily within the Power Plant areas in
ground or near surface storage structur es.  The justification for this alternative is that technological 
development may bring with it better methods of arranging the waste management.  The most significant 
draw back of indefinite interim storage is that it assumes that future societies will remain stable and
capable of maintaining the stores. 
  
53.       The Committee was also  informed that, nowadays, most of the countries that use nuclear energy
have a programme for the final dispos al of high level wastes in bedroc k.  As a host rock for disposal, 
granite, salt, clay, clay stones and tuff  formations are being invest igated.          In ‘direct final disposal’, 
encapsulated fuel rod assemblies are disposed of as such.  In ‘reprocessi ng’, high-level waste is 
solidified in glass before final disposal.  
  
54.       Other alternatives for the geological dispos al of high-level waste are final di sposal in deep 
boreholes or in the seabed.  These alternatives are practically permanent solutions unlike facilities in 
bedrock.   High-level waste could be brought back on the surface from deep repositories if required.  
However, the Committee feels that this would be very costly. 
55.       The Committee is of the opinion that bedroc k or seabed at a depth of  several kilometers would 
probably isolate radioactive substances effectively.  However, th e Committee feels th at afterwards it 
would be difficult to  verify the safety of thes e disposal methods.  There is no certainty that waste 
canisters would remain intact in the depths of ocea n or bedrock.  Besides, it would most probably be 
difficult to win international approval for final disposal of wastes in seabed. 
56.       There are two fold spent nuclear fuel canisters.  The inner canister of nodular cast-iron is 
surrounded by external canister made  up of copper that is about 5 cm. thick.  The canisters are lowered 
into the final disposal repository.    The repository  comprises a network of tunnels.  The tunnels are 
excavated in bedrock at a depth of 400 to 700 meters. 
57.       Spent nuclear fuel is isolated from the environment by multiple safety  barriers.  For example, 
corrosion resistant waste canisters and the surroundin g bentonite cla y isolate nuclear waste from

necessary to decrease the waste volume by evaporating as much water as possible from the crusty
sludge.  This will make the transport of the waste easier and storage less costly.   
59.       Since there is a clear relationship between chemical composition of th is waste material and the 
data from the spectrometer, Ra man spectrometer method could be developed into a fiber optic
instrument that would allo w testing of materials in the tanks fr om a distance.  The Raman spectromete r 
method possibly could act as a sophisticated type of l itmus paper, or a colour coded pH sensor to detect
undesirable chemical composition. The high level nuclear waste such as spent fuel from nuclear reactors
could be stored in containers that hold up for approximately hundred years but stowing nuclear waste for
the long run will require containm ent materials that can resist leaching and radiation damage fo r
thousands of years. 
60.       Typically, radioactive emissions jostle the at oms out of their careful ly ordered arrangements
within the storage material.  The material eventu ally becomes unstable and thus prone to cracking,
swelling or structural change. 
61.       The key seems to be that atoms in the stru cture of the material are re latively disordered and can 
shift positions with ease, thereby tolerating minute defects caused by radiatio n.  Therefore, looking fo r 
better storage materials li ke ceramics which are called ‘complex oxide’ are proper because it shares a 
basic chemical formula i.e. two di fferent pairs of metallic cations i.e. positively charged ions and 7
Oxygen atoms.  Depending on their size, the cation pairs may give these materials either a highly 
ordered or a somewhat disordered st ructure.    Pyrochlore, which is a brown material, is extremely ideal 
because atoms within it cannot easily trade places.  Brown pyrochlore structures are promising for use in 
waste containment because th ey are chemically compatible candidate with waste constituents.  Purple 
fluorite structure also does well u nder irradiation because atoms within this mate rial can shift around to
accommodate the defects with little effort.  Except  pyrochlore and fluorite type crystalline materials, 
other crystalline materials with rela tively disordered struct ures may be resistant to radiation damage as
well.  In many countries including Ja pan, Russia and some countries in  Europe, crystalline materials are 
preferred as candidate for nuclear waste storage containers.  However,  in USA vitreous glass like an d 
cemented materials are used for storage of nuclear material. 
62.       The Committee is of the view that ‘Fluorite Ceramic’ materi als show promise as  safe, radiation 
proof materials and should be further developed to contain nuclear wastes. 
63.       The highly radioactive wastes are either extracted by a solution that does not mix with the waste 
solution; a process called solvent extraction or is re moved by ion exchangers.  The high level wastes are 
then to be immobilized in a special glass, placed inside steel drums and buried about 1000 ft. deep in salt
mines, in sites to be designate d.   The remaining low-level waste may then be encased in cement an d 
stored on site. 
64.       Inorganic ion exchangers can also be used  in nuclear medicines.  Radioactive elements with 
short half lives currently are used to determine blood flow or to locate a tumor.   With the ion exchanger, 
it might be possible to be tter target the tumor by sparing surr ounding healthy cells.  Inorganic materials 
exchange ions more efficiently than organic materials and they can withstand radiation better. 
65.       In transmutation, very long-lived radio active substances could be separated from waste and 
destroyed.  Transmutation means that radioactive sour ce material is transforme d stable, short lived or 
fissile.   Transmutation would be used to destr oy those substances of spent nuclear fuel that have very
long half-lives, even of millions of years.  Among these substa nces there are Iodi ne-129, Technetium-
99, Caesium-135, Selenium-79 and ma ny substances heavier than Uranium which are also known as
‘Transuranic’nuclear substances. 
66.       The Committee is of the opinion th at transmutation is researched all the time.  It seems to be 
difficult to develop industrial scale transmutation processes for nuclear waste management.  In any case, 
transmutation would be onl y a partial solution sinc e it does not destro y a l l  n u c l e a r  w a s t e s .  T h e
