Recommendation 
  
            For minimizing the high level nuclear waste volume for pe rmanent storage and eventually
determining what happens to the ma terial when it leaks out of th e tank, the Committ ee feels, it is
necessary to decrease the waste volume by evaporating as much water as possible from the crusty
sludge.  This will make the transport of the waste easier and storage less costly.   
  
(Para58)
Action taken by the Department  
  
The practice of decreasing the volume of high le vel waste by evaporation is being followed in
our  spent fuel reprocessi ng plants as well as in high level waste vitrificati on facilities. Evaporation by
concentration in specially designed thermo-syphon evaporators is an integral part of the basic flow sheet
of all these plants. We are, thus, able to reduce the waste volumes substantially. 
  
As regards the storage of HLW in  the liquid form, this is done in high integrity stainless steel
storage tanks with cooling and instrumentation provisions. Our experience of HLW storage in tanks over
last more than three decades  is excellent from safety point of view with not a single instance of leakage
of any of the tanks. 
  
In order to avoid transportation of HLW, care  has been taken during the plant design by co-
locating reprocessing and vitrification plants. Transfer of waste among reprocessing plant, waste storage
tanks and vitrification plant is done through underground shielded piping system to avoid radiation
exposure to operation personnel. 
  
Thus, aspects of volume reduction of  HLW, its safe storage and tran sfer are an in tegral part o f
the design of our facilities and their safe performance has been demonstrated during last more than three
decades of operations.

Recommendation 
  
            Since there is a clear relationship be tween chemical composition of this waste material and the
data from the spectrometer, Ra man spectrometer method could be developed into a fiber optic
instrument that would allo w testing of materials in the tanks fr om a distance.  The Raman spectromete r
method possibly could act as a sophisticated type of l itmus paper, or a colour coded pH sensor to detect
undesirable chemical composition. The high level nuclear waste such as spent fuel from nuclear reactors
could be stored in containers that hold up for approximately hundred years but stowing nuclear waste for
the long run will require containm ent materials that can resist leaching and radiation damage fo r
thousands of years. 
(Para 59)
 
Action taken by the Department  
  
Raman Spectrometer is in use for analysis of va rious solid samples and necessary facilities have
been developed at BARC, Trombay fo r this application. Essentially, Ra man Spectrometer is capable  o f
analyzing chemical composition.  However, the accuracy of measur ement by Raman Spectrometer is
generally in the range of milligm/litre against our requirement of microgm/litre   
Page 10 of 19137th Report of Committee on S & T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/137threport.htm

  
HLW is stored in our faciliti es in specially designed tanks of high integrity with various
provisions including that for liquid sampling. Thes e samples are remotely withdrawn, diluted and
analysed for various radiochemica l properties. The analysis require s measurement of radioactivity
content and identification of various isotopes present in the waste. Other properties like density, acidity,
alkalinity, total salts, etc. are also  analysed. Extensive analysis of va rious elements and radicals present
in the waste is also done. All this analysis is done in the laboratory with the help of various analytical
and nuclear instruments like spectrophotomet er, inductively couple plasma atomic mission
spectrophotometer and radioactivity c ounters. Since waste storage tanks ar e stored in shielded area, the
chemical analysis signals through opt ical fibres have to be routed  to the spectrometer. Aspect o f
attenuation of signal through a lengt h of 50-60 m of optical fibres needs to be considered alongwith
other issues like radiation stability for deployment of Raman spectroscopy in HLW analysis. 
As regards, containment material for disposal of spent fuel, this  issue is not applicable to ou r
programme in view of closed fuel cycle approach adopted by India. 
  
  
Comments  
  
            The Committee notes the reply of the Department. 
  
Recommendation 
  
            The Committee is of the view th at ‘Fluorite Ceramic’ materials show promise as safe, radiation 
proof materials and should be further developed to contain nuclear wastes. 
  
  
(Para 62)
  
Action taken by the Department  
  
            BARC has already taken up a program me for development of ceramic matrices for incorporation
of long lived radionuclides. The matrix being developed is basically a  assemblage of various crystalline
formations containing  minerals like hollandite, pervoskite and  zircolonite. ‘Flourite Ceramic’ belongs 
to zirconolite family and is a form  of crystalline phase present in the matrix formulation to immobilize
long lived Plutonium isotopes. At present, the work in BARC is being carried out in the laboratory scale
to study  the properties of the wast e product. In parallel, developmen t of technologies for separation o f
long live radionuclide from high level waste and their immobilization is also being carried out. 
  
Comments  
  
            The Committee notes the reply of the Department .  The Committee appreciates the fact that the 
programme for development of Florite Ceramic matrices for inco rporation of long-l ived radionuclide 
has already been taken up by the BARC. The Committee is of the view that after carrying out laboratory
scale-study to identify the nuclear properties of radionuclide, the same could be used for the purpose o f 
treatment of Cancer which will give a functional dimension for th e use of nuclear waste products fo r
medical applications. 
  
Recommendation 
  
            The highly radioactive wastes are either extracted by a solution th at does not mix with the waste 
solution; a process called solvent extraction or is removed by ion exchangers.  The high level wastes are

then to be immobilized in a special glass, placed inside steel drums and buried about 1000 ft. deep in salt
mines, in sites to be designate d.   The remaining low-level waste may then be encased in cement an d 
stored on site. 
(Para 63)
Action taken by the Department 
Disposal in 1000 feet salt mines is not being considered in India since massive deep salt deposits
are not present in the country. Dis posals in salt mines is being studied in few c ountries like Germany
and USA where such deposits are available. 
  
Comments  
  
            The Committee notes the reply of the Department. 
  
Recommendation 
            Inorganic ion exchangers can also be used in nuclear medicines.  Ra dioactive elements with
short half lives currently are used to determine blood flow or to locate a tumor.   With the ion exchanger,
it might be possible to be tter target the tumor by sparing surr ounding healthy cells.  Inorganic materials
exchange ions more efficiently than organic materials and they can withstand radiation better. 
(Para 64)
Action taken by the Department  
            Process based on ion exchange are be ing  used in our radioactiv e waste management plants fo r
separation of certain isotopes fr om various waste  streams. Inor ganic ion exchanges like naturally
occurring ion-exchanger known as vermeculite have been used ex tensively in India for cesium 
separation from radioactive waste. However, inorganic ion exch angers are used in once - though made. 
They have better radiation stabili ty than organic ion exchangers . DAE has developed organic ion
exchangers for separation of cesium and strontium from  intermediate level alkaline waste. Compared to
inorganic exchangers, these have ma ny superior qualities like very high selectivity for specific isotope
and re-usability after regeneration. This technology has been used for industrial scale application both at 
Tarapur and Trombay. Based on separated 137Cs isotope, design and installation of facility fo r 
encapsulation of cesium in glass matrix as well as fabr ication of assemblies have  been initiated for use
in blood irradiation.  
Therefore, ion exchange proces s is basically employed for sepa ration of various isotopes from
radioactive waste.  
  
Comments  
            The Committee notes the reply of the Departme nt. The Committee is happy to note that organic 
ion exchanger technology has been used for industria l scale application both at Tarapur and Trombay.
Since ion exchange process is pr imarily aimed for separa ting radio-isotopes from  Nuclear wastes, the 
Committee hopes that in future thes e isotopes will be used for the purpose of productive application in
the field of Nuclear Medicine, particularly in the treatment of Cancer. 
  
Recommendation 
  
            The Committee is of the opinion th at transmutation is researched all the time.  It seems to be
difficult to develop industrial scale transmutation processes for nuclear waste management.  In any case,
transmutation would be only a part ial solution since it does not de stroy all nuclear wastes.   The
Committee feels that final disposal  of nuclear waste must  not ever cause hazar dous radiation or othe r
damage to the environment or property. 
  
(Para 66)
Action taken by the Department

            DAE has embarked upon a long-range pl an for the development of Accelerator Driven System 
(ADS) which, besides other applications, has the potential of use in tran smutation of long lived
radionuclides.  As a preparatory st ep, process development for separa tion of long-lived radionuclides  
from HLW has been taken up. The separated radionuclides will be subjected to transmutation fo r

            In line with the thinking of the Committee, it is the basic objective of radi oactive waste
management practices adopted in the country that  final disposal of vitr ified high level waste in
geological formation must be safe from the point of view of protec tion of human  and his environment.
To meet this objective, a systems appr oach is followed  so that release to the environment is well within
the prescribed limit. Various compone nt of this disposal system are vitrified high level waste, caniste r

Mathematical models  and the data  of characteristics of individual component of the repository are used

            Unlike at Nuclear Power Plants, there are no high temperatures or pressures at the encapsulation
plant. Spent nuclear fuel cannot expl ode by itself.   They are not eas ily flammable substances in the

            The Committee notes the reply of the Department. 
  
Recommendation  
  
            The Committee has been given to understand that  the Universal Extraction, or UNEX, process 
which is being studied in USA by Idaho National Engineering and Environmental Laboratory (INEEL)
engineers which is a subsidiary of US Department of Energy has developed the first demonstrated
technology of its kind capable of removing multiple radio active elements from high level nuclear waste
in one step.  Just a sprinkling of radioactive el ements turns volume of a largely harmless waste into
‘high level radioactive waste’ subject to rigorous and expensive storage standards.   
  
            Such waste is a byproduct of nucle ar energy and weapons developm ent and usually contains a
mixture of intensely radioact ive fission products like Stront ium-90, Cesium-137 and long lived 
radioactive elements like plutonium and Americiam plus hazardous and toxic materials. Separating most
of the radioactive elements  from the other materials can shrink volume of high-leve l waste, reduce the 
total disposal cost and minimise potential harm to the people and the environment surrounding it.  The
Committee is of the opinion that an extractant is required that works in one step and removes radioactive
strontium, cesium and other Actinides at once. 
  
            Using the UNEX process, trimming th e volume of high level waste at least twenty fold, each
gallon of waste shrinks to less than a cup and the twenty fold vol ume reduction leads to a corresponding
reduction in disposal costs.  The ma jority of the waste left over afte r a   UNEX sepa ration is far less
expensive to treat and store than the highly radioactive portion. 
  
            The Committee would like to suggest that this unique UNEX process of squeezing the volume of
enormous nuclear waste to  size less than a cup should be studi ed to depth by DAE and Atomic Energy
Regulatory Board (AERB) so that the benefit of the reduction of disposal cost could be enjoyed by the
Department as an economy measure for treating, managing and storing all types of radioactive waste e.g.
low level, intermediate level and high level nuclear waste etc., and a subsequent  feasibility report could
be submitted before the Committee for perusal and examination, partic ularly keeping in view the cost
effectivity aspect  of the project. 
( Paras 70, 71, 72 & 73)
  
Action taken by the Department 
  
In various countries several solvent extraction process have been developed for the separation o f
long-lived radionuclides, Stront ium-90 and Cesium-137 from acidic radioactive waste solution. These 
processes use different types of solvent employing solvent-extraction equipment of different designs.  
  
Universal Extraction (UNEX) process being studied by Idaho Nati onal Engineering and
Environment Laboratory (INEEL), USA employs a large number of  centrifugal  contactors  in a cascade
manner. In this process,  a universal solvent containing Ch roninated Co balt Di carbollide (ChCoDic) 
with polyethylglycol (PEG) to remove 137-Ce sium and Strontium-90 and C arbamoylmethyl Phosphine 
Oxide (CMPO ) to remove long-lived radionuclides is used. 
  
India has developed extens ive expertise during last  four decades in extr action  of uranium and
plutonium from acidic solutions gene rated during spent fuel reprocessi ng. The solvent used is 30%  tri-
butyl phosphate (TBP) + dodecane  in pulse agitated  columns. Plants  based on this solvent extraction
technology are in o peration at Tromba y, Tara pur and Kal pakkam from 1965 onwards. Presentl y,

research and development is being carried out for separation of minor actinides as well as fission
products from reprocessi ng waste for which various solvents have and are being developed and
evaluated. 
  
 Feasibility study for using a “combined solvent extraction flow sheet”, for extraction of Cs 137, 
Sr90 and long-lived radionuclides from various types of liquid waste st reams forms a pa rt of on-going 
development strategy review. 
  
Comments  
  
            The Committee notes the reply of the Departme nt.  The Committee is  of the opinion that

undertaken by DAE for an in-depth f easibility study in this respect fo r extracting other long lived radio-
nucleotide like Co 60   from high-level Nuclear Was tes which could be used fo r applications in Nuclea r
Medicine.

(AERB) envisages three distinct modes of final disposition in respect of radioactive wastes:-

b)      Deep geological disposal for high level and Alpha bearing wastes; and

adequate infrastructure at all stations to train co astal states about the adva nced tools and techniques fo r
planning coastal zone management sy stems. Besides, modern tools su ch as GIS, Remote Sensing and
Mathematical Modelling should be fr equently used to predict the cro ss-impact of various activities 
under the programme.

        The Committee would like the De partment to actively participat e in international events and 
expositions so that our scientists get exposure to the developments and innovations taking place in other
countries. It will also help in exchanging knowledge about th e scientific deve lopments of othe r

expositions to enable its scientists to get necessary exposure.

OCEAN OBSERVATION & INFORMATION SERVICES (OOIS)  
Recommendation 
        The Committee commends the activities being pur sued by the Indian Nati onal Centre for Ocean
Information Services (INCOIS) in the field of Ocean info rmation and observations. However, being the
nodal agency for providing coastal and ocean data  and value added products to the users, the
Department should monitor the performance a nd work-mechanism of the INCOIS to process an d 
disseminate ocean data and data pr oducts to user communities like fi sheries, weather, climate, ports,
shipping etc. on a regular basis so that ocean weather forecasting is precise.

chairmanship of Secretary, DOD, which consists of 15 members incl uding Heads of institutions of 11
national agencies pertaining to Science & Technology and 2 expert s who would provide advice on
generation and dissemination of coastal and ocean data products and value added services to a variety of
user community. The recently cons tituted Research Advisory Commi ttee (RAC) of the Department is
also monitoring the performance of INCOIS. In add ition, the progress of various activities of INCOIS is
also being reported on quarterly  basis to the Planning Commissi on by quarterly pe rformance review
under the chairmanship of the Member (S&T). Signi ficant achievements are also reported on monthly
basis to the Cabinet Secretary. Thus the achievements  of INCOIS are effectivel y monitored to make the
advisory services of INCOIS as a part of value added chain among the potential user communities.

OCEANOGRAPHIC RESEARCH 
        The Committee is pleased to not e that the Department is mainly using two Ocean Research
Vessels, namely, Sagar Sampada and Sagar Kanya for deep sea re search. These vessels are using
Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV ) and Autonomous Underwater Vehi cle (AUV) to study about deep
sea life forms at considerable depth. However, the Committee feels that scope of deep sea research could
be more challenging and informative if machiner ies could dive beyond a de pth of 6000 metres. The
Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that for a real deep sea study Advanced Tethered Vehicle (ATV)
is needed by Department, which is an unmanned ve hicle equipped with latest  advanced technology and
which can easily undertake researches beyond a de pth of 6 thousand metres. The most striking
advantage for using the ATV for underwater research is that it is extremely helpful to make researches at
extreme depth where it is dangerous  for divers to venture. The Co mmittee is given to understand that
such vehicles are cost affective and can be used in ocean abyss with much flexibility. It is observed that
the vast majority of the ocean depths are bone chilling cold, completely dark and have ambient pressures
equivalent to the weight of the hundreds of atmosphe res. The exploration of th e deep sea is, therefore,
impossible without a substantial i nvestment on latest te chnology. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that the Department may use Advanced Tethered Vehi cle (ATV) for the purpose of deep
sea research in view of its deep sea advantages a nd cost effective applicati ons. This vehicle will be
extremely helpful for researches at  ocean benthos where gr eater variety of biotic  and abiotic elements
are available and a study of which could add consid erably to the store house of human knowledge about
ocean depth.                                                                                                                                      (Para
58) 
Action Taken by the Department 
        The Department is already pursui ng the design and developm ent of Unmanned Tethered
Submersible, upto a water depth of  6000m. This programme has been en trusted to National Institute of
Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai fo r implementation. NIOT is in the process of designing and
developing such deep sea unmanned tethered submer sible with the help of a Russian Institute EDBOE,
RAS, MOSCOW. The system is likely to be ready by May, 2005 for demonstration.

        Keeping in view its deep  sea advantages and cost  effective applications, the Committee hopes that 
sustained efforts would be made to develop Advanced Tethered Su bmersible. The Department should
devise better ways and means to achieve the objective.

        The Committee feels that Gas Hydr ates have the potential of pr oviding energy security to the
country. Therefore, the Department  should encourage excellence in national laboratories to focus on

        The Honourable Committee observes that the Gas Hydrates have the potential for providing energy
security to the country and hence the Department should encourage excellence in national laboratories to
focus on nice areas of Hydrate research with special emphasis on Environmental impacts and technology
development. 
        The Gas Hydrate programme is progressing at brisk pace and considerable progress has already
been made. The programme is being implemented through active participation of 3 of the major national
laboratories - National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIO T), National Geophysical Research Institute 
(NGRI) and National Institute of Oceanography (NIO). The emphasis is on basic and applied research in
this field. NIOT is developing tw o technologies for underwater auto mated coring system (capable o f
coring up to 150m at depths 2500m) and underwater support submersi ble. These equipments will be
extremely useful in exploration of  the gas hydrates. Also NIO is wo rking on the possible environmental
impact of Gas Hydrate exploitati on. Some of other niche areas be ing covered under the programme are
physical properties of Gas Hydrates, advanced multi channel seismic data processing, economics of Gas
Hydrates, Ocean Bottom Seismometer etc.

The Committee notes the reply of the Department.  
PERSISTENT ORGANIC POLLUTANTS  
Recommendation 
        The Committee feels that Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) are the most common sea pollutants
which are constantly affecting the Ocean environm ent and optimal marine ecology. The POPs usually
gets generated in the deep sea envi ronment from the dead biotic orga nisms. When the particles of this
organisms get sink in the sea bed, a degradation of organic matrix occurs a nd consequently POPs get
released in the surrounding water. Under anoxic conditions, sediments containing organic carbon
releases contaminants into the surrounding water. POPs not only aff ect microbial food chain but also
coastal environments which are the most productive  areas of the sea. PO Ps are also ubiquitous.
Accordingly, it is an extreme th reat towards maintenance of opt imal sea ecology and it has high
exposure to humans also. Keeping the gravity of the situati on into active consideration, the Committee
feels that Sagar Purvi and Sagar Paschimi, two ocean research vessels, which are monitoring research on
ocean pollution may also direct a major chunk of their study towards the understanding of POPs
behaviour and subsequent control of the same from spreading on the sea benthos so that the entire biotic
community of ocean flora and fauna could be effectively preserved from environmental pollution. 
        The Committee also feels that two of th e main POP group namely dioxi n and furans which are the
principal threat to humanity should also be studied as a part of th e pollution control programme by the
Department. 
                                                                                                                                               (Para 63)

benthos so that the entire biotic community of ocean flora and fauna could be effectively preserved.

Recommendation 
The Committee has observed that given the present state of Wild Life Conservation in India,
there are a lot of work to be done in the field to gi ve the word ‘Conservation’ a real meaning.  Over the
years, the Committee has noted that  the basic requirements for conserva tion of wild life have not been
fulfilled to its best by the Minist ry of Environment & Forests and neither much importance has been
attached for the preserva tion of endangered species of animal and flora which constitute the heart o f
nature in India. 
            In order to give a thrust to the real  understanding of the meaning of  the term ‘Conservation’, the 
term Wild Life will have to be interpreted in a different perspectiv e in the broadest sense possible to
include scientific work, field wo rk, planning and manage ment, control of poach ing and illegal trade,
awareness, education and extensi on of work, eco-development, captive breeding and zoo management 
etc. 
            In order to give a more thrust  on the crux of the above definition, the Committee feel that
following priorities for wild life conservation should be designed by the Ministry during the current plan
period:- 
1.                  Control of poaching and illegal trade in wild life and wild life produc ts made of wild life
parts; 
2.                  Development of protected areas network.; 
3.                  Welfare measures for wild life staff; 
4.                  Eco tourism; 
5.                  Wild life conservation outside protected areas; 
6.                  Prevention and reduction of damage to wild life;  
7.                  Establishment of second home for the Asiatic lion in Gir. 
So long as the Asiatic lion population remains restri cted to a single location, it is at constant risk
from catastrophic natural events li ke forest fire, flood, earthquake et c.  Accordingly, efforts should be
under way to establish a second population of this enda ngered species in a suitable animal habitat.  As
per the Committee’s categorised opi nion, Palpur –Kuno in Madhya Prades h could be identified as the 
most viable alternative for this purpose.

Legal Protection against Wildlife Poaching and Trade  
  
            Govt. of India enacted a comprehensive legislat ion “Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972”with the 
objective of effectively controlling poaching and illegal trade in wildlife and its derivatives. This has
been amended in January, 2003 and puni shment an penalty for offences  under the Act have been made
more stringent.  
Offences pertainin g to huntin g of endan gered species and alterin g of boundaries of protected
areas. 
  
            For offences relating to wild an imals (or their parts a nd products) included in schedule- I of part 
II of Schedule –II  and those relating to hunting or altering the boundaries of a sanctuary or national park
the punishment and penalty have been enhanced, th e minimum imprisonment pres cribed is three years
which may extend to seven years, with a minimum fine of Rs. 10,000/-. For a subsequent offence of this 
nature, the term of imprisonments shall not be less than three years but may extend to seven section (51-
A) has been inserted in the Act, making certain conditions applicable while granting bail: 
            When any person accused of the commi ssion of any offence relating to Schedule I or Part II o f
Schedule II or offences relating to hunting inside the boundaries or National Park or Wildlife Sanctuary
or altering the boundaries of such parks and sanctuaries, is arrested under the provisions of the Act, then
not withstanding anything containe d in the Code of Cr iminal Procedure, 1973, no such person who had
been previously convicted of an offence under this Act shall be released on bail unless- 
            (a)  The public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity of opposing the release on bail; and  
            (b) Where the Public Prosecutor oppos e the application, the Court is  satisfied that there are
reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty or such offences and that he is not likely to commit
any offence while on bail.  
            In order to improve the intelligen ce gathering in wildlife cr ime, the existing provision fo r
rewarding the informers has been increased from 20% of the fine and composition m oney respectively

measures.

dilution, dispersion, wind base d movement, dry deposition, precipitation and chemical
transformation of pollutants generated.

Recommendation 
The Committee feels that Yamuna Action Plan fail s to achieve its twin objectives of making the
environment clean and using the trea ted effluent for irrigation for the benefit of the farmers.  As the
major problem with regard to the pollution of River Yamuna has been lack of minimum flow of water,
the Ministry should devise ways a nd means to constantly monitor the release of a minimum flow of 10
cubic meters per second of fresh water.  All the ripa rian states should ensure release of their share fo r
maintaining the minimum flow in the river.  This step will help in improving the water quality of the
River.                                                                (Para 60) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) wherever completed have helped in improvement o f
environment in those towns and in improvem ent of water quality of the river Yamuna.  Wherever 
possible, the treated effluent from STPs is being used for irrigation to  the extent possible.  For works
under National River Conservation Plan including Yamuna Action Plan, only the treated effluent
channel is included as a part of the project.  The work fo r carrying the treated effluent to the irrigation
fields through irrigation channels is to be done by th e State Govts. themselves.  The farmers are picking
up/lifting the treated effluent of STPs from the effluent channel, drains for irriga tion as and when
required. 
A High Powered Committee under the chairm anship of Member, Planning Commission
constituted in 1998 monitored the as pects on maintenance of minimum fl ow in river Yamuna.  All the
riparian States were asked to release their share of water as per the ratio decided by the Committee. 
While the States of Haryana and UP  filed the affidavits regarding discharge of required quantities o f

PROTECTION OF TAJ MAHAL 
Recommendation 
The Taj Mahal at Agra is  one of the most important monuments  of not only in India but also the
whole world.  In recent years owing to  growth of satellite industries, the ambient air quality particularly
within the Taj Trapezium Area (TTZ) has become more and more vulnerabl e to severe pollution
generating a serious threat to the qua lity of white marble stones of this  remarkable structure. This most
celebrated monuments viewed from  a distance, looms on the banks of  a stinking river almost always
enveloped in a haze of dust and smog from be lching smokestacks and exhaust fumes from the
surrounding industries.  The Committeefeels with a painful heart that this soot and fumes will eventually
turn the gleaming white building black. 
It is, therefore, obvious from the above, that in the recent year s the corrosive impact of the
polluted air on Taj Mahal ha s become a matter of grave concern.  Accordingly, the committee feels that
corrosive impact of pollutants and emissions from surroundings industrial conclave and running vehicles
within the vicinity of the monument is required to be addressed on extreme priority basis.

INTRODUCTION 
  
I, the Chairman of the Commi ttee on Science and Tec hnology, Environment and Forests, have been
authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present this 14th Report of the
Committee. This Report deals with  the Detailed Demands for Grants  (1994-95) of the Department o f
Electronics. 
  
2 The Committee held in all three meetings on 6 th , 7 th  and 22 nd April, 1994 (Appendix). In the 
meeting held on the 6th April, 1994, the Secretary and other repres entatives of the Department o f
Electronics gave a brief account of the allocations on different activiti es/projects of the Department as
proposed in its Detailed Demands for Grants and Members sought clarificati ons thereon. On the 7th
April, 1994 the Committee discussed in detail the Demands for Grants of the Department on the basis of
the documents made available to it and the submissions made befo re it by the Secretary and othe r
officials of the Department and the officials of the Department replied to the clarifications sought by the
Members. 
  
3. The Committee considered and adopted this report at its meeting held on the 22nd April, 1994. 
  
4. The Committee expresses its appreciation for the officials of the Department for their cooperation
and making available the material whenever required by the Committee. 
  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 
                                                                                     REPORT 
In the modern world if there is any area, which has affected our life most, it is the field of electronics
and information technology and all th e related disciplines that underpin it. There is hardly any area o f
human endeavour where electronic ga dgets have not reached; and ther e is hardly any industry, which
does not depend for its efficiency and productivity on the application of electronics in its different
manifestations. Innovations are taki ng place in this field on a revol utionary, continuing and breath-
taking basis, and the world over. Computers, communicati ons, control systems, consumer, industrial,
entertainment, defence and space el ectronics are all surging ahead. Th e Department of Electronics has
been vested since the early 1970s w ith the responsibility of formulat ion and implementation of national
policies in this sector, promoti onal measures for the development of appropriate new technologies
through R&D Programmes and coordinati on of the various appl ications of electronics. The aims, which
this Department seeks to achieve, are two-fold namel y, to bring the benefits of electronics to every walk 
of life and to every part of the country; and to develop the Indian Electronics as a major global player. 
  
2. In its sittings spread over two days, the Committee had occasion to examine the Detailed
Demands for Grants of the Department for the ye ar 1994-95 at some lengt h, particularly from the 
broader angle of its mandate and objectives. In this process the Committee has made an evaluation of the
plans and programmes of this Department in the larger framework of the Eighth Five Year Plan. 
  
3. The Secretary of the Department, in his presen tation before the Committee, outlined the measures
being taken by the Department on the application of th e electronics in different sectors; and in this
context cited some of th e recent attainments of his Department. Among these he cited the development
of design for Solid State Indicat or Signal with an energy saving between 15-20% for use by the 
Railways; Project "Vivek Darpan" which, through the use of audio visual medi a, aims at promoting
literacy, particularly amon g women; Industrial Elect ronics Promotion Pro gramme, the idea behind

which is to select some sectors li ke paper, steel, railways, avionics etc. and to render necessary help
in fields such as training, engineering, R&D, us e of electronic instruments and instrumentation,
productivity, quality improvement, development of  indigenous technology etc., and the technology-
based programme for sub-titlin g of films in Indian language s launched through the Centre fo r
Development of Advanced Computing. 
  
4. After listening to the presentation made by the Secretary of the Department, the Committee went
into the specifics of the budgetary allocations of the Department for its di fferent programmes as con-
tained in the Detailed Demands for Grants. The Committee has noted that as against the total Plan outlay
of Rs. 713.98 crores for the Depart ment's Eighth Five Year Plan, Rs. 67.70 crores for 1992-93 and Rs. 
164.00 crores (Revised Estimates) fo r 1993-94 have already been allo cated to the Department and fo r 
the year 1994-95, the Department has sought an allocation of Rs. 140.10 crores. This implies that for the
first three years of this Five Ye ar Plan period, the total allocati on comes to Rs. 371.80 crores, and about
Rs. 342.18 crores will be left with the Department  to pursue its programmes during the remaining two
years of this Plan period. The comp arative figures of allo cations programme/activity-wise are given in 
Annexure. 
  
5. In comparative terms, the Pl an allocation of Rs. 140.10 crores for 1994-95 is less by about Rs. 24 
crores as compared to the year 1993-94. It was stated  that the major reason for this is that, during the 
year 1993-94, there was an allocation of a substantial amount to  the tune of Rs. 75 crores through
supplementary grants for partiall y meeting expenditure on rebuild ing of the Semiconductor Complex
Limited (SCL) Mohali. In the year  1994-95 a budgetary provision of Rs . 27.18 crores has been kept fo r 
this purpose. Therefore, if the amount of Rs. 75 crores made ava ilable to SCL th rough supplementary
grants and the amount of Rs. 27.18 crores earmarked for SCL duri ng the year 1994-95 is excluded, then 
an increase of about Rs. 24 crores is reflected in the budgetary estimates for 1994-95 in the Plan sector. 
6. In the course of the submissi ons made by the Secretary and othe r officials of the :Department
before the Committee, the constant refrain was that the Department's  projected dema nd for its various
projects, both ongoing as well as new, had either been met only partially by the Planning Commission or
no allocations at all had b een made, particularly for new projects.  It was mentioned that for Technology 
Missions theprojected demand of th e Department during the Eighth Plan  was for an amount of Rs. 519
crores against which a meager am ount of Rs. 25 Crores was allocate d. Similarly, sixteen new projects
for 1994-95 involving a budgetary s upport of Rs. 19.87 crores were submitted, which related to: 
providing employment opportunities for women in electronic sector; R&D in agri-electronics; Computer 
Graphic Development; and Survey of IT industry in India. No allocations whatsoever were made for any
of these projects. 
7. The Committee, however, did not f eel satisfied with these arguments . It was clearly visible to the
Committee that even during the ye ars 1991-92 and 1992-93, the Department  had not been able to fully 
utilise the funds allocated for di fferent projects/scheme s. For example, duri ng the year 1991-92, the 
utilisation was Rs. 123.10 crores ( both Plan and Non-Plan) as agai nst the allocation of Rs. 137.25 
crores; and in 1992-93, it was Rs. 87.12 crores against Rs. 104.61 crores. In so far as the year 1993-94 is 
concerned, the same trend of under utilisation of al located funds appears to be continuing, though signs
of marginal improvement are there.  The reasons given by the Department  for the shortfalls in expendi-
ture in most of the cases are th at the saving was due to insufficie nt number of R&D projects of the
requisite quality (which the Committee found to be very surprising, cons idering the contrary situation in
most other areas that the Commit tee has examined, and this appear s to be a reflection of the poo r
promotional attitudes towards R&D in the Department) or release of less funds owing to delay in getting
approval of the competent authority (which again th e Committee found to be su rprising, considering the
powers available to scientific depa rtment). The Committee feels that in some of the cases there may be
genuine reasons for non-utilisation or under-utilisation of allocated f unds, but if this becomes recurring
feature in respect of use of budgeta ry allocations every year, it does not portray the Department in a
good li ght and will surel y result in some kind of hesitation to provide enhanced allocations in

consequence of which new initia tives may not succeed. The Commi ttee, therefore, strongly urges
upon the Department of Electronics to take urgent steps to improve  its performance in promotion o f
R&D and the use of budgetary allocations. 
8. The Committee finds that so me of the programmes for whic h major allocations have been
provided for in the Budget Estimates for 1994-95 are Standardisation Testing and Quality Control (Rs.
14.19 crores), Advanced Technology Programmes in Co mputer Networking (Rs.  12 crores), Special
Manpower Development Programme (25.20 crores), Technology Missions (Rs. 10.00 crores), Computer
Maintenance Corporation Limited (Rs. 10 crores), Society for Applied Micro Wave Electronics
Engineering and Research (SAMEER) (Rs. 5.65 cror es), Centre for Elect ronics Design Technology
(CEDT) (Rs. 3 crores), C-DAC (Rs. 6.80 crores),  Software Export Promot ion Programme (Rs. 4.60
crores) and Fifth Generation Com puters System (FGCS) Developm ent Programme (Rs. 8 crores).
Besides, a budgetary provision of Rs. 27.18 crores has been made to meet the expenditure on the
rebuilding of SCL, which, as coinmuni cated to the Committee, is expect ed to be  completed by the end
of 1994 
9. The Committee has observed that  the budgetary allocations for the standardisation Testing and
Quality Control Directorate (STQC) during the ye ars 1993-94 and 1994-95 have  been reduced consecu-
tively, whereas during the year 1992-93, the util isation for STQC was al most double the allotte d
amount. The Committee, therefore,  wanted to know the reason for lower allocations for STQC and
whether it no longer had the same priority which it hitherto had been having. The e xplanation given by
theDepartment was that the actual utilisation for STQC Directorate shown in the year 1992-93 was more 
than the allocated amount due to the fact that additional amount wa s requested in the Supplementary 
Grants for book adjustment of FRG Aid. In the B.E. for 1992-93, an amount of Rs 10.00 crores was 
projected for the book adjustment, but only Rs. 1.60 cr ores were allocated. Du e to the augmentation o f
the Project, the amount of Aid from the German si de for hardware was increased, and accordingly
additional funds were requested in Supplementary Grants. This was duly appr oved by Finance Division
of DOE and additional provision was made in the Supplementary Grants. 
  
10. In the year 1993-94, the BE of Rs. 17.13 crores included a provision of Rs. 10.78 crores for book 
adjustment of FRG aid. This provisi on was reduced to Rs. 7.00 crores in  R.E. as the Project which was
to end on 31.12.1993 has since been extended to 31.12.1995. 
  
11. This extension has been duly approved by the Government of I ndia, Department of Economic
Affairs and German Government. Accordingly the procurement of equipment has been replanned to
cover the extended period upto 31.12.1995. A provision of  Rs. 4.00 crores has been kept for the boo k
adjustment in the total provision of Rs. 11.90 crores. The amount provided in the German Aid will be
fully utilised till the end of the Project. 
  
12. In this connection the attention of the Depa rtment was also invite d by the Committee to the
contract awarded by EEC to KEMA, Holland to prepare a feasibility report for upgrading the STQC and
its laboratories in five years at pa r with the European Standards, a nd the visit undertaken by the experts
from KEMA to STQC Headquarters and selected ST QC laboratories during A ugust, 1993, whereafter a
draft upgradation plan has been prepared by KEMA. The Committee wanted to know as to whether any
further progress has been made in" this regard, and where the matter stands at present. The Committee
was told that the third and fina l phase of the appraisal by M/s KE MA for upgradation of seven STQC
Labs (the four ERTLs a nd the ETDCs at H yderabad, Bangalore and Madras ) has been completed. M/s
KEMA have prepared Draft upgradati on plan in the areas of: a) Safe ty, b) EMT/EMC, c) IECQ, d) EN
45001, and e) EN 450011/450012, On which STQC have sent  their comments for preparation of the
feasibility report. Three different scenarios A, B, & C have been propos ed by KEMA in  their report.
Scenario A includes upgradation of three ERTLs (East, West and North), ETDC Bangalore and STQC
Hqrs with a budget of ECUs 14.055 Million. Scenario B include s all the four ERTLs, three ETDCs
(Hyderabad, Bangalore and Madras) and STQC Hqrs with a budget of ECUs 18.567 Million. Scenario C

includes all the seven STQC labs with the additional support for upgradation of "Industrial
Calibration Service" with a tota l budget of ECUs 19.205 Mi llion. The duration of the project is five
years. Presentation of the feasibility report by KEMA to EC Hqrs is expected shortly. 
  
13. The Committee is of th e view that the area of STQC is of the greatest importance, considering
the imperative need for exports, wh ich call for products of the highes t quality and reliability, and the
increasing global competitiveness. However, Govern ment needs to have an overall national policy in
this area. The Committee has obser ved that the investments in diff erent areas of quality control unde r
different departments/agencies are highly disparate, and need to be harmonized. There is also the ques-
tion whether industry, being the bene ficiary, should not contribute to the investments and pay for the
services in a market oriented econo my. It would appear that at presen t, this Department is not obtaining
any Extra Budgetary Resource on this account. 
This, in the view of tile Committee is not corr ect. The Committee also feels that the progress o f
Centre for Electronics Test Engi neering (CETE), Calcutta under STQC has been tardy and this should
not be delayed any further. 
  
14. It was pointed out to the Secretary of the Department that, as reflected in the World Bank Report,
in the total software market of $250 billion, the share of co untries like India is not more than 3 to 4
%,but it is possible for India to raise software export from $660 Mi llion to $1 billion by 1996 if the
facility of high speed te lecommunication network and adequately trained manpow er is made available.
In the budgetary estimates for, 1994-95, however, the plan allocati on for Software Export Promotion
Programme has been reduced from Rs. 8 crores to just Rs. 4.60 crores, it appeared that the Department is
not concerned about raising softwa re export and earning valuable foreign exchange. The World Ban k
report has also laid empha sis On the need for adequately trai ned manpower, but the Department also
seems to have ignored this asp ect as the budgetary allocation fo r special manpower development
programme during the year 1994-95 ha s also been substantially reduced. In its reply, the Department 
listed some of the steps taken by it to boost softwa re exports such as remo val of double taxation on
software, exemption given to soft ware export earnings from income-t ax, the reduction in customs duty 
on the software import, rationalisation of export obligation formula for software exporters and import of
computers for training at reduced customs duty. It was also submitted, that Rs. 27.70 crores have already
been invested by the Government in setting up Softwa re Technology Parks as infr astructure facility and
for datacom. Besides Satellite Earth Stations have  already been commissione d at STPs at Bangalore,
Hyderabad and Thiruvananthapur am and are being commissione d at two more places namely
Bhubaneshwar and Gandhinagar. The software exports , as submitted to the Committee have shown
substantial growth over the past three years, the figures for the years 1991, 1992 & 1993 being worth Rs.
3,300, 5,000 & 7,000 million rupees respectively. The re ason for comparatively lesser allocation fo r
Software Export Promotion Program me during the year 1994-95 is th at an amount of Rs. 15.09 crores 
has already been utilised during the years 1991-92, 1992-93. 
15. In other words the Department will be utilising the entire Eighth  Five Year Pl an allocation fo r
Software Export Promotion Programme  during the first three years of Eighth Plan and it is not clea r
whether any, substantial allocations for this programme will  be available to the Department during the
remaining two years of this plan period. As regard s allocations for the Speci al Manpower Development
Programme, the explanation given by the Department is  that the budgetary plan  allocation for the yea r
1994-95 is at the same level .as th e revised estimate for the year 1993-94. Augmentation of this budget 
can be revised when the Revised Es timates are finalised. Si nce this project is li kely to be extended by
one more year, the budgetary provision should be avai lable for the extension period, which is likely to
spin off to 1995-96 and 1996-97. 
  
16. While the Committee appr eciates these steps in that dir ection, the net amount of earning 
through  software and that it has ta ken a number of share in the world of exports is  still very small and
more concerted action is re quired to raise India's soft ware market substantiall y u pwards and in this
Page 9 of 1914th Report of Committee on S&T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/14threport.htm

context the Department has to i nvolve industry on a larger scal e. The Committee is aware that
though large efforts have been  put into the development of software  technology parks, the major part o f
software exports-around 80% have been by a few large enterprises operating outside this system. 
  
17. The Committee finds that th e Department's scheme to la unch Eighth Technology Missions in
selected core areas is an ambiti ous programme but a budgetary provision  of just Rs. 10 crores has been
made for the year 1994-95. The Comm ittee accordingly wanted to kn ow as to how the Department 
would be able to achieve the ai ms of Technology Missions with th is amount. The Secretary of the
Department clarified that the Department had projec ted a demand of Rs. 519 crores for these
Technology Missions during the Eight h Plan period which are a mix of both fundamental as well as
Applied Research. Against this, however, Rs. 25 crores were sa nctioned for the whole project. In
comparison, however, other Science departments were given sizeable allocations and the increase was as
good as 100%. The reason for this Department getting only 55% increase was that Electronics was
considered an industry and not science & Technology Department. The matter was nonetheless pursued
with the planning Commission whic h held the view that the issue for revising the allocations upwards
would be taken up only when the mid-term review of the Eighth Plan was undertaken. It, however, 
suggested that the Depart ment could get additiona l resources through multil ateral or bi-lateral 
assistance. The Budget allocations as of now take into account inte rnal generation and extra budgetary
resources and what the Depa rtment is suggesting is that if they  are able to get aid from some othe r
sources, it should not be ta ken within the limit  of the Budget. Elaborating on this, the Secretary stated
that for Control Instrumentation the foreign aid expected during th e Eighth Plan was Rs. 7 crores, an d
they got Rs. 21 crores. In addition the UNDP extended assistance for their jute project. Besides, there
are organisations like SCICI and TDICI which too are extending assistance. SAMEER, for example, has
got an assistance of Rs. 4.5 crores. This type of external assistance may, for example, not be reflected in
the Budget. 
  
18. The Committee feels that in an era when ra pid technological advances, particularly in the
Electronics Sector are taking place and the need for country is to make quantum jump in this vital sector,
the Department's requirements for vi able projects have to be met s ubstantially and resource constraints
should not hamper the pr ogress which the country can make. In th is context, the Co mmittee would like
to reiterate its earlier recommenda tion that such of the missions as are of a crucial nature should be
identified. There should be clear cut and detailed project proposals on these, including investments, time 
frames and other agencies which would collaborate.  The Committee is not satisfied that the present
Technology Missions of the Department have been developed in this manner. 
  
19. The Committee has noted that there has been substantial in crease in financial outlay fo r
Advanced Technology Programme in  Computer Networking and Fift h Generation Computer System
(FGCS) Development programme as compared to the allocations for these programmes during the
previous year (1993-94). For the former programme during the ye ar 1994-95, a provision of Rs. 12 
crores has been made whereas during the year 1993-94, the amount ea rmarked for this programme was
just Rs. 1.50 crores. Similarly for the later programme viz FGCS budge tary allocation of Rs. 8 crores
has been provided during th e year 1994-95 as against just Rs. 50 lakhs during 1993-94. Asked to give 
reasons, it was explai ned by the Department th at ERNET (ATPCN ) allocation for 1994-95 is Rs. 12 
crores, out of this Rs. 10 crores is toward book ad justment for transfer of  UNDP equipment as pe r
mandatory requirements for the terminal year of UNDP funding. The budgetary support for the project is
thus only Rs. 2 crores. It is not cl ear to the Committee what exactly th is project will achieve and why it
is needed in the context of many other networks of  NIC, CMC, INFLIBNET etc.  that have been set up.
There is need for more coordination in respect of networks  before public funds ar e allocated to more o f
them. 
  
  
Page 10 of 1914th Report of Committee on S&T

20. Knowledge Based Computer Sy stem (KBCS) project funded by UNDP has been closed on 31st
March, 1994. It is not clear  to the Committee Why this has been  done and what will happen to all the
expertise generated through this in an important area.  It is apparently propos ed in initiate a Second
Phase Project with a total cost of  Rs. 5 crores. In addition to this  the Department has also done boo k
adjustment of Rs. 7.9 crores for the transfer of title of equipment purchased from UNDP. 
  
21. The Committee is not happy with this situati on as higher allocations are sought giving the
impression as if the proj ects are of a crucial natu re, but in reality substa ntial amounts therefrom are
diverted towards book adjustments. 
  
22. The Committee has noted that pho tonics has been iden tified as a thrust area demanding special
attention by the Steering Group on Science and Technology for the formulation of Eighth Plan as well as
by the erstwhile Science A dvisory Council to the P.M. The allo cation of an amount of just Rs. 1.70
crores for the year 1994-95 for th e Photonics Developm ent Programme, however , does not appear to
reflect the importance the Department attaches to this area. On being asked about the reasons for smaller
allocations for this sector, the explanation give n was that in view of  limited funds, Photonics
Development Programme has been prioritised and pursued. At pres ent, emphasis has been given to
develop projects and programmes wh ich are in priority areas and in and around institutions where
discerned capabilities and infrastructure already exists and are of immediate relevance to industry. These
have been supported for specific goals essentially to consolidate the efforts in the country. In view of the
limited funds, major initiatives c ould not be taken in the new emer ging areas. The Committee finds that
the efforts of the Depart ment relating to the Photonics Devel opment Programme, appear at several
different places in the demand for gran ts and it is, therefore,  difficult to discern an  integrated picture o f
the thrust of the Department in this area. 
  
23. R & D is an important area in the field of Electronics and the Committee wanted to know from
the Secretary of the Department as to how much of the total amount was being spent on R & D projects
as a whole. The Committee was informed that the total amount on R & D projec ts earmarked during the
year 1994-95 was to the t une of Rs. 67.43 crores. Th e Secretary also informed  the Committee that the
Department looks on R & D projects  from two angles. Firstly, whatever technology is developed should
be used. In other words, only thos e projects are recommended which have a ready user. Secondly, the
Department expects the contribution to  come from either user Department  or a personal us er so that the
small capital of the Department acts as a catalyst to attract investment . It is not clear to the Committee
why this argument has not been applied to the STQC programmes. 
  
24. A question was posed to the Secretary as to whether the Department was getting the right type of
projects from the educational institutions. The repl y was that the Department  has started a number o f
programmes and interacted  with Electronic Industry Associati ons such as ELCINA, CETMA, IEEMA.
The Department has got Proposals from Punsami indu stry for aluminum capac itors and other proposals
are also coming. This, of course, does not relate to educational instituti ons. It was then stated that the
Department as a matter of fact wants to put in every professional college teaching Science & Technol-
ogy as well as engaged in R &D one computer at least to link it with the Telecom Network and Satellite
Communication; every college will th en have the facility of documen t transfer and the access to data
base. Of the amount allocated for        R & D 60% of the Department's  budget goes to meet the
requirements of applied research and 40% to fundame ntal research. The project s are selected such that
India has an advantage parallel pr ocessing and Photonics etc. The in tention of the Department is to
strengthen the country's infrastructure in order to apply indigenous technology effectively. 
  
25. The Committee feels that out of  the total Plan outlay of the Department for the year 1994-95 
which is Rs. 140.10 crores, almost 50%  appears to be spent on R & D projects, but the performance o f
the Department up till now in the R & D sector has not been ver y commendable. The exce ptions are
Page 11 of 1914th Report of Committee on S&T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/14threport.htm

major activities like on parallel processing SA MEER, HVDC. No major projects in the hardware
sector appear to be on the anvil as may reassure the country about Department's playing the role o f
makingIndia a global player in term s of either productivity  or competitiveness. As pointed out by the
Secretary of the Department himself Electronics is a strategically important area and as an instrument o f
economic development; it has, therefore, to be taken up as a national priority. The Department, however,
has failed to realise its objectives, only partly because of lack of resour ces. Largely this is because of a
lack of vision relating to the role  of technology in area of hitech with rapid change and obsolescence
where there is need for self reliance. The Department, no doubt, has endeavoured to establish linkage
with industry but the industry does not seem to have  been very enthusiastic about using the technology
development efforts of the Department. On the contrary the response fr om Government Mini-
stries/Departments such as Rural Development, Water Resources, Public Enterprises, Women and Child
Development, Family Welfare, Agri culture, to use its inputs seem s to be more encouraging. The
Secretary of the Department made a forceful plea before the Committee that the Department had requisi-
te technological inputs and if an amount of Rs. 1000 cr ores is spent on steel, cement, fertilisers, paper,
etc. return would be as much as 5000 crores of rupees. If that is so  then the Committee is of the view
that the Department must make an analysis as to where it has"  gone wrong. This is, however, not to
belittle Department's achievements such as of the Centre for Materials for Electronics Technology (C-
MET), a society under the Depart ment, which include the Successful Development of Silicon
Tetrachloride for Optical Fibre A pplications, POC-13 for Solar Cell  Applications, Barium Carbonate
and Strontium Carbonate for Electro Ceramic Industry. Efforts are now under way to transfer these tech-
nologies to the Industry. By the turn of the century the import of Electronics material is expected to be at
the level of 40% as compared to the present level of 80%. Besides, as many as 17 projects are now under
development. 
26. In the course of the scrutiny of the budgetary demands of the Department it has come to the
notice of the Committee that the allocations during the year 1994-95 for Rural Electronics an  R & D 
Agricultural Electronics have been substantially brought down as compared to those for these
programmes during the year 1993-94. Rs. 50 lakhs we re allocated during 1993-94 for Rural Electronics 
whereas in 1994-95, the amount allotted is just  Rs. 10 lakhs. Similarly, for R & D Agricultural
Electronics Rs. 20 lakhs were earma rked during 1993-94 and no provision has altogether been made in 
the Budget Estimates for 1994-95. Conf ronted on this question, it was explained that the Department 
had projected a demand of Rs. 1.60 crores for Rural Electronics ag ainst which indications were given at
the time of discussions with the Pl anning Commission that the provision wi ll be kept at the level of last
year viz. Rs. 50 lakhs but finally it was reduced to Rs. 10 lakhs. None theless, quite a few proposals are,
at present, stated to be under Financial Adviso r's consideration, which would require funds to be
released. However, with the provision of Rs. 10 lakhs as it stands on date, th e Department may have to
take a decision either not  to support these proposal s or to suitably enhance the budgetary provision. As
regards the R &D Agricultural Electronics, the De partment submitted to the Committee that the
Planning Commission applied its own inter-se priority and decided not to allocate any amount for this
programme in 1994-95. The Committee fails to understand as to how th e Department would achieve its
objective of bringing the benefit of electronics to ev ery walk of life and every part of the country if the
rural sector is ignored in  this way and even smaller allocations  are not given. The Committee therefore,
strongly recommends that in the matt er of allocations the Electronics projects for the rural sector should
be given high priority. 
  
27. The Committee has observed that among the ne w projects submitted by the Department to
Planning Commission one related to employment opportunities for women in electronic sector for which
an allocation of Rs. 10 crores was sought. In this c ontext, a point was raised about the serious crisis
being faced by 13 women's co-operati ves in Kerala which had an em ployment force of 700 persons and
there was fear of their becoming jobless because selling their product was a big problem, there being no
buyers. The Secretary expl ained the position by saying that the solution to the problem lay in an
encouraging private companies which had a foot-hold in the market to use the product of such women's
Page 12 of 1914th Report of Committee on S&T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/14threport.htm

co-operatives as an input and for that it was necessa ry to give incentives to such private companies. 
For example, in China and Japan large and ancillar y industries work together and the necessity is to
evolve similar strategies in our country. In so far as women's co-operatives in Kerala are concerned, they 
have enjoyed excise duty concession, but it has lately  been withdrawn for the reason that they started
producing under some other brand na me. The matter has been taken up by the Department with the
Ministry of Finance. The Committe e feels that it is a laudable obj ective to make women a strong wor k
force in the electronics se ctor, and pursuant to that objective it is all the more necessary that suitable
linkages are established with th e industries to use the produce being manufactured by them. This
proposition can be viable and mean ingful only if due patronage on duty concessions are given to such
co-operatives. 
  
28.  The Department of El ectronics has not only to make an anal ysis of the problems and define the
reasons for the difficulties encount ered, but play an important promot ional role in achieving solutions.
While the Department of Electronics seems to have a large technical staff of high quality, the impression
that the Committee has gathered in its discussion is more of efforts of an administrative nature, as would
be expected from a regular Governme nt department concerned with i ndustry rather than with science
and technology. There is need to cha nge this approach. The Department  also does not have a full time
Secretary in contrast to the earli er period when this area had a high powered Electronics Commission.
The Committee notes that the funding for majo r areas of R & D under National Radar Council,
Technology Development Council, Na tional Microelectronics Council  (NMC), EMDC is relatively
small. 
  
29. The Department has allotted the re sources available to it significantly on infrastructural facilities
rather than on R&D and links with  sectors powerful in electronics like DRDO , ISRO, Department o f
Atomic Energy appear to be wea k. The Performance Budget does not i ndicate in clear terms the actual
utilisation of allocated funds which would give a picture as to how the money has been spent and results
achieved. It gives just details of the project and does not highlight the actual physical targets laid out and
achieved. The Department of El ectronics aims at India becomi ng a significant global player in
electronics. The Committee does not see in the progr ammes of the Department  presented to it, any
integrated approach to achieve this. In the absence of such a vision  and major self-reliant strength in the 
country progress towards this is unlikely. The Commit tee would urge Government  to lay greater stress
on this area of opportunity.

COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR)
 
12.       The Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR), a premier autonomous Research & Development
 organization, is a multi-disciplinary, multi-locational set-up, comprising 38 laboratories and 47 regional centres, has
 completed sixty-three years of its existence. Nourished, fostered and supported, since its inception, CSIR is now recognized
 internationally as an institution, which is moving speedily towards achieving global excellence without diluting local
 relevance. In India, it symbolizes a culture that links science with society through technology and industrial infrastructure.
 
13.       The detailed functions assigned to the CSIR are as follows:
(i)
                  Promotion, guidance and coordination of scientific and industrial research in India, including the institution and
 financing of specific researches;
(ii)                Establishment or development and assistance to special institutions or departments of existing institutions for
 scientific study of problems affecting particular industries and trade;
(iii)               Establishment and award of research studentships and fellowships;
(iv)              Utilization of the results of the researches conducted under the auspices of the Council towards the development
 of industries in the country and the payment of a share of royalties arising out of the development of the results of
 researches to those who are considered as having contributed towards the pursuits of such research;

15.       The creation of major and innovative knowledge networks across and beyond CSIR laboratories, is a key feature of

16.       This year also saw an all-time high in CSIR’s journey so far as science papers, patents and earnings are concerned.  In

17.       The guiding principle for CSIR during the Tenth Five Year Plan is to provide scientific industrial R&D that maximizes
 the economic, environmental and societal benefits for the people of India.  The Tenth Five Year Plan of CSIR and the Annual
 Plans have been formulated with the background of 8% growth rate envisaged by the Planning Commission and Government
 policy to invest 2% of GDP on Science & Technology.

22.       National Laboratory scheme is operated through 38 National Laboratories and 47 field Centres. The research
 programmes/project/activities of the National Laboratories have been categorized into thirteen major socio-economic sectors
 viz.  Aerospace, Biology and Biotechnology, Chemicals, Earth Resources and Natural Hazards Mitigation, Ecology &
 Environment, Electronics and Instrumentation, Energy, Food & Food processing, Health Care, Drugs & Pharmaceuticals,
 Housing & Construction, Information Dissemination and Products, Leather, Materials, Metals, Minerals and Manufacturing.
 
23.       Basic research is the major source of advancement of knowledge in science and provides the foundation for
 development of newer generic technologies for the future. CSIR has to continuously upgrade its core competencies and
 research areas to be planned so as to provide the needed strength for successfully competing in emerging technologies for the
 years to come. The core competencies to be continuously developed are in the areas of aerospace science & technology,
 modern biology and biotechnology, chemistry, geophysics, oceanography, material science, computer aided studies, expert
 system, parallel computation etc. Since the CSIR infrastructure was built or acquired more than thirty years ago, selective
 refurbishment and renovation of existing infrastructure will be carried out during the 2005-2006.

 to meet the ongoing and new commitments of the 38 National Laboratories and its out reach centers which undertake

 Plan CSIR seeks to foster the organizational value of excellence in science, global competitiveness in technology based on
 high science local relevance in tune with socio-cultural and economic ethos of the people and innovation ranging in all

 in network mode and this increase is essentially to provide support to the approved projects during the Tenth Plan. The Non-
plan increase of  Rs. 8.86 crore is to partly meet normal increase under salary and other maintenance expenditure.

INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY AND TECHNOLOGY MANAGEMENT
30.       The objective of the scheme is to enhance the volume and value of Intellectual Property (IP) generated by CSIR and to
 share the best innovation and technology management practices organizationally and with the Indian S&T community at
 large. The volume of IP rights secured by CSIR has greatly increased over the time. The major task, however, is to realize
 adequate and appreciable value from the IPR.
 
31.       It is also felt that necessary skills and knowledgebase of those in CSIR engaged in the IPR game need to be
 refurbished, particularly, in some still unresolved issues such as  ‘traditional knowledge’, ‘genomic sequences’, ‘copyright on
 the Net’ etc. It is proposed to advise the policymakers appropriately on the new development and changes proposed in
 international IP rights arena.
 
32.       It has been informed that CSIR’s  position in IP rights arena is quite noteworthy. CSIR has made Intellectual Property 
 as its pursuit, for it continued to be at number one position securing Patents in India and abroad. During 2001-2004, CSIR
 was granted 390 patents in USA, a feat unmatched by any other Indian firm or organization in the country and it has filed
 1223 Foreign and 827 Indian Patents. It is thus by far the largest patent holder in India and ranked at first position along with
 Samsung in PCT filing from developing countries in the year 2002 and ranked third in 2003. It is expected that CSIR would
 be able to file 400 patents in India and 500 patents abroad during 2004-05.
 
33.       For the first time, CSIR instituted the Diamond Jubilee Invention Awards for school going children upto the age of 18.
 A two tier rigorous selection procedure was followed and fourteen inventions were selected for five categories of prizes. To
 protect IP rights, provisional patent applications have been filed for these inventors.
 
34.       In order to refurbish skills within CSIR community a series of awareness workshops/ training courses were organized.
 Significant ones were Capacity building in the area of IP management, Conference cum workshop on the theme Leveraging
 Intellectual Property for Organizational Strategy, advanced IP training program on Negotiating, Contracting and Valorization
 of IP, and International seminar on International Enactments and Practices on Intellectual Property Rights.
 
35.       To expose the participants to the world's current practices on IPR and to enable them to plan their strategies in the new
 IPR regime, the joint effort brought together a team of internationally renowned experts. The seminar provided a unique
 opportunity to the participants to closely interact with Experts from different establishments like Patent County Court, U.K.,
 European Patent Office and Patent Attorneys of leading IPR firms from USA, UK and Japan.For the first time in the country,

INFRASTRUCTURE RENOVATION AND REFURBISHMENT
 
41.       The CSIR has translated the S&T goals into viable, low risk and profitable choices. These are multi-location/multi-
institution programme with well-defined tasks. The tasks identified in each programme and their linkages form a matrix of
 inter-related milestones and activities with identified inter-disciplinary teams at different locations/institutions. Managing
 information and computational requirements at various levels in the execution of these milestones/activities is the key to
 success. Therefore, effective and timely access to computing resources across laboratories/disciplines becomes imperative in
 the management of these milestones/activities.
In order to expedite research through network approach the vital components are:
(i)         Strengthening of computation and data resources'
(ii)        ICT support to S&T programmes and R&D areas
(iii)       Inter-laboratory networking
(iv)       Cross boundary information and compute resource sharing
(v)        Information access (intra and inter) laboratory
(vi)       Utilisation of generated knowledge
(vii)      ICT Infrastructure in Labs
(viii)      Monitoring and assessment of CSIR Networked Projects
(ix)       E-enabled uniform system for business development, inventory control, purchases, personnel management and human
 resource development
(x)        Information system to support insight to the R&D issues
 
42.       These requirements necessitate that CSIR set-up an efficient Scientific Knowledge Management System by creating a
 CSIR wide Grid consisting of functional virtual Grids related to areas of concern. These virtual sub-Grids may consist of
 labs/institutes, where specialists and data together form a complete resource in an area of research. These may be managed
 and used systematically to conduct globally competitive R&D.

 Communication Technology (ICT) Infrastructure, renovation & Refurbishment of National Laboratories.  The ICT

 researchers and work on real time and online basis.

 intensive products.
                 (viii)   To promote and strengthen consultancy capabilities for domestic use and export requirements.
                    (ix)   To support and use mechanisms, both national and international, towards transfer of technology, both within and
 outside the country.
                      (x)   Generate endogenous capacities for the development and utilization of digital information resources for providing
 inputs to scientific & industrial research in the country.
 
47.       In reply to a question regarding the reasons for the reduced allocation at R.E. stage during the year 2004-2005, the
 Committee has been informed that after the Expenditure Finance Committee approved the TPDU programme in March 2004,
 the operationalization of new scheme at the level envisaged at the time of Budget preparation took time. The financial
 progress in the first two quarters of the year was on the lower side, as the focus during the period was on conceptualization
 and evaluation of different components of the new programme. It involved organization of meetings of experts, to identify
 areas of operation, setting up and organization of meetings, technical advisory committees, advertising of programmes for
 inviting proposals, preparation of brochures, evaluation of the on-going projects, etc.  Thus the expenditure upto the third
 quarter was less.  In the fourth quarter only one-third of the B.E. has been allowed to be spent as per the instructions of the
 Ministry of Finance.  The R.E. was, therefore, reduced to                   Rs. 10.23 crores.
 
48.       The Committee feels that the Department should initiate action to coordinate the research work undertaken by the
 CSIR laboratories and the industrial houses and an atmosphere of co-operation should be generated so that both stand to
 benefit from each  other’s expertise.
 
DEVELOPING NEW GENERATION FUELS
 
49.       The Committee has been informed that CSIR has initiated research activities in the areas of new alternate fuels. 
 Through a network programme on Developing new generation fuel and lubricants, research activities are directed towards
 development of Gas to Liquid Technologies for Dimethyl ether and Fischer Tropsch Fuels; Liquid Fuels and Ethanol
 Production from Biomass; Catalysts for Atmospheric Residue Processing; Performance Evaluation of New Generation
 Automotive Fuels to meet emission norms.
 
50.       Under Hydrogen fuel the research activities are on Thermo-catalytic conversion of Biomass to Hydrogen;
 pyrolysis/decompositon of methane to Hydrogen; application of Hydrogen in Internal Combustion(IC) engine by developing
 Compressed Natural Gas(CNG) Hydrogen Blend and Hydrogen-Ethanol blend.
 
51.       A project on PEM (Proton Exchange Membrane) based fuel cells was initiated under NMITLI with focus on (i) Fuel
 processor for the production of hydrogen; (ii) Cell stack assembly; and (iii) Control & instrumentation systems.  One-
demonstration unit of 5KW based on H
2  reformer with Liquefied Petroleum Gas LPG as fuel has been installed at National
 Chemical Laboratories.  Efforts are on to develop other types of fuel cells.
 
52.       In the area of Biofuels the activities are conversion of non-edible oils like Jatropha curcas, Salvadora, Pongamia,
 Mahdhuca Indica etc. to methyl ester (biodiesel) and its performance evaluation on IC engines; chemical transesterification of
 Oils to Bio Diesel and recovery of By-product; process development of biodiesel (ethyl esters) of jatropha curcas and its
 evaluation on IC engines and field trials on diesel cars; recovery of hydrocarbons from biomass & their conversion to liquid
