 fuels; pyrolysis of Biomass and Biomass to Ethanol; diesel Blends and Emulsions; gas to liquid Fuels.
 
53.       With reference to Jatropha, the Secretary, DSIR has informed that National Botanical Research Institute (NBRI) is
 promoting model plantation at various sites; making genetic selection for superior strains that have high seed output and high
 oil content; and optimization of extraction, storage, filtration and purification of oil.  It is also developing site-specific strains
 and extraction of biofuel.
 
54.       The Central Salt and Marine Chemicals Research Institute has successfully cultivated elite varieties of Jatropha
 Curcas on marginal land to assess practically realizable seed yields.  Orchards are simultaneously being raised in Orissa
 (Huma & Mohuda villages) and Gujarat (Chorvadla village) to make elite germplasm available in sufficient quantity so that
 cultivation can subsequently be taken up in larger (100-200 hectares) tracts of wasteland.
 
55.       A simplified process has also been developed for production of biodiesel from the oil complying with Euro 3
 specifications for free fatty acid methyl ester.  The biodiesel has been evaluated at Daimler Chysler AG and found to be
 matching to all specifications.  Two C-class Mercedes Benz cars with our neat biodiesel are successful running.   The
 biodiesel in neat form and also as blend was evaluated in tractor engine by Massey Ferguson.
 
56.       A project on “Genetic Improvement of Jatropha curcas for Drought Tolerance and Oil Yield” has been initiated under
 the NMITLI Scheme that aims at selection and improvement of J. curcas germplasm for developing plant types characterized
 for higher survival, adaptability to drought and salinity, high seed and oil yield and optimization of low-cost agro-
technologies for different agroclimatic regions.  This will help address the major issue for making jatropha oil an economically
 feasible alternative to petroleum diesel.
 
57.       The Committee notes that the research regarding biofuels is still at a research stage and commercial production is yet
 to begin. However, the initiative taken by the Department to produce biofuel, specially from ‘Jatropa Curcus ‘ plant is
 commendable in view of the fact that large tracts of wasteland in the country can be utilized and the farmers can benefit a lot
 from the commercial production of this plant. The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be made towards
 early commercialization of the technology, which will benefit the farmers as well as the consumers.  
 
NATIONAL GEOPHYSICAL RESEARCH INSTITUTE (NGRI), HYDERABAD
 
58.       The Committee is happy to learn that NGRI is developing a special groundwater management strategy for coastal fresh
 water aquifers, endangered by saline incursion and in certain industrial belts for mitigation of groundwater pollution.
 
59.       The Committee is further happy to know that NGRI under a global attempt has taken a lead to prepare a Seismic
 Hazard Map covering the entire Himalayan Belt and Seismically active regions of India, under Global Seismic Hazard
 Assessment Programme (GSHAP).
 
60.       Apart from this, NGRI as a premier institute is handling considerable original researches in engineering geophysics,
 redox-history of the planet and in several important areas of radioactive and geochemical properties of earth.
 
61.       The Committee, however, has noted that in a few prominent areas where research is necessary to understand the
 anatomy of earth’s inner core, the Institute has not so far undertaken any scientific investigation which are as follows:
a)
                  Heat generating capacity of Radiogenic isotopes of potassium which may  power convection in the core of the
 earth and drive the magnetic field in the earth’s crusts;
b)                  The earth’s dynamo action; and
c)                  Geo-neutrino picture of earth’s interior for its better comprehension.
 
62.       The Institute has stated that since geo-neutrino study is not within the purview of NGRI’s research activities, the
 Institute has not attempted any research work in this field.  The Committee, however, sees no reason why such an important
 study has not been kept within the purview of the research activities of the Institute while in other parts of the world the study
 of geo-neutrino imaging of earth crusts is being given primary importance.  The Committee feels that geo-neutrino imaging
 can give vital information about earth’s core that may prove to be extremely useful for Institute’s preparation of Seismic
 Hazard Map on which the Institute has already taken a lead under a global attempt.
 
63.       Moreover, some neglected areas like the understanding of the heat generating capacity of Radiogenic Isotopes and
 greater understanding about earth’s dynamo action may be of considerable help for the Institute to establish a perfect
 intelligibility of the anatomy of earthquake and its accurate prediction which is still eluding the scientists the world over.

ii)                   Geo-neutrino imaging of earth’s interior; and

 anatomy of heat flow from core to mantle, driving convection motion in the outer core that could be linked with generation of
 earthquake.
 
NATIONAL RESEARCH DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION (NRDC)
 
65.       The Committee has been informed that the National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) was established in
 December 1953 as a company, under Section 25 of the Companies Act to commercialise the Research and Development
 results of publicly funded R&D institutions as well as to promote the growth of indigenous technology.  The Corporation
 provides comprehensive technology transfer services and acts as a catalyst for transforming innovative research into
 marketable industrial products. NRDC is a unique organization in that and it is the only public enterprise wholly dedicated to
 transfer of technologies from R&D laboratories to industry. During the past five decades of its existence, the Corporation has
 developed strong links and network with various R&D organizations in the country as well as abroad for transfer of
 technologies.  Its operations cover the entire spectrum of industrial technologies ranging from chemicals to metallurgy,
 mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, electronics, biotechnology and so on.  Its promotional and commercial
 objectives are:
                              (i)      Promotion and commercialization of inventions;
                            (ii)      Commercialisation of Laboratory Know-How;
                           (iii)       Financing Technology development;
                          (iv)      Development and Commercialisation of Rural Technology;
                            (v)      Promotion of Export of Technology; and
                          (vi)      Dissemination of Information on Technology Transfer.
 
66.       The Committee has been informed that the budgetary Plan allocation for NRDC is Rs. 1.00 crore for the year 2005-06. 
 It is a premier organization engaged in development, promotion and also acts as a catalyst for transforming innovative
 research into marketable industrial products. Keeping in view the specialized activities of NRDC, the Committee feels that
 the present allocation is too meagre. The Committee, therefore recommends that the Plan allocation should be substantially
 increased from the present Rs. 1.00 crore to at least Rs. 4.00 crores.
PROMOTION OF SCIENTIFIC TEMPER
67.       The Committee has been informed that the CSIR has been organizing, from time to time, training and demonstration
 programmes, workshops, exhibitions and participating in “Kisan Melas’, to disseminate its developed and available
 ‘knowledgebase’.  It would further accelerate these efforts through self-motivated training programmes at identified village &
 taluk levels in association with concerned developmental agencies. In addition, CSIR also published 2188 papers in journals
 for promotion of Scientific temper.
68.       In a country where a sizable population is barely literate, inculcating a scientific temperament and rational outlook is
 not an easy task. However, to improve the quality of life of the people and removing backwardness and superstitious thinking,
 science popularization is of utmost importance. Therefore, the Committee feels that the Department should not only focus on
 the transfer of technologies but also disseminate basic scientific knowledge to the people through various popular media like
 Television, Documentary Films, frequent melas and demonstrations throughout the country.
69.       After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research and assessing the
 various programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs.1557.00
 crores, as sought by the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research for the year 2005-2006 under Demand No.83, may be
 approved.

 variation in them.  The Committee is not convinced with the reply of the Department in this regard and is of the considered
 view that the Department needs to evolve a mechanism to maintain  uniform pace of expenditure, to the extent possible,
 throughout the year.                                                              (Para 11)

REPORT
The spectacular achievements in the new frontier technology of Space during the last three decades have firmly established
 its capability for bringing out a socio-economic revolution in the world because of its potential to transform even stagnant
 societies in a most cost effective and timely manner.  With the unique ability of a Space platform to provide a synoptic view of the
 universe in the entire electro-magnetic spectrum, Space exploration has been virtually extended to the very end of the universe and
 the very beginning of time, providing for the first time a breath taking glimpse of interplanetary space, solar planetary system and
 the deeper space filled with hitherto unknown exotic celestial objects like quasars, pulsars, neutron stars, X-ray stars and black

 operationally extend over communication, meteorology, television broadcast, education, agriculture, industrial growth, resource
 management, environmental pollution, disaster mitigation, flood and drought management, health and entertainment virtually
 touching every fact of human endeavour.
2.         The primary objective of the Indian Space Programme is to promote the development and application of space
 technology and space science for the socio-economic benefit of the nation through establishment of operational space services
 in a self-reliant manner. The main thrust areas of the programme are:
§                     Satellite-based communication for various applications.
§                     Satellite-based resources survey and management and environmental monitoring.
§                     Meteorological applications
§                     Development and operationalisation of indigenous satellite launch vehicles and  associated ground segment
 for providing these space-based services.
 
3.         Government of India set-up the Space Commission and the Department of Space (DOS) in 1972.  The Department is
 responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space Commission.  These are carried out through the Indian   Space
 Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Grant-in-aid institutions viz., National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), Physical
 Research Laboratory (PRL), National MST Radar Facility (NMRF) and North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC).
4.      The Secretariat of the Department of Space and the Headquarters of ISRO are located in Bangalore.   Programme Offices
 at ISRO Headquarters co-ordinate the overall programmes like satellite communication, earth observation, launch vehicle,
 space science, space industry development, disaster management support, international co-operation, publications and public
 relations, budget and economic analysis and human resource development.
5.         The major Centres, Units and establishments of ISRO/DOS, responsible for carrying out research and development
 activities as well as for undertaking the various projects and programmes, are given below:
§
         Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, provides the technology base for the country’s
 indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development.
§         Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities at Bangalore, Thiruvananthapuram and Mahendragiri,
 is responsible for development of liquid propulsion and cryogenic propulsion systems for satellite and launch
 vehicles
§
         Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the launch base.  Also, it provides
 the facilities for processing of solid rocket motors.
§         ISRO Satellite Centre (ISAC), Bangalore, is entrusted with the prime responsibility for the satellite development. 
 The Laboratory for Electro-Optics Systems (LEOS), Bangalore of ISAC has the responsibility for development
 and production of electro optical sensors for satellites.  ISRO Radar Development Unit (ISRAD), Bangalore of
 ISAC has the responsibility to develop the Radar systems for ISRO and other emerging radar systems for national
 development.
§
         Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad carries out research and development in space applications as well
 as development of application payloads.
§         Development and Educational Communication Unit (DECU), Ahmedabad is involved in the conception,
 definition, planning and socio/techno-economic evaluation of development communication programmes.

SATELLITE NAVIGATION
36.       The Committee was informed that  the Ministry of Civil Aviation has decided to implement an indigenous Satellite-
Based Regional GPS Augmentation System also known as space-Based Augmentation System (SBAS) as part of the Satellite-
Based Communications, Navigation and Surveillance (CNS)/Air Traffic Management (ATM) plan for civil aviation.   A
 national plan for satellite navigation including implementation of Technology Demonstration System (TDS) over the Indian
 airspace as a proof of concept, has been prepared jointly by Airports Authority of India (AAI) and ISRO.  The TDS is the first
 step towards implementing an operational SBAS system.
37.       The Indian SBAS is planned to be implemented in three phases: Technology Demonstration System, Initial
 Experimental Phase and Final Operational Phase.  The Indian SBAS is expected to bridge the gap between the European
 EGNOS (European Geo Stationary Navigation Overlay System) and the Japanese MSAS (MTSAT Space Augmentation
 System) to provide seamless navigation of aircraft from west to east and vice-versa.  When implemented, the Indian SBAS 
 system will play an important role in the introduction of satellite based navigation services in the Asia Pacific region.  The
 Indian SBAS system has been given an acronym-GPS And GEO Augmented Navigation (GAGAN).  The first navigation
 payload is being fabricated and it is proposed to be flown on the GSAT-4 satellite expected to be launched in 2006-07
38.       The Committee feels that the phase when India can become a major hub in air navigation and be able to operate air
 services from India, there is a greater need for superior space based navigation and as India is  placed at the axis of routes
 connecting Europe with Southeast Asia and  by having an indigenous Satellite-Based Regional GPS Augmentation System
 can gain both in terms of market and strategic importance.
SPACE CAPSULE RECOVERY EXPERIMENT (SRE)
39.       The Committee was informed that Space Capsule Recovery Experiment (SRE) is intended for demonstrating the
 capability to recover an orbiting space capsule. The experiment envisages the development of a 500 kg recoverable capsule
 and the associated technologies. SRE is intended to test reusable thermal protection system, navigation, guidance and control,
 hypersonic aero-thermodynamics, management of communication blackout, deceleration and floatation system, recovery
 operations, etc. SRE will be launched as a copassenger of CARTOSAT-2 on board PSLV during the second half of 2005-06.
40.       SRE comprises aero-thermo structure, spacecraft platform, deceleration and floatation system and micro-gravity
 payloads. It has a sphere-cone-flare configuration with a spherical nose of about 0.5 m radius, base diameter of 2 m and 1.6 m
 height. The capsule is made of mild steel. The parachute, pyro devices, avionics packages of triggering unit and sequencer,
 telemetry and tracking system, sensors for measurement of system performance parameters are placed inside SRE capsule.
41.       After its launch by PSLV, SRE will remain in orbit for a few days during which it will be used to perform experiments
 in micro-gravity environment. The capsule will then be de-orbited and it reenters the earth's atmosphere.  On reentry, after
 initial aerodynamic braking, a parachute system will reduce the touch down velocity. SRE will splashdown in the Bay of
 Bengal, about 140 km east of Sriharikota coast. A floatation system will keep SRE afloat and enables its recovery.
42.       During the year, three airdrop tests have been conducted successfully using aircraft for testing deceleration and
 flotation system. Three drop tests of the instrumented SRE were successfully conducted using a helicopter during June-
August, 2004 from SDSC SHAR.
43.       The Committee feels that the success of this method would save a lot of costs for the nation as the single space capsule
 could be used again for different experiments.

CHANDRAYAAN-1 
49.       Chandrayaan-1 is India’s first scientific mission to moon to be undertaken during 2007-08.   The mission is aimed at
 expanding the scientific knowledge about the moon, upgrading India’s technological capability and providing challenging
 opportunities for planetary research to the younger generation.
50.       The scientific objectives of Chandrayaan-1 are the high resolution remote sensing of the moon in the visible, near
 infrared low energy X-ray and high-energy X-ray regions for preparing a 3- dimensional atlas of regions of scientific interest
 with a high spatial and altitude resolution of 5-10 m and chemical mapping of the entire lunar surface for elements such as
 magnesium, aluminum, silicon, calcium, iron and titanium with a spatial resolution of 10 km and elements of high atomic
 numbers (z), such as 
222 radon, uranium, thorium and gadolinium with a spatial resolution of 20 km.
51.       The spacecraft for Chandrayaan-1 will be a 1.5 m cuboid with a dry weight of 525 kg in its final lunar orbit.  It will be
 3-axis stabilized and powered by solar array generating 750 W of electrical power.  It will have a Lithium-Ion battery back up
 for operation during eclipse.  The spacecraft will use a bipropellant propulsion system for transferring it from GTO to lunar
 orbit and for orbit and attitude maintenance.
52.       PSLV will launch the spacecraft into GTO.  Two consecutive in-plane perigee manoeuvre, using the Liquid Apogee
 Motor (LAM) on board the spacecraft, will raise the apogee to 3,86,000 km. which is very close to the moon (Lunar Transfer

ALTERNATIVE ROCKET PROPULSION TECHNOLOGIES
58.       In India the rocket propulsion is generally classified into two main areas based on the propellant use, for example,
 Liquid Propulsion and Solid Propulsion.  The Liquid Propulsion is further broadly classified into Earth Storable Propulsion
 and Cryogenic Propulsion System based on the type of propellant used.  Earth Storable Propellant can be stored in the liquid
 form under normal pressure and temperature conditions.  Generally, these are called liquid propulsions, e.g. N2O4
 (DiNitrogen Tetroxide and UDMH (Unsymetrical Dimethryl Hydrazine) (CH3) (2NNH2).    Cryogenic propellants are stored
 at very low temperature i.e. below 120K.  Since they are in gaseous form under normal pressure and temperature conditions
 due to low Boiling Point (BP) e.g. Liquid Hydrogen (LH2) – BP = 20K Liquid Oxygen (LOX) – BP 90K.
59.       Rocket stages using the above propellant combination are classified as earth storable stages and cryogenic stages
 respectively.  Auxiliary Propulsion Systems are  used for controlling the rocket and are also known as control systems.  These
 are small liquid rocket engines positioned at specific locations to control the trajectory of Launch vehicles during its flight.
60.       It is, however, clear from the above that the propulsion system mainly used for the rocket engines by the Department
 of Space, that is, liquid, solid,  auxiliary and cryogenic system,  involves the following problems:
The liquid hydrogen being used for cryogenic propellants is highly flammable.
It produces invisible cold flame.
It is liable to produce large volume of explosive gas cloud sensitive to ignition due to high liquid vapour expansion.
Earth Storable Propellants are toxic in nature.
Hydrazine is also difficult to handle and is highly toxic.
Any exposure to human being is extremely dangerous and environmentally fatal.
61.       The Committee is of the opinion that  any use of these propulsion systems require elaborate safety measures in order to
 avoid any environmental disaster that may arise due to the nature of the systems being used by the Department of Space for
 putting rockets into space.

62.       The Committee has been informed that the objectives of Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS) project, sanctioned in April 
 1994, is to develop and qualify an indigenous cryogenic stage for the upper stage of GSLV and the cryogenic engine has been
 successfully developed and tested for its flight duration.  The engine has logged more than 7000 seconds of accumulated test
 duration.  The integration of the cryogenic engine with propellant tanks and other subsystems, which together form the
 Cryogenic stage  is in progress.  As most of the materials, components and fabrication services required for the cryogenic
 stage has already been realised.
Safety Measures Against Cryogenic Propellants
63.       The cryogenic propellants, especially liquid hydrogen is highly flammable and produces invisible cold flame.    Due to
 high liquid vapour expansion, it is liable to produce large volume of explosive cloud which is very sensitive to ignition.  The

SPACE PHYSICS LABORATORY AND AEROSOL ISSUES
64.       The Committee has been given to understand by the Vikram Sarabhai Sapce Centre that specific findings of Space
 Physics Laboratory are focussed on Atmospheric Dynamics, Aerosols and their environmental and radiation effects by
 undertaking spatial studies in Boundary Layer Physics.  In addition to fixed ground based experiments, studies were carried
 out using mobile experiments and also by using satellite data for studying the temporal variation in the spatial distribution of
 atmospheric aerosols, clouds and water vapour to understand the basic chemistry of the dynamic changes in atmospheric
 processes.
65. One of the most important findings of the SPL is that this ABL study is an important approach to climate modelling. The
 Atmospheric Boundary Layer (ABL) is the lowest region of atmosphere which is directly affected by surface processes like
 turbulences vertical and horizontal transport of momentum and moisture.  The Committee is, therefore, convinced that
 Atmospheric Boundary Layer (ABL) is directly affected by the anthropogenic activities on the bio-sphere of the planet.  The
 Space Physics Laboratory has tried to study particularly the coastal ABL to SODAR, LAWP etc. and it has been founded that
 coastal ABL depth varies from 200 to 300 meter and particularly just above the bio-sphere spanning upto to a distance of 1.5
 to 3 kilometers.
66.       The altitude structure of ABL aerosols concentration is modeled for different seasons and its association with boundary
 layer processes was established.  During southwest monsoon period, the ABL aerosols system over Thiruvananthapuram is
 mostly governed by oceanic aerosols, while during the winter &summer periods, it is of continental type.  The columnar
 loading atmospheric aerosols is measured through a multiwave length solar radiometer (MWR).  This is measure of total
 aerosol leading in this atmosphee.  Studies made over last 15 years show an increasing  trend in aerosol loading indicating an
 increase in environmental pollution.  Satellite data revealed intense advection of aerosols from the Indian continent to oceanic
 region especially during the winter/summer period.  During the monsoon period significant mineral dust is being transported
 over to the Arabian Sea sector from the Gulf region.  SPL is the nodal agency for the study of the regional distribution of
 aerosols over the continent using the MWR network of 13 stations under the ISRO-Geosphere-Biosphere Prgoramme
 (IGBP).  Using a high power IDAR, studies were carried out or tropospheric and stratospheric aerosols as well as on high
 altitude clouds.
67.       Atmospheric waves of periodicities and horizontal scales in the lower atmosphere propagate upwards playing a
 prominent role in the momentum and energy budget of the middle atmosphere, (the Atmospheric Dynamics) and in turn
 influence the weather and climate.  Making use of temperature and wind measurements using balloons and rockets (from
 TERLS & SHAR) along with LIDAR and RADAR measurements from TERLS & NMRF, the properties of these waves are
 being characterized.
68.       The Committee is of the opinion that since the findings of the Space Physics Laboratory have a direct bearing over the
 quantum of environmental pollution due to aerosol eroding in the immediate atmosphere over the biosphere of the earth and
 also its influential impact over the predictions of the weather pattern and climate pattern in the atmosphere, any conclusion of
 the findings could be submitted to the IMD under DST for a further study for controlling of air pollution and predicting
 weather and climate changes in the near future.

71.       The Committee has been given to understand that Ammonium Perchlorate Experimental Plant (APEP) was established
 in 1979 at Aluva, Kerala with production capacity of 110 ton per annum. The Ammonium Perchlorate (AP) is being used as
 oxidizer in solid motors used for blasting  rockets into space.  The plant capacity was enhanced to 220 ton per annum during
 1998 for catering to the needs of motors being used in PSLV and GSLV.  This plant is functioning to its full capacity.
72.       The capacity of the plant was further increased to 440 ton per annum in 2003 towards meeting the increased demand of
 launches of PSLV and GSLV.  Additional production plant with a total capacity of 800 ton per annum is planned for meeting
 the future requirements of GSLV Mk III.  APEP is also manufacturing Strontium Perchlorate (SP) which, in solution form, is
 used as injectant in the Secondary injectant Thrust Vector Control System of Launch Vehicles for rockets.  APEP has so far
 made more than 3300 ton of AP and 50,000 liters of Strontium Perchlorate Injectant.

 Perchlorate (SP) are necessary as oxidizer in solid motors and for injectant for Thrust Vector in control system of Launch
 Vehicles for rockets,  necessary precautionary measures should be taken by Department of Space due to environmental
 pollution potential of AP & SP before using them as oxidizer and injectant in motors for rockets.

2.         The programmes being pursued by DAE emanate from the following mandate:
 
Ø      Increasing share of nuclear power through deployment of indigenous and other proven technologies, along
 with development of fast breeder reactors and thorium reactors with associated fuel cycle facilities. The
 three-stage Nuclear Power Programme is achieved through-
 
(i)         Setting up of pressurised heavy water reactors (PHWRs) and associated fuel cycle facilities;
 
(ii)
                Setting up of fast breeder reactors (FBRs) backed by reprocessing plants and plutonium-
based fuel fabrication plants and
 
(iii)
               The third stage that would be based on the thorium-uranium-233 cycle where Uranium-233
 is obtained by irradiation of thorium.
 
Ø      Building and operation of research reactors for production of radioisotopes and carrying out radiation
 technology applications in the field of medicine, agriculture and industry;
Ø      Developing advanced  technologies such as accelerators, lasers, supercomputers, advanced materials and
 instrumentation, and encouraging transfer of technology to industry;
Ø      Support to basic research in nuclear energy and related frontier areas of science; Interaction with universities
 and academic institutions; Support to research and development projects having a bearing on DAE’s
 programmes, and International cooperation in related advanced areas of research; and
Ø      Contribution to national security.
3.         The atomic energy programmes comprise three sectors, namely, ‘Nuclear Power Sector’, ‘Industries & Minerals
 Sector (I & M Sector)’ and ‘Research & Development Sector(R & D Sector)’. The Plan and Non-Plan outlays of the
 Department are formulated under power sector, industries and minerals (I&M) sector and Research and Development
 sector. The financial supports for the activities of the Department are provided by budgetary support. The public sector
 undertakings, namely Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd.(NPCIL), Mumbai, Indian Rare Earths Limited (IRE),
 Mumbai, Uranium Corporation of India Limited (UCIL), Jaduguda and Electronics Corporation of India Limited (ECIL),
 Hyderabad and Bhartiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Ltd.(BHAVINI), Kalpakkam of the Department provide Internal and
 Extra Budgetary Resources (IEBR) in addition to budgetary support to the capital and infrastructural developments.       
4.         The Nuclear Power Sector of the Department deals with design, construction and operation of commercial power
 reactors with associated safety in all its phases.  This comprises building of Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWR) and
 development of Fast Breeder Reactors (FBR) and Thorium Reactors on commercial scale.  Associated waste management
 and environment monitoring and technology development relating to operation and maintenance of the reactors also form
 part of the programmes.
5.         Industries & Minerals Sector is involved in industrial application of technologies developed in the R&D facilities and
 includes- programmes related to nuclear fuel cycle covering design, construction and operation of industrial plants for
 refining ores, fabrication of fuel, production of heavy water, instrumentation and control, etc. needed for sustained operation
 of the power reactors; and applications of radioisotopes, radiation, laser and accelerator technology for development in
 industry, medicine, agriculture and food preservation.
6.         Research & Development Sector provides R & D support to the Nuclear Power Programmes of the Department.  The
 R & D efforts of DAE are in multidisciplinary high technology areas.  Significant achievements have been made in building
 technical capabilities in the design, construction and operation of Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWR); exploration,
 mining extraction, purification and conversion of nuclear materials; production of fuel element for nuclear reactors;

CHOICE OF FUEL FOR FAST BREEDER REACTOR (FBR)
 
25.       The Committee has been given to understand that Department of Atomic Energy  (DAE) is planning to use metallic
 fuel for future Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR).  The metallic fuel has high breeding ratio i.e. high electricity generating
 capacity through breeding process and shorter doubling time.
25.1     The Committee welcomes the idea and feels that this advanced fuel will reduce the cost of production of electricity
 through FBR and not only that by reducing the capital cost of production of electricity the plant life span will also increase
 by incorporating better safety features for these reactors.  Faster the breeding, quicker will be the rise in the FBR’s capacity.
 Other nuclear fuels for FBR and PFBR (Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor) like oxide, nitride and carbide fuels may now take
 the back seat for being used as fuels for FBR.
25.2     The choice of fuels for breeder reactors, the Committee feels, is a choice between doubling time versus the cost of
 production. The Committee, however, feels that oxide fuel with a ratio of 30% plutonium oxide and 70% uranium oxide is a
 well-proven fuel world over.  In India, however, mixed oxide fuel (MOX) could be used for prototype Fast Breeder Reactor
 (PFBR).
25.3     The Committee, on the other hand, feels that carbide fuel is very difficult to fabricate on a large scale as it is highly
 pyrophoric and is highly susceptible to oxidation and hydrolysis.  Moreover, reprocessing of spent carbide fuel is difficult
 as it is difficult to dissolve in nitric acid and leaves behind organic complexes.  Apart from this, the carbide fuel  has low
 burn up value in comparison to oxide fuel. The fuel ‘burn-up’ in a nuclear reactor refers to the amount of energy extracted
 from the fuel before it is discharged for storage or reprocessing.  Higher the burn-up, lesser will be the fuel cycle cost.
25.4     The Committee understands that cost of power production comes down with increased burn up value.  Also oxide
 fuel is easy to fabricate as it is not pyrophoric and hence needs no inert atmosphere during fabrication.  The Committee is,
 therefore, of the opinion that use of oxide fuel would be more vital for making a foray into fast breeder power plants.
25.5     The Committee understands that breeder technology works on the principle of self-sustenance and ability to produce
 more plutonium than it actually consumes to produce power.  The breeding ratio, which is 1.1 in case of oxide fuel, is 1.2 –
 1.4 in case of carbide and nitride fuels.  While it is maximum in case of metallic fuel i.e. 1.4 – 1.5 and hence doubling time
 (i.e. surplus plutonium produce to start a new reactor) is shortest in case of a metallic, carbide and nitride fuels respectively 
 in comparison to oxide fuel.
25.6     The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that doubling time becomes paramount when the country goes on
 commissioning new reactors.  Hence, the stress on using advanced fuel is necessary.  The Committee feels that making
 technology available for producing power at cheaper cost may gain more public acceptance, which is vital to breeder
 programme.
25.7     The Committee is of the opinion that lower burn up by using carbide fuel is not economical since fabrication and
 reprocessing would increase cost of power production.  However, the Committee feels that long-term strategy calls for fuels
 with shorter doubling time.  Sometimes it is felt that nitride fuel seems to be more preferable due to its easier reprocessing
 and improved performance.
25.8     The Committee recommends that the Department of Atomic Energy may like to consider the following choices:-
 
i)                    High breeding ratio and shorter doubling time

 world speaks for four different approaches for preventing, detecting, diagnosing and treating the disease. Researches all
 over the world have recognized that body’s own biology could be a powerful weapon to fight against cancer by
 manipulating body’s own mechanism against the disease.
 
27.       Although the Committee feels that TMC is providing state-of-the-art treatment against this killer disease, it would
 still like to recommend for a new line of research in the field of oncology. The Committee feels that Gene Therapy
 experiment is the most important therapy for finding a permanent solution against the disease.  In  Gene Therapy  process,
 the healthy copy of the missing gene is inserted into the cell using a virus known as Adeno-Associated Viral Vector that is
 no longer harmful and as such it could be termed as a disabled virus.  Cells that have been successfully changed by this
 gene therapy process are separated out, grown and returned to the patient’s body to fight against the disease.  In other cases,
 disabled viruses are used to deliver healthy gene directly to cells within the patient’s body.

 and deep attention.
a)
                  Role of angiogenesis inhibitors in Cancer treatment;
b)                  Role of Tumour Suppressor Genes like pRB and p53 in Cancer Control and
c)                  Role of Farnesyl Transferase Inhibitors (FTIs) – Tumour Necrosis Factor(TNF) and Endothelial
 Growth Factors Receptors(EGFs) in promoting neoplastic transformation.
 ANTI-SENSE THERAPY AND CANCER CONTROL
29.       In this connection, the Committee would like to draw the attention of the ACTREC research group to  a finding
 achieved by a group of scientists working in Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, (CCMB)  Hyderabad where they
 have been working on RNA interference (RNAi) based therapy for nearly three years. During the visit of the Committee to
 Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, (CCMB) the Committee was apprised that  scientists of the institute has
 pioneered in the field in isolating this unusual transgene silencing in animals.  This gene has been targeted in several viral
 diseases and had successful delivery on human applications.  This group of scientists has successfully showed that RNAi
 controls heterochromatin formation and cell cycle progression.  They found a way to control diseases like cancer which are
 related to cell-cycle progression and cell proliferation which take place almost in different types of tumor formation in
 cancer.  They have also worked on short interfering siRNAfor viral inhibition and has generated siRNA for Human
 Pappilloma Viruses (HPVs).  In HPV they have  targeted  a combination of E6 and E7 genes and coat protein of the virus. 
 Apart from this, this group has also generated a new generation of  adeno-associated viral vectors (AAVV) for better
 delivery of siRNA in different tissues.  The Committee feels that such researches may provide a meaningful solution in
 understanding the mechanism of carcinogenesis and their subsequent control through wider clinical trials of such findings
 and ultimately  applications on human voluteers.

FOOD IRRADIATION
 
33.       It is well-known that incidence of food born diseases can be reduced by food irradiation techniques.  It can also
 inhibit post-harvest sprouting in potatoes and onions – disinfect fruits and vegetables, delay ripening in fruits, can eliminate
 outrightly the food borne  pathogens which can be kept for a long time without refrigeration before substantial
 consumption.  In addition, the irradiation technology can be used for eliminating pests nuisance etc.
34.       Although irradiation technology could have   outright advantages, there could be  certain health risks that might be
 involved in the application of the technology of the following nature:
·
        Food irradiation can result in loss of nutrients.
 
·        When food is exposed to high doses of ionising radiation, the possible changes in chemical composition and nutritional
 content of food damage  DNA in humans.
 
·
        The food irradiation does not necessarily inactivate dangerous toxins which have already been produced by bacteria
 prior to irradiation.
 
·
         Irradiated food products like chicken meat, etc could mislead consumers into thinking that they are biologically safer for
 consumption.
 
35.       The Committee therefore feels that some precautionary measures should be taken by the Department of Atomic
 Energy while irradiating foods so that the possible health risks involved before consumption of irradiated food could be
 effectively dealt with. In this connection, Radiological Safety, Microbiological Safety, Nutritional adequacy and
 Toxicological Safety measures may be kept in view.
36.       The Committee also feels that long term effects of irradiated food should be studied thoroughly from the point of
 view of the fact that how  ionizing radiation alters chemical structure of food material.  This could be managed if a

 adopted for improving the operational efficiency of the irradiating machine through lowering cost of irradiation, control
 over accidental spillage of radiation from place of work and transportation to construction site for placing food irradiation
 technology that may include high voltage electorn beam generated from linear accelerator but also by placing proper safety
 label on irradiated food products for its increased public acceptance through informing the consumers  adequately and
 extensively  by educating them more about the health advantages of irradiated food.

 production is derived at least possible opportunity cost.
(Para 25.9)
17.       Although the Committee feels that TMC is providing state-of-the-art treatment against this killer disease, it would
 still like to recommend for a new line of research in the field of oncology. The Committee feels that Gene Therapy
 experiment is the most important therapy for finding a permanent solution against the disease.  In  Gene Therapy  process,
 the healthy copy of the missing gene is inserted into the cell using a virus known as Adeno-Associated Viral Vector that is
 no longer harmful and as such it could be termed as a disabled virus.  Cells that have been successfully changed by this
 gene therapy process are separated out, grown and returned to the patient’s body to fight against the disease.  In other cases,
 disabled viruses are used to deliver healthy gene directly to cells within the patient’s body.
(Para 27)
18.       The Committee is also of the opinion that following fields in Cancer Research apart from the above needs research
 and deep attention.
a)
      Role of angiogenesis inhibitors in Cancer treatment;
b)      Role of Tumour Suppressor Genes like pRB and p53 in Cancer Control and
c)      Role of Farnesyl Transferase Inhibitors (FTIs) – Tumour Necrosis Factor(TNF)
 and Endothelial Growth Factors Receptors(EGFs) in promoting neoplastic
 transformation.
 
(Para 28)
19.       In this connection, the Committee would like to draw the attention of the ACTREC research group to  a finding
 achieved by a group of scientists working in Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, (CCMB)  Hyderabad where they
 have been working on RNA interference (RNAi) based therapy for nearly three years. During the visit of the Committee to
 Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, (CCMB) the Committee was apprised that  scientists of the institute has
 pioneered in the field in isolating this unusual transgene silencing in animals.  This gene has been targeted in several viral
 diseases and had successful delivery on human applications.  This group of scientists has successfully showed that RNAi
 controls heterochromatin formation and cell cycle progression.  They found a way to control diseases like cancer which are
 related to cell-cycle progression and cell proliferation which take place almost in different types of tumor formation in
 cancer.  They have also worked on short interfering siRNAfor viral inhibition and has generated siRNA for Human
 Pappilloma Viruses (HPVs).  In HPV they have  targeted  a combination of E6 and E7 genes and coat protein of the virus. 
 Apart from this, this group has also generated a new generation of  adeno-associated viral vectors (AAVV) for better

 understanding the mechanism of carcinogenesis and their subsequent control through wider clinical trials of such findings
 and ultimately  applications on human voluteers.
(Para 29)
20.       In view of the importance of the research, the Committee would like to strongly recommend TMC research group
 and CCMB research group to work in collaboration with  each other on such findings so that an effective targeted drug
 could be designed which may answer the complexities of cure of many forms of cancer with greater successes.
(Para 30)
21.       The Committee understands that one of the greatest sources of extraction of anti-cancer medicine are the oceans and
 seas of the world.  Keeping this in view, the Committee in its 128
th Report on Demand for Grants 2004-05 for the
 Department of Ocean Development recommended for initiatives to be undertaken by the Department for extraction of
 potentially anti-cancerous drugs from the depth of  the ocean.  The Committee further recommended that bulbous yellow
 soft coral that disrupts erratic cell divisions in cancer cells and ocean molds that live in sea grasses are the great source of
 anti-cancerous drugs.  The Committee further recommended that sea sponges are the real source of anti-cancerous drugs
 and drugs like Didemnin-B that could be isolated from sea squirt, Bryostatin-I that could be isolated from Bugula,
 Dolestatin-10 that could be derived  from Indian Ocean Mollusk and Dolabella, a sea hare are also potential sources of
 drugs for anti-cancer treatment and other incurable diseases.  In response to these recommendations  of the Committee, the
 Department of Ocean development has replied that possibilities are being explored for participation of more and more
 institutions under the “Drugs from Sea” programme for extraction of potentially anti-cancerous drugs from the depth of the
 ocean from these microalgae as mentioned above.  They have further stated that for understanding the  details of Didemin-B
 from sea squirt, Bryostatin-1 from Bugula and Dolestatin-10 from Indian ocean Mollusc & Dolabella//Seabella the focus
 from the year 2005-06 onwards would be strengthened to frame  comprehensive action plans to study the extraction of
 these  drugs for cancer treatment and pain management etc.
(Para 31)
22.       In pursuance of the above, the Committee would like to recommend strongly that research wing of the ACTREC
 should jointly collaborate with the Department of Ocean Development for an active participation in the drugs from sea
 programme for extraction of this potentially anti-cancerous drugs as mentioned above.  They should also collaborate with
 the Department of Ocean Development for a comprehensive action study for giving this extraction of drug project a head
 start from 2005-06 onwards so that the nature’s prized possession  in the form of anti-cancer drugs in sea biology could be
 utilized functionally to find out a potential answer in curative medicine for the treatment of this dreaded disease named
 “Cancer”.
(Para 32)
 
 
23.       The Committee therefore feels that some precautionary measures should be taken by the Department of Atomic
 Energy while irradiating foods so that the possible health risks involved before consumption of irradiated food could be
 effectively dealt with. In this connection, Radiological Safety, Microbiological Safety, Nutritional adequacy and
 Toxicological Safety measures may be kept in view.
(Para 35)
24.       The Committee also feels that long term effects of irradiated food should be studied thoroughly from the point of
 view of the fact that how  ionizing radiation alters chemical structure of food material.  This could be managed if a
 monitored  safe label  of exposure of food to radiation is laid down by the Department of Atomic Energy.
(Para 36)
 
25.       The Committee feels that high voltage electron beams generated from linear accelerators which could be a better
 alternative for food irradiation technology than application of Cobalt-60 and cesium 137  because the penetration depth of
 gama irradiation is not there and with shorter exposure time, the food could be safe with this method.  With all other
 existing methods of food irradiation, the Committee feels only low efficiency could be maintained combined with high cost
 of production of irradiated foods.  
(Para 37)
26.       The Committee feels that in order to make the food irradiation a success,  the  following factors for judging the
 bactericidal efficacy of a given dose of irradiation may be adopted:
 
2.

 number of organism present in the food.
4.      Composition of the food.

Created in 1985, the Ministry of Environment and Forests acts as the nodal Ministry in the Government of India for

 planning, promotion, coordination and overseeing the implementation of various environmental and forestry programmes.
 The Ministry’s mandate also includes  environmental management to promote health considerations, to focus on poverty
 alleviation by enhancing access of the poor to natural resources for livelihood, and to heighten the awareness regarding
 environmentally sound living process by focusing on nature-man synergy.  The Ministry has been designated as the nodal
 agency in the country for the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), and the International Centre for
 Integrated Mountain Development, and looks after the follow-up of the United Nations Conference on Environment and
 Development (UNCED). Within the overall framework of its mandate, the main activities of the Ministry are conservation
 and control of pollution, afforestation and regeneration of forests in degraded areas, protection and conservation of forests
 and wildlife and protection of environment.
The tasks assigned to the Ministry are achieved through environmental impact assessment, eco-regeneration,
 assistance to organizations implementing environmental and forestry programmes, promotion of environmental and
 forestry research, extension, education and training for capacity building, dissemination of environmental information,
 international co-operation, creation of environmental awareness among all sections of the country’s population.  These
 objectives are supported by a set of legislative and regulatory measures aiming at preservation, conservation and
 protection of environment.  Some of these are the Wildlife  (Protection) Act, 1972, the Water (Prevention and Control of
 Pollution) Act, 1974, the Forests (Conservation) Act, 1980, Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the
 Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, National Forest Policy, 1988 the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, a National
 Conservation Strategy and Policy Statement on Environment and Development, 1992, a Policy Statement on Abatement
 of Pollution, 1992, the National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995, the National  Environment Appellate Authority Act,
 1997, the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 2001. The Bio-Diversity Act 2002 has been passed and Rules 2004 have
 been finalized.
 
The following are the broad objectives of the Ministry:
i)
                    Conservation and survey of flora, fauna, forests and wildlife,
ii)                   Prevention and control of pollution,
iii)                 Afforestation and regeneration of degraded areas,
iv)                 Protection of the environment, and
v)                  Ensuring the welfare of animals.

POLLUTION FROM COAL BASED METHANE AND CLEAN COAL TECHNOLOGIES
 
11.       Among the fossil fuels, coal has acquired the dubious distinction of being the dirtiest one.  Such an attribute is on
 account of severe environmental damage and acute pollution problems caused during mining operation, processing of the
 mineral till its end use and pollution arising out of coal based wastes.
 
12.       Land subsidence in underground mines, ugly scars of land in abandoned open cast mines, emission of fly ash
 during combustion of coal and huge quantities of ash generated from boilers of coal based power plants and industrial
 units are among the hosts of multi-facial problem associated with handling and subsequent productive use of coal. 
 Emission of carbon dioxide, an important component of green house gases (GHGs) and global warming is another
 emerging concern linked with the burning of coal.
 
13.       The Committee is of the opinion that although the coal constitutes a major source catering to the country’s energy
 needs, possibly with proper technologies and new initiatives for better management, it is possible to reduce the hazards of
 coal production which is being otherwise caused due to extraction of this mineral without proper planning.  Through
 scientific mining practices followed by land reclamation, beneficiation for ash reduction at source, improvement in
 combustion methods, use of efficient electrostatic precipitators, bag filters for trapping of fly ash emission and effective
 management of ash including its utilization for bricks, cement and such other purposes, many of the problems can be
 prevented and controlled.
 
14.       The Committee feels that Central Pollution Control Board should lay down the environmental guidelines for coal
 mining activities prescribing the use of beneficiated coal with lower ash content in power plants and lay down specific
 norms for emission and effluents from coal combustion system.
 
15.       In India out of the total land area of 3.29 million sq. km., only 0.45% area, that is, about16,000 sq. kms. is coal
 bearing  and out of this coal bearing area, active coal mining area is about 2500 sq. kms.  The Committee feels that
 maximum land degradation in coal mining is caused by open-cast mining.  Since the productivity is higher in open cast
 sector, this pace of growth cannot be sustained for long since the stripping ratios will increase the mining operations
 which may consequently run into  land access and other environmental problems.

16.       Air pollution in coalmines is chiefly due to the fugitive emission of particulate matter and gases including methane,
 sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.  The mining operations like drilling, blasting, movement of the heavy earth
 moving machinery on haul roads, collection, transportation and handling of coal, screening, sizing and segregation units
 are the major sources of such emissions. Underground mine fire is also a major source of air pollution in some of the
 coalfields.
 
17.       High levels of suspended particular matter increase respiratory diseases such as chronic bronchitis and asthma
 while gaseous emissions contribute towards global warming besides causing health hazards to the exposed population
 
18.       Methane emission from coal mining depends on the mining methods, depth of coal mine, coal quality and
 entrapped gas content in coal seams.  The proper management of methane emission should be one of the important factors
 which should be handled by the miners and mining authorities to reduce its emission into the atmosphere.
 
19.       The major source of water pollution in the coal mines is the carry over of the suspended solids in the drainage
 system of the mine sump water and storm drainage and in some of the coal mines acidic water is also found in the
 underground aquifers.  In addition, waste water from coal preparation plant and mine water are other source of water
 pollution which requires immediate control.
 
20.       The main sources of noise pollution, are blasting, movement of heavy earth moving machine and drilling and coal
 handling plants and the effective monitoring of all these issues are necessary for reducing noise pollution.
 
21.       Subsidence of surface takes place due to extraction of coal by underground mining.  Subsidence is exhibited by
 cracks on surface and lowering of land in the worked out areas compared to surroundings.  The surface is rehabilitated by
 dozing and sealing  of cracks followed by plantation of trees.  The subsided areas with medium sized depressions are ideal
 for developing water pools and sustain green vegetation and also to meet the water needs of local people.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the mined areas, which are backfilled, should be rehabilitated for development of vegetation. 
 In the quarried areas water reservoir is developed for water harvesting.  The big voids created by open-pit mining can
 cause land degradation which, the Committee feels, could be gainfully utilized to serve water reservoirs which will
 provide moisture for vegetation in the surrounding areas and the water could be used for domestic supply after necessary
 treatment.
 
22.       It is understood that major coal projects are required to obtain Environmental Clearance from the Government. 
 Mitigative/control measures are identified to reduce the adverse impacts on environment.  It helps to integrate
 environmental considerations into mining and related operations right from the planning stage.  For this purpose, the
 project proponent needs to prepare an Environmental Impact Assessment Report and an Environmental Management
 Plan.
 
23.       The Committee is of the opinion that for abatement of the pollution problems associated with the coal mines, the
 Central Pollution Control Board needs to develop National Environmental Standards and Code of practice for coal mines
 which should be given due consideration by the Ministry of Environment & Forests and given a legal framework.
 
24.       The Committee is of the opinion that supply of  high ash laden coal to power plants not only poses environmental
 problems but also causes poor plant performance and high cost for ash disposal. The Committee, therefore, strongly
 recommends that Ministry of Environment and Forests should evolve a mechanism for suggesting measures for improving
 the quality of coal supplied to the power plants.
a)         Particularly power plants located beyond 1000 kms. from pit head; and
b)         Power plants located in critically polluted areas, Urban sectors and in ecologically sensitive zones.

OPTIMAL HYDRO-CARBON ENERGY MANAGEMENT THROUGH CLEAN DEVELOPMENT
 MECHANISM (CDM)
 
27.       In the wake of implementation of Kyoto Protocol in February, 2005 stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations
 in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system appears to
 be one of the challenging subjects before the country in the current global environment scenario.  The Committee would,
 therefore, like to invite the attention of the Ministry of Environment and Forests in conjunction with the oil sector
 that investment in low emissions technologies is the demanding need of the hour and the problem should be
 addressed in such a fashion that long term national emissions reduction should be made one of the priority areas.
 
28.       In order to give an effective implementation of the above proposal of the Committee, the following model may be
 considered by the Ministry of Environment & Forests:
·
        The solubility of additional carbon dioxide in the ocean surface water decreases with rising concentrations. 
 Thus, the relative oceanic uptake of carbon dioxide is reduced at higher concentrations.
·        The land vegetations may serve as an additional medium term sink for anthropogenic carbon emissions.
·        The radio-active greenhouse forcing grows only logarithmically with increasing carbon dioxide and Green
 House Gases (GHG) emissions.
 
29.       The environment friendly performance objectives and mechanisms for tracking progress in achieving the prime
 objective of the aforesaid model for the growth of the oil industry on the one hand and socio-economic sustainability on
 the other, the implementation of socio-environmental policies involving oil companies and the Ministry of Environment &
 Forest requires combination of technological advances and innovative approaches.
 
30.       The Committee is of the opinion that for addressing the key issues pertaining to the transition of a carbon based
 economy to a hydrogen economy, the Ministry of Environment and Forests needs to promote the following:
§
         Promote more rapid dissemination and use of efficient, existing commercial technology in strategic and
 environmentally sensitive areas of the country.
§         Encourage the development and use of innovative, currently non-commercial technologies.
§         Enhance the ability of all oil sector companies to achieve and utilize advanced and efficient technologies, and
§         Improve scientific understanding by addressing well-known uncertainties, in the adoption and implementation of
 efficient technologies.

 flowering and fruiting of herbs, shrubs and trees of the region.  In certain specialised ecosystems, like cold deserts in the

 habitat (terrestrial epiphytic, epiphyllous, saprophyte, parasite,  aquatic etc.) local name uses, if any, abundance and such
 features which will not remain in herbarium specimens  as colour of the flower/leaf, bark, etc., fragrant, height/girth and

WILDLIFE CONSERVATION
PROJECT TIGER
44.       Project Tiger was launched in 1973 with a mandate to conserve tigers in a holistic manner.  These are fulfilled by
 facilitating focused, concerted management of ecotypical reserves in various states, constituted on a ‘core-buffer’ strategy
 through funding the technical support, including site-specific inputs to elicit local community support for conservation.
 Initially, the project was launched in nine tiger reserves, covering an area of 16,339 sq. km. which has now increased to
 28 tiger reserves, ecompassing 37761 sq. km. of tiger habitat distributed in 17 States.

 Reserve and requested the Ministry to furnish a status note on the poaching and disappearance of Tigers. In response, the
 Ministry has informed the Committee that there has been considerable media coverage recently speculating a country
 level decline in tiger population in the wake of claims that tigers have not been spotted in recent months in the Sariska
 Tiger Reserve of Rajasthan.  Based on field visits by senior officials of the Ministry of Environment & Forests, the
 Rajasthan State was asked to carry out an intensive search for tigers in and around Sariska, apart from ensuring
 compliance of directives issued from Project Tiger for protection, regulation of tourist visitation inside the reserves and
 systemic  improvement.  Though no direct sighting of tigers or pug marks were seen during the search, the State has
 reported collection of some indirect evidence like droppings.  The State has been advised to send the collected samples to
 the Wildlife Institute of India for species identification.  The Wildlife Institute of India has also been directed to carry out
 a detailed ecological study in the Sariska Tiger Reserve for an appraisal of the status of tiger, prey animals, the

46.       The Ministry also expressed some concerns and observations based on the field visit, which are as follows:-
(a)        Non-compliance of Government of India Guidelines/Directives.
            Despite guidelines and repeated requests from the Ministry of Environment & Forests, there appears to be a general
 lack of will on the part of the State for compliance, which would have otherwise ensured the desired degree of protection
 in the Sariska Tiger Reserve.  From the middle of June, 2004 to mid September 2004 there was no Deputy Director
 functioning in Sariska, since the incumbent proceeded on leave.  The DCF level officer (Deputy Director) is the cutting
 edge, as far as field implementation of Project Tiger is concerned.  Therefore, this absence has also contributed to the
 collapse of the day-to-day administration and protection within the reserve.  Further, the CF & Field Director of Sariska
 also proceeded on leave in September and a junior officer of the level of ACF was made responsible for management of
 the reserve during the said period.  The State Government could have entrusted this task to a trained senior officer.
(b)        Disturbance caused to the Reserve by heavy vehicular traffic and the human influx:
            There is a State Highway (No.29) passing through the Sariska Tiger Reserve which links Sariska to Dausa.  The
 vehicular traffic on this road during day time has gone up considerably, especially during the free entry days earmarked
 for Hanuman (PANDU POL) temple visit twice a week (every Tuesday and Saturday).  The vehicular traffic during the
 free entry days has increased from 14706 in 2002 to 27982 (April, 2004 – January, 2005).  Likewise, the pilgrim visitation
 inside the reserve has also gone up from 138342 to 177580 during the period.  The influx of pilgrims on annual meal day
 in the month of ‘Sawan goes considerably high toughing as high as 30000 on a single day.  This is the major cause of
 disturbance to wild animals and no initiatives have been taken to regulate this traffic of vehicles as well as human beings,
 despite clear directives from the Ministry of Environment & Forests for containing the visitation within the carrying
 capacity.  The State highway 13 (Alwar-Jaipur), carrying a very large traffic of goods vehicles, was reported to have been
 diverted to the new road built with a central assistance of Rs.3.5 crores to avoid road hits of wild animals on the old route
 which passes through the core of the Reserve.  However this still remains to be implemented.
(c)        Heavy human and cattle population
            As many as 196 villages are situated in and around the Sariska Tiger Reserve with a cattle population of 275414. 
 Further, 28 villages are located within the Tiger Reserve itself with 11 villages in the core of the Reserve. The State has
 hardly taken any initiative for relocating these villages despite the fact the funding support for such initiatives are
 provided under the Project Tiger.  It is noteworthy that the people who were relocated earlier in 1976 from the Kraska
 village have returned to their original settlement area.  Likewise, some families of another earlier relocation (village
 ‘Karnakavas’) have also returned to the fringe area of the Reserve.  No effort seems to have been made by the State to
 redress the situation.

 population of wild elephants in India.
iii)                 Ecological restoration of existing natural habitats and migratory routes of elephants of elephants.
iv)                 Promotion of measures for mitigation of human – elephant conflict in problem areas and moderating pressures
 of human and live stock on crucial elephant habitats.
v)                  Eco-development and veterinary care.
vi)                 Research on issues relating to elephant conversation.
vii)               Public education and awareness programme and capacity building  of field staff, mahouts and veterinarians.
 
52.       The Committee feels that Project Elephant is a major project of the Ministry but getting less importance. The tusk
 is as precious as tiger skin and not immune from Poachers. Therefore, the Committee recommends that Elephants should
 also be protected from the poaching and effective strategy should be evolved for their preservation. In view of decline in
 Tiger population in Sariska, the Committee suggests the Ministry to undertake an evaluation of Elephant population and
 take corrective measures accordingly.
 
53.       The Committee recommends that sufficient allocation must be provided to various States for habitat management
 mitigation of human-elephant conflict, payment of ex-gratia relief for loss of human life and crops caused by wild
 elephants, strengthening of anti-poaching measures, capacity building of the field staff, registration of domesticated
 elephant using microchips etc.
 
54.       The Committee recommends that endangered species need to be preserved while the population of other animals
 should be sustainably managed.  The Ministry should generate data and information on maintaining a sustainable
 population of each animal for their scientific management.  Research initiatives in the field of sustainable use of wildlife
 products are needed.  The Ministry should cover not only wildlife research and training but also the socio-economic
 aspects of wildlife conservation.
 
55.       While the Committee is concerned about the protection of wildlife in the Protected Areas, it feels that wildlife
 should also be protected outside the Protected Areas and sufficient allocation should be made for the purpose.

 thrust areas are as follows:

98.       The Committee is of the view that 90% of the country’s medicinal plants occur in forest habitats.  The most
 important strategy for conserving the medicinal plant gene pools is to establish a nation wide network of forest gene banks
 (average size 200-500 ha in tropical forest and 50-100 ha in high altitude forest) across the different forest types and
 altitudinal range in all bio-geographic regions of the country.  In view thereof, the Committee recommends that Ministry
 should urgently initiate programmes or in-situ conservation of genetic diversity. The Committee also feels that
 conservation of genetic diversity and documenting the entire traditional medicinal plants should be undertaken in such a
 manner so as to plan for development of traditional medicinal plants.  Besides, the Ministry, in collaboration with CSIR,
 DST, DBT and Ministry of Rural Development, should support community owned enterprises based on medicinal plants. 
 
TROPICAL BOTANIC GARDEN AND RESEARCH INSTITUTE, (TBGRI), THIRUVANTHAPURAM
 
99.       Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute (TBGRI) with its mandate for conservation and sustainable
 utilization of tropical plant diversity is recognized as a National Centre of Excellence in ex –situ conservation of tropical
 plants.  TBGRI also functions as the National Gene Bank for medicinal and aromatic plants of peninsular India and has a
 Bioinformatics Distributed Information Centre.
 
100.     TBGRI is the only organization in India, which maintains a 300 acre conservatory garden for the wild tropical plant
 genetic resources of India, besides a well integrated multidisciplinary R&D system dealing with conservation,
 management and sustainable utilization of tropical plant resources.  The Institute is ideally located at the foothills of the
 Western Ghats.  The institute has 121 acres of forest land with hills and hillocks, portions of evergreen, decidous, marshy
 and riverine vegetation in addition to grass lands and rocky areas.  All of them to large extent provide different
 microclimatic conditions for different species.  The Institute also have a well-organized Arboretum, Palmetum,
 Bambusetum, Orchidarium, Medicinal plant garden and Field Gene Bank of wild plant collections to which new additions
 are being carried out from the topical areas of the country.  The Institute has about 20 major projects at operational stage
 on survey and inventory conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources in India.  TBGRI is accredited
 to UNCED and enjoys the membership of Botanic Gardens Conservation International.  The Institute is the coordination
 and National Database Center for All India Coordinated Research Project on Ethnobiology sponsored by the Ministry of
 Environment and Forests, Government of India.  TBGRI also harbours a well-established herbarium of vascular plants
 and fungi and a group of well-trained taxonomists.
 
101.     Keeping in view above the facts, the Committee considers it as an institute of national importance and, therefore,
 recommends that the TBGRI should be elevated to a national institute under the administrative control of Ministry of
 Environment & Forests.
 
102.     After considering the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Environment & Forests and assessing the progress of
 various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the budgetary allocation
 of Rs.1388.19 crores, as sought by the Ministry for the year 2005-2006, under Demand   No. 30, may be approved.

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS
1.         Therefore, the Committee recommends that as there has been greater emphasis on North-East region, the Ministry
 should make a lump sum budgetary support under one head equal to 10% of Plan funds for the North-Eastern Sector
 including Sikkim and not under separate heads as has been made in this financial year. 
(Para 5.2)
2.         The Committee is of the view that expenditure should be evenly spread over all the four quarters of the financial
 year. The Committee is of the considered opinion that any variation in the expenditure is mainly due to inherent lacunas in
 the budgetary mechanism of the Ministry, which requires urgent attention and a well-planned action plan to ensure full
 utilization of allocated budget in a uniform manner spreading over all the four quarters of the financial year. The
 Committee therefore suggests that the Ministry may examine the existing procedure and see weather it can be further
 streamlined to make the expenditure uniform in all quarters.
(Para 10)
3.         The Committee is of the opinion that although the coal constitutes a major source catering to the country’s  energy
 needs, possibly with proper technologies and new initiatives for better management, it is possible to reduce the hazards of

 combustion methods, use of efficient electrostatic precipitators, bag filters for trapping of fly ash emission and effective
 management of ash including its utilization for bricks, cement and such other purposes, many of the problems can be
 prevented and controlled.
(Para 13)
4.         The Committee feels that Central Pollution Control Board should lay down the environmental guidelines for coal
 mining activities prescribing the use of beneficiated coal with lower ash content in power plants and lay down specific
 norms for emission and effluents from coal combustion system.
(Para 14)
5.         The Committee feels that maximum land degradation in coal mining is caused by open-cast mining.  Since the
 productivity is higher in open cast sector, this pace of growth cannot be sustained for long since the stripping ratios will
 increase the mining operations which may consequently run into  land access and other environmental problems.
(Para 15)
6.         The mining operations like drilling, blasting, movement of the heavy earth moving machinery on haul roads,
 collection, transportation and handling of coal, screening, sizing and segregation units are the major sources of such
 emissions. Underground mine fire is also a major source of air pollution in some of the coalfields.
(Para 16)
7.         The proper management of methane emission should be one of the important factors which should be handled by
 the miners and mining authorities to reduce its emission into the atmosphere.
(Para 18)
8.         In addition, waste water from coal preparation  plant and mine water are other source of water pollution which
 requires immediate control.
(Para 19)
9.         The main sources of noise pollution, are blasting, movement of heavy earth moving machine and drilling and coal
 handling plants and the effective monitoring of all these issues are necessary for reducing noise pollution.
(Para 20)
10.       The Committee, therefore, recommends that the mined areas, which are backfilled, should be rehabilitated for
 development of vegetation.  In the quarried areas water reservoir is developed for water harvesting.  The big voids created
 by open-pit mining can cause land degradation which, the Committee feels, could be gainfully utilized to serve water
 reservoirs which will provide moisture for vegetation in the surrounding areas and the water could be used for domestic
 supply after necessary treatment.
(Para 21)
11.       It is understood that major coal projects are required to obtain Environmental Clearance from the Government. 
 Mitigative/control measures are identified to reduce the adverse impacts on environment.  It helps to integrate
 environmental considerations into mining and related operations right from the planning stage.  For this purpose, the
 project proponent needs to prepare an Environmental Impact Assessment  Report and an Environmental Management
 Plan.
(Para 22)
12.       The Committee is of the opinion that for abatement of the pollution problems associated with the coal mines, the
 Central Pollution Control Board needs to develop National Environmental Standards and Code of practice for coal mines
 which should be given due consideration by the Ministry of Environment & Forests and given a legal framework.
(Para 23)
13.       The Committee is of the opinion that supply of  high ash laden coal to power plants not only poses environmental
 problems but also causes poor plant performance and high cost for ash disposal. The Committee, therefore, strongly
 recommends that Ministry of Environment and Forests should evolve a  mechanism for suggesting measures for
 improving the quality of coal supplied to the power plants .
(a)
    Particularly power plants located beyond 1000 kms. from pit head; and
(b)   Power plants located in critically polluted areas, Urban sectors and in ecologically sensitive
 zones.
(Para 24)
14.       The Committee during its study visit to Regional Research Laboratory, Bhubneshwar, held a meeting on 31 st
 January, 2005 with the management of the laboratory and the scientists thereof.  During the course of the meeting, inter
 alia the Committee was informed that a certain section of the research of the laboratory is being directed towards
 biological desulfurisation of coal for reducing the sulfur dioxide  and nitrious oxide emissions i.e.  SO2 and NOX into the
 atmosphere during extract of coal from mines and their subsequent burning.  The Committee was also informed that

 priority areas.
(Para 27)

 considered by the Ministry of Environment & Forests:
