        The solubility of additional carbon dioxide in the ocean surface water decreases with rising concentrations. 
 Thus, the relative oceanic uptake of carbon dioxide is reduced at higher concentrations.
·        The land vegetations may serve as an additional medium term sink for anthropogenic carbon emissions.
·        The radio-active greenhouse forcing grows only logarithmically with increasing carbon dioxide and Green
 House Gases (GHG) emissions.
(Para 28)
18.       The environment friendly performance objectives and mechanisms for tracking progress in achieving the prime
 objective of the aforesaid model for the growth of the oil industry on the one hand and socio-economic sustainability on
 the other, the implementation of socio-environmental policies involving oil companies and the Ministry of Environment &
 Forest requires combination of technological advances and innovative approaches.
 (Para 29)
19.       The Committee is of the opinion that for addressing the key issues pertaining to the transition of a carbon based
 economy to a hydrogen economy, the Ministry of Environment and Forests needs to promote the following:
§
         Promote more rapid dissemination and use of efficient, existing commercial technology in strategic and
 environmentally sensitive areas of the country.
§         Encourage the development and use of innovative, currently non-commercial technologies.
§         Enhance the ability of all oil sector companies to achieve and utilize advanced and efficient technologies, and
§         Improve scientific understanding by addressing well-known uncertainties, in the adoption and implementation of
 efficient technologies.
(Para 30)
20.       The Committee is happy to note that Global Positioning System (GPS) is also being used for recording the
 coordinates of the collection site and mapping the distribution in the area. 
(Para 31)
21.       The Committee is also  given to understand that person undertaking survey is at least M.Sc. in Botany  with good
 knowledge of herbarium methodology and taxonomy and also has a very sound physique and normal sight, and should be
 ready to trek in remote, inaccessible areas.
(Para 32)
22.       BSI has further intimated that survey reports normally contain a general information about the area surveyed
 including a small vegetational account, significant features of flora of the region supplemented with photographs and total
 number of samples collected during the survey.
(Para 33)
23.       The Committee while appreciating the process adopted by the Botanical Survey for framing survey methodology
 including norms for designing survey report would also like to suggest that the Ministry  should examine and review the
 guidelines in view of their experiences and problems faced.
(Para 34)

25.       Moreover, IFPS is of significant importance not only for the maintenance of existing forest cover and natural
 regeneration but also achieving the National goal of achieving forest and tree cover to 25% by 2007 and 33% by 2012. 
 But the transfer of the scheme to the States may not help in achieving the stipulated 33% target as some States always
 complain about the hindrance of development activities due to thick forest cover in their States. In all likelihood, such
 State may refrain from utilizing the allocation on the IFPS and money can be utilized for some other purpose. The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that IFPS should not be transferred to the States and continues to be administered as a
 Centrally-Sponsored Scheme.
(Para 40)
26.       The Committee recommends that to accelerate the pace of research and to provide expertise in different fields of
 forestry research, the Ministry should impart forestry education and develop forestry curricula at various levels. It should
 also strengthen the infrastructure and technical capabilities of the universities providing forestry education with necessary
 grants. The Ministry should also organize seminars and workshops, besides conducting special courses on various forestry
 themes for the academic advancement of the foresters and those interested in the field of forestry.
(Para 43)
27.       The Committee expresses its serious concern over the sudden disappearance of the Tigers from Sariska Tiger
 Reserve. The Committee feels that the negligence of Forest staff coupled with the large scale poaching has cost the
 country dear. Conditions in most of the national parks are more or less same, posing a clear danger to protected animal
 species. Poaching is not a new phenomenon but the poachers are now more advanced with latest weapons and very
 powerful communication network, making the lackadaisically managed tiger reserves easy picking. In contrast, forest
 guards are usually equipped with a wooden stick and most of the times without any means of communication. Taking note
 of this alarming situation, the Committee is of considered opinion that a Special Task Force at the central or state level
 with the involvement of para-military forces must be constituted to combat the menace of poaching of wild-life.
(Para 49)
28.       Moreover, the Ministry should also involve the villagers living in and around National parks/Tiger reserves to
 prevent the poaching as they are aware of the tentative movement of the poachers but because of poachers’ threats or any
 other compulsion, they refrain from coming out openly to help the forest Department to catch the poachers.  The
 Committee strongly recommends that all vacant positions should be filled immediately and at no time any tiger reserve in
 the country should be left with the junior officers.
 
(Para 50)
29.       The Committee feels that Project Elephant is a major project of the Ministry but getting less importance. The tusk
 is as precious as tiger skin and not immune from Poachers. Therefore, the Committee recommends that Elephants should
 also be protected from the poaching and effective strategy should be evolved for their preservation. In view of decline in
 Tiger population in Sariska, the Committee suggests the Ministry to undertake an evaluation of Elephant population and
 take corrective measures accordingly.
(Para 52)
30.       The Committee recommends that sufficient allocation must be provided to various States for habitat management
 mitigation of human-elephant conflict, payment of ex-gratia relief for loss of human life and crops caused by wild
 elephants, strengthening of anti-poaching measures, capacity building of the field staff, registration of domesticated
 elephant using microchips etc.
(Para 53)
31.       The Committee recommends that endangered species need to be preserved while the population of other animals
 should be sustainably managed.  The Ministry should generate data and information on maintaining a sustainable
 population of each animal for their scientific management.  Research initiatives in the field of sustainable use of wildlife
 products are needed.  The Ministry should cover not only wildlife research and training but also the socio-economic
 aspects of wildlife conservation.
(Para 54)
32.       While the Committee is concerned about the protection of wildlife in the Protected Areas, it feels that wildlife

 should also be protected outside the Protected Areas and sufficient allocation should be made for the purpose.
(Para 55)
33.       The Committee is of the opinion that the destruction and depletion of forests will not only lead to loss of our
 vegetation but will also result in widespread deterioration of environment with fatal consequences to the very existence of
 all forms of life. Therefore, the Ministry should evolve mechanisms for ecological restoration of degraded forest areas and
 adjoining lands through systematic planning and implementation, in a cost effective manner. The Ministry should also
 restore fuelwood, fodder, timber and other forest produce on the degraded forest and adjoining lands in order to meet the
 demands for these items and local population including tribals should be allowed to share its products without 
 compromising the preservation of our national forests.  In addition, the Ministry should also create general awareness and
 help foster a people’s  movement for promoting afforestation and eco-development with the assistance of voluntary
 agencies, non-governmental organizations, Panchayati Raj Institutions and others and promote participatory and
 sustainable management of degraded forest areas and adjoining lands.
(Para 59)
34.       The Committee is also of the view that the Ministry should formulate an effective strategy to consider all activities,
 current and potential,that can influence forests and related social, economic, and environmental outcomes.  More focussed
 interventions are required that address issues relating to opportunity, empowerment, and livelihood security of the poor
 people who depend on forests in different ways.  A broader livelihood approach, covering productive capacity,
 institutional and legal structures, market access and tenure must be adopted that puts forests into the broader context of
 rural development.  The focus should be on improving governance (especially correcting major distortions in incentives
 and markets that are reducing the value of the forest resource), and the development of efficient markets and encouraging
 competitive private sector participation in the sector.  More focused interventions are required for maintaining natural
 forests for eco-system protection and sustaining the global and local forest values.
(Para 60)
35.       The Committee recommends that the Ministry should have taken the initiative for strengthening Environment
 Education in the formal educational curriculum and for this purpose, it should vigorously interact with the University
 Grants Commission (UGC), the National Council for Educational Research and Training (NCERT), the Ministry of
 Human Resource Development, All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) and the State Education Department
 to ensure integration of environmental concept into the curriculum. Moreover, talented persons should be encouraged with
 remunerative schemes and attractive pay scales to do research on environment related issues.
(Para 63)
36.       The Committee also recommends that to promote and awareness among the students, the scientists, planners,
 policy makers, etc., and also for exchange of information and knowledge on different aspects of ocean science and
 technology, the Ministry should sponsor, organize and conduct seminars/workshops/symposia, etc.  These measures will
 help the Ministry in building up a skilled human resource base in environmental science, besides augmenting existing
 infrastructure facilities.  
(Para 64)
37.       The Committee recommends that National Mangrooves Afforestation Programme should be designed so that new
 research projects on the priority areas of mangrove and coral reef conservation for supplementing Management Action
 Plan of strategically identified mangrove areas is accorded importance.
(Para 70.1)
 
38.       The Ministry has submitted that it is most unlikely to achieve the target of cleaning of major rivers by 2007 and it
 may extend the target to XI Plan.   On this submission of the Ministry, the Committee express its serious concern on the
 tardy pace of execution of river cleaning project and recommends that all causative factors for the slow progress of the
 project be identified and sorted out expeditiously and all out efforts be made to accelerate the momentum required to
 achieve the stipulated targets within their scheduled time limit and cost estimates.
(Para 78)
39.       The Committee feels that lakes are critical in sustaining the environmental health of our country.  Acting as a huge
 reservoir, they not only provide water but also recharge and replenish the ground water and prevent floods.  Besides, their
 importance from the point of view of beauty, and aesthetics are well acclaimed. But the Committee is not satisfied with
 the lackadaisical approach of the Ministry in undertaking the lake conservation schemes.  They are moving without any
 specific targets and objectives.  The Committee is anguished to note that even after repeated recommendations of the
 Committee, the Ministry has not come out with any specific targets to be achieved during a particular period.  The
 Committee expresses its serious concern and recommends that the Government should formulate short-term and long-
term plans on lake conservation with specific targets and should proceed further in that direction as per those targets. 
(Para 84)

BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2005-06
Recommendation
The Committee finds that the pace of expenditure by the Department has not been uniform. However, it notes that
 Department has sustained the tempo of its activities and made optimum utilization of the funds allocated to it in third and
 fourth quarter.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that meaningful and relevant programmes and policies should be
 formulated for regular infusion of funds in various projects/schemes in all quarters of the financial year and the total
 utilization of plan outlays.                                                                                                                                                           
 (Para 8)
Action Taken by the Department
            The variation in the expenditure, particularly in the third and fourth quarter of 2004-05, is primarily due to making a
 single payment towards acquisition of new research vessel for which the final approval was obtained in the second quarter
 of 2004-05.  Besides, the four new programmes undertaken during the 10
th Plan were cleared in all aspects only in the year
 2003-04 for which initial payments had to be in lumpsump particularly towards infrastructure.  Secondly, the low
 expenditure in the first quarter has also resulted due to adjustments of previous unspent balance available with the
 participating agencies.    Currently, efforts are also underway to re-formulate some of the programmes and policies towards
 achieving regular infusion of funds in all the quarters of the financial year and total utilization of plan outlays.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply of the Department. 
POST-TSUNAMI ASSESSMENT OF CORAL HEALTH IN ANDAMAN WATERS AND   INDIAN OCEAN
Recommendation
The Committee has been given to understand that massive influx of seawater borne by Tsunami on 26/12/2004
 severely affected several section of coral population in Andaman & Nicobar and in certain strategic areas of Indian Ocean. 
 The Committee has been further given to understand that four research vessels, namely, Sagar Purvi, Sagar Paschimi, Sagar
 Sampada and Sagar Kanya of the Department of Ocean Development were commissioned in these waters to undertake,
 interalia, a detailed assessment of destruction inflicted by Tsunami on the coral health of these regions.
The Committee, however, finds that assessment with regard to the impact of Tsunami on coral reefs in Andaman &
 Nicobar Islands is somewhat contradictory.  As per the Annual Report of the Department for 2004-05, coral reefs have been
 severely affected by Tsunami whereas Secretary of the Departmentin his presentation before theCommittee on the 1
st April,
 2005, maintained that by and large coral reefs were unaffected.  The Committee, therefore, feels that a detailed physical
 verification of coral health is necessary to assess accurately the status of their health in post-Tsunami scenario.  The
 Committee would like to have a factual note in this regard, inter-alia, giving the future contingency plan in case of such
 natural eventuality.
(Para 10)
Action Taken by the Department
            The activities relating to the assessment of the damages caused to the coral reefs in Andaman and Nicobar islands
 including undertaking coral reef habitat restoration projects etc. fall within the purview of the Ministry of Environment and
 Forests (MoEF).  The Department of Ocean Development (DOD), under the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area
 Management Programme, has taken up only mapping of coral reefs using GIS, mainly to demonstrate the use of the GIS

 technique in coral reef mapping and monitoring in Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands.
Point raised by the Committee
What are the procedure and benefits of Coral reef mapping and monitoring in    A&N Islands and Lakshadweep
 under the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM)? What are the actual benefits derived therefrom?
Clarification by the Department
The Department of Ocean Development, under the ICMAM Programme, has proposed to demonstrate the use of GIS
 in mapping of coral reefs in Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshdweep.  The procedures for coral reef mapping and
 monitoring include qualitative and quantitative analysis of coral reefs using Line Intersect Methods (LIT) with the help of
 SCUBA diving equipment.  During the survey, accurate position of investigating area is recorded using the sophisticated
 GPS equipment namely Arc Pad.  The data collected is brought into GIS Environment with the help of Software called Arc
 Info and Arc View.  The plotted data with respect to coordinate indicates the status of the corals at the time of
 Investigation.  This technique is useful in monitoring the health of the corals in the subsequent years by the local
 authorities.  The ICMAM Directorate has already developed this technique for Andaman and Nicobar Administration and
 Lakshadweep Administration through training programmes so as to facilitate them for continuously monitoring the health of
 the corals.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
The Committee apprehends that certain branching corals like Acropara Cytherea also known as stag horn corals
 which are common in Andaman waters might have been affected severely by the Tsunami onslaughts.
The Committee is, however, of the opinion that unless comprehensive planning is made, neither proper and deep
 assessment of the heart of coral in these areas could be made nor any critical measures could be designed to remedy the
 health of these corals in the affected areas.  The Committee, therefore, understands that in order to have a very successful
 picture of the entire assessment scenario, the following measures need to be considered by the Department before
 undertaking major audit of coral health in these areas:
i)
                    Norms of audit through symbiotic studies of coral health will have to be mapped.
ii)                   New insights into the role of cell suicide and apoptosis in bleaching of corals should also have to be
 developed.
iii)                 A detailed mapping of coral stress tolerance is necessary to be assessed and mapped.
iv)                 The Behavior of coral reef fish is needed to be assessed on a comparative pilot-scale basis in coral areas
 which are severely affected by Tsunami and areas which are less affected or are not affected at all by the
 Tsunami onslaught.
v)                  Since reef bleaching and mortaity are highly co-related, the study of coral bleaching in detail is also
 necessary since this could be linked to global climate change specially elevated sea water temperature and
 high solar irradiance.                                                                                                      (Para 11)
Action Taken by the Department
            The Department of Ocean Development (DOD) under the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management
 Programme has taken up only mapping of coral reefs using GIS, mainly to demonstrate the use of the GIS technique in
 coral reef mapping and monitoring in Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep islands.  However, the subject of coral reefs
 pertains to Ministry of Environment and Forests (MoEF) and all the recommendations made by the Committee are pertinent

Recommendation
The Committee feels that successful restoration and management of coral health require a more realistic and
 historically informed understanding of the ecology of near-pristine condition of coral reefs that can only be obtained by a
 combination of retrospective analyses, modeling and intensive studies of eco-systemstructure andfunction of the very few
 isolated reefs that have escaped intensive exploitation by Tsunami onslaughts.  The Committee understands that studies
 based on an index known as DI, i.e., comparative Deterioration Index of community for corals will have to be undertaken
 for deriving a comparative picture of analysis of the health deterioration of different corals groups in these regions.  The DI
 values can show the likelihood of some of the corals getting rehabilitated early and some corals more at a later stage which
 is proportional to the destructive index of each coral communities following the Tsunami onslaughts.  The training should
 be given to surveyors  for fast yielding of elaborate data based upon deterioration index of these coralcommunities so that
 relatively accurate picture could be framed for the subsequent restoration.  Moreover, the DI approach can serve as an
 efficient tool for Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) Selection and Management.  The Marine Protected Areas (MPA) is the
 primary form of protection in the marine coastal zone and could be used as a spearhead for marine conservation including
 the restoration of coral health.  The MPA could be directly linked with DI index and the coefficient of the DI picture can
 give details for restoration of the marine protected areas.  Apart from this, identification of new Heat Shock Protein (HSP)
 of marine invertebrates is expected to enable rapid and accurate quantitative monitoring of short term and long-term
 fluctuations in marine eco-system. The expression of specific stress proteins present in certain coral community can be
 identified as early warning system for future changes in coral communities following Tsunami disturbances and also the
 ability of reef eco-system to withstand global changes could also be
 assessed.                                                                                                                                                    (Para 12)
Action Taken by the Department
            The activities relating to  the need to assess the damages caused to the coral reefs including mapping of coral reefs,
 undertaking coral reef habitat restoration projects etc, are the subject matters pertain to Ministry of Environment and Forests
 (MoEF).  The Department of Ocean Development (DOD) has taken up only mapping of coral reefs using GIS, mainly to
 demonstrate the use of the GIS technique  in coral reef mapping and monitoring in Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep
 islands under the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management programme.
Recommendation
The Committee also feels the turbidity and terrigenous which have been transported by the Tsunami to different coral
 reefs from other areas should also be measured to understand the coefficient of DI (Deterioration Index).
            Apart from this, the comparative gene flow, migration of sea bio community from other areas and relative return of
 the elementary sea bio community to their original coral habitats following Tsunami can also give some idea about
 comparative health of the coral resources.                                                                                                               (Para 13)
Action Taken by the Department
            The subject of coral reefs pertains to Ministry of Environment and forests (MoEF).  The recommendations made by
 the Committee are being undertaken by MoEF.  The Department of Ocean Development (DOD) under the Integrated
 Coastal and Marine Area Management programme has taken up only mapping of coral reefs using GIS, mainly to
 demonstrate the use of the GIS technique in coral reef mapping and monitoring in Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep
 islands.
Recommendation
The Committee further feels that while assessing coral health, the incidence of coral diseases may also be studied

 because in most cases etiology of greater number of coral diseases are still unclear and the nature of relationship between

The Committee would also suggest the development of coral nursery project by the Department because this will

            The development of technologies in Mining and Metallurgy under the programme on polymetallic nodules is aimed

Recommendation
The Committee recommends that the Department should study the icy continent’s atmospherics and ozone

Action Taken by the Department
Studies on ozone hole, ice core and climate changes
Studies undertaken by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and National Physical Laboratory (NPL) have
 provided insight to understand the temporal and spatial dynamics of ozone hole phenomenon. Analysis of ice cores obtained
 by Indian Scientists have provided insights into the changes in the earth’s climate during the past two centuries.  A high-
tech Ice-core laboratory has been established at NCAOR, Goa under its long term ice-core-drilling & research programme. 
 Palynostratigraphic studies of lake sediments have thrown light on the nature and dynamics of paleoenviroments.  Satellite
 imageries and GPS based studies are included to expand the scope and dynamics of Antarctic ice sheet and sea-ice. 
 NCAOR, Goa has recently published an Atlas on Antarctic Sea-Ice using satellite data over a period of two years.

 have been studied by national institutes.  Out of 125 new microbes found in Antarctica, 20 microbes have been identified by

 survival of life forms in extreme cold conditions and research on cold adaptation of bacteria has led to technological
 innovation in biodegradation of wastes in extreme cold conditions.  Recently, the Department has organized a National
 seminar in collaboration with Ocean Science and Technology Cell (OSTC), Microbiology, Goa University to work out a
 detailed research programme in Antarctic and Marine Microbiology.  Besides, frontier institutes like Birbal Sahni Institute
 of Paleobotany, Lucknow and IIT, Kanpur has undertaken palynological studies in schirmacher Oasis using lake sediments. 
 It has generated valuable data which will help to understand the changes of vegetation over a period of time.
Relation of the Antarctic plate with the Indian plate.
Premier organizations like Geological Survey of India (GSI), National Geophysical Research Institute (NGRI) have
 undertaken studies on the relation between the Antarctic plate and India plate.  There are strong evidences suggesting that
 the Indian Eastern Ghat Mobile Belt (EGMB) and Enderby Land, East Antarctica shared a common Mesoproterozoic (1100
 Ma) evolutionary history.  The east Gondwana Land, then comprised of India, part of East Antarctica and Australia while
 the west Gondwanaland comprised a small fragment of South India, Africa, South America and central Droning Maud
 Land, east Antarctica (area in which Indian Antarctic Station, Maitri is located).  Indian earth Scientists have been working
 in the area of exposing rocks which have been involved in the Pan-African orogeny.  The Indian base has offered a unique
 opportunity to study the processes that were responsible for amalgamating east and west Gondwana. This, in turn, has also
 helped them to understand the processes involved in the evolution of continents through geological past with co-relatable
 implication on the evolution of Indian subcontinent.  Geochronological studies have helped to trace back the chronology of
 tectonometamorphic events.

Clean energy technology.

 340-watt wind turbine was installed near ‘Nanda Devi’ hut for performance study.  Valuable data was collected on the
 installation and performance of the wind battery charger etc.  A new data retrieval software was designed and installed. 
 NCAOR is developing plan to upgrade facilities at Maitri and also for a new research base, where clean energy technology
 will be a priority, as also mandated under the Environmental Protocol of Antarctic Treaty.
Impact of human activity on Antarctica.

 permanent environmental monitoring laboratory has also been set up by NCAOR in Maitri.  Baseline studies on the major
 wild animal population in the area of Indian operation have been carried out by the Wildlife Institute of India and a long
 term monitoring programme is in place.

Recommendations
The Committee is of the opinion that any change in ocean geochemistry/bio-chemistry during the extraction or
 drilling of the gas from the hydrates should be viewed from the point of view of its potential polluting capacity.      ( Para 50
 )
The Committee is of opinion that methane can appear in the marine environment not only due to microbial and
 biochemical decomposition of the organic substance in bottom sediments, but also as a result of the natural bottom seepage
 of combustible gases from shallow oil and gas bearing structures.  The entire process can lead to intensive vertical flows of
 hydrocarbon gases from the bottom to the sea surface accompanied some times by gas hydrates decomposition. ( Para 57 )
The Committee is also of the opinion that an important anthropogenic source of gas hydrocarbons in the water
 environment is the offshore drilling accidents.  The environmental consequences of offshore drilling accidents can be very
 hazardous.  Such accidents may cause long-term release of large amount of natural gas into the water accompanied by self-
inflaming of the gas.                                                                                                                  ( Para 62 )
The Committee, in view of the above, recommends that the Department of Ocean Development while dealing with

 Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
The repercussion of gas leakage on ocean fishes are extremely sensitive.  The fish response to a toxic gas leakage is
 extremely high in comparison to its response to other dissolved or suspended toxicants.  The gas could rapidly penetrate
 into the organism of the fish through the gills and disturb the main functional systems. There is external evidence of its
 disturbance which changes the behaviour of this aquatic animal like fish excitement etc.  The Committee has also been
 given to understand that the time interval between the moment the fishes come in contact with such toxic gas and the first
 symptom of poison surfacing on these organisms are extremely short.  The entire toxicological effect could be assessed by
 the nature of the toxicant, its toxicity in water, exposure time and evaluating by environmental degradation.  Gas emboli
 could be the general effect typical to all types of fishes.  These include rupture of tissues, enlarging of swim bladder,
 disturbances of circulatory system and a number of other pathological changes.  The Committee would, therefore, like to
 recommend that deep study of water toxicology of saturated aliphatic hydrocarbons of methane should be undertaken by
 Department of Ocean Development.  The Committee further urges for the development of toxicity data on different gaseous
 poisons which could reveal some general features of interaction between gaseous traces and marine
 organisms.                                                                  ( Para 63 )

CHOICE OF FUEL FOR FAST BREEDER REACTOR (FBR)
Recommendation
The Committee welcomes the idea and feels that this advanced fuel will reduce the cost of production of electricity through
 Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR) and not only that by reducing the capital cost of production of electricity the plant life span will
 also increase by incorporating better safety features for these reactors.  Faster the breeding, quicker will be the rise in the
 FBR’s capacity. Other nuclear fuels for FBR and PFBR (Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor) like oxide, nitride and carbide
 fuels may now take the back seat for being used as fuels for FBR.                     
(Para 25.1)
The choice of fuels for breeder reactors, the Committee feels, is a choice between doubling time versus the cost of
 production. The Committee, however, feels that oxide fuel with a ratio of 30% plutonium oxide and 70% uranium oxide is a
 well-proven fuel world over.  In India, however, mixed oxide fuel (MOX) could be used for Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor
 (PFBR).                                                                                                                                             (Para 25.2)
The Committee, on the other hand, feels that carbide fuel is very difficult to fabricate on a large scale as it is highly
 pyrophoric and is highly susceptible to oxidation and hydrolysis.  Moreover, reprocessing of spent carbide fuel is difficult
 as it is difficult to dissolve in nitric acid and leaves behind organic complexes.  Apart from this, the carbide fuel  has low
 burn up value in comparison to oxide fuel. The fuel ‘burn-up’ in a nuclear reactor refers to the amount of energy extracted
 from the fuel before it is discharged for storage or reprocessing.  Higher the burn-up, lesser will be the fuel cycle cost.          
                                                                     (Para 25.3)
The Committee understands that cost of power production comes down with increased burn up value.  Also oxide fuel is
 easy to fabricate as it is not pyrophoric and hence needs no inert atmosphere during fabrication.  The Committee is,
 therefore, of the opinion that use of oxide fuel would be more vital for making a foray into fast breeder power
 plants.                          (Para 25.4)
The Committee understands that breeder technology works on the principle of self-sustenance and ability to produce more
 plutonium than it actually consumes to produce power.  The breeding ratio, which is 1.1 in case of oxide fuel, is 1.2 – 1.4 in
 case of carbide and nitride fuels.  While it is maximum in case of metallic fuel i.e. 1.4 – 1.5 and hence doubling time       
 (i.e. surplus plutonium produce to start a new reactor) is shortest in case of a metallic, carbide and nitride fuels respectively
 in comparison to oxide fuel.                                                      (Para 25.5)
The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that doubling time becomes paramount when the country goes on
 commissioning new reactors.  Hence, the stress on using advanced fuel is necessary.  The Committee feels that making
 technology available for producing power at cheaper cost may gain more public acceptance, which is vital to breeder
 programme.   (Para 25.6)
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that lower burn up by using carbide fuel is not economical since fabrication and
 reprocessing would increase cost of power production.  However, the Committee feels that long-term strategy calls for fuels
 with shorter doubling time.  Sometimes it is felt that nitride fuel seems to be more preferable due to its easier reprocessing
 and improved performance.                                                                                                        (Para 25.7)
 
The Committee recommends that the Department of Atomic Energy may like to consider the following choices:-
i)          High breeding ratio and shorter doubling time
ii)         High burn up value and less fuel cycle cost
iii)         Faster breeding and quicker capacity of fast breeder reactor
iv)        High burn up value and low production cost of power; and between
v)         Easy fabrication and reprocessing and low cost of power production before ending itself finally by choosing the most
 ideal fuel for its FBR and PFBR programme.                                                             (Para 25.8)
 
The Committee feels that without choosing the best options from among the above series, the choice of fuel for future
 reactors of the Department of Atomic Energy may not be optimally fulfilled unless maximum efficiency in power
 production is derived at least possible opportunity cost.

 140,000 MWd/t without any fuel pin failure.  The Reprocessing Group at IGCAR has also successfully demonstrated the
 capability to reprocess mixed carbide fuel of 50,000 & 100,000 MWd/t burn-up.
However, it is to be noted that the reprocessing technology for carbide fuel has not been established on a commercial scale
 in any country. Also, since the carbide fuel is air-sensitive, difficulties are envisaged in the large scale manufacture of
 carbide fuel. On the other hand, the performance of mixed oxide fuel in fast reactors has been proven in other countries and
 sufficient technical data is also available in published literature on their properties. Also, the fuel has been fabricated and
 reprocessed on a commercial scale in other countries. Considering the difficulties associated with fabrication and
 reprocessing of carbide fuel on a commercial scale as well as the lack of international experience on carbide fuel cycle, the
 well proven mixed oxide fuel with lower PuO
2  content ( 21% PuO2  in inner zone and 28% PuO2 in outer zone) has been
 selected for the 500 MWe PFBR.
 It is envisaged that in addition to PFBR, 4 more FBRs of 500 MWe capacity are planned to be constructed by the year 2020
 as part of DAE Vision 2020 Programme.  Since the main objective of these reactors is to prove the techno-commercial
 viability of the FBR technology when multiple units are constructed, mixed oxide fuel has been considered for these
 reactors also. However, through the use of better materials and design, it is aimed to improve the burn-up of the oxide fuel
 as well as the breeding ratio in these reactors.
It is realized in the department that the rapid growth of fast reactors is only possible through adoption of fuels and fuel
 cycles which would ensure higher breeding and consequently, lower doubling time. It is therefore necessary to switch over
 to fuels like metallic fuel, which has higher breeding ratio. It is at the same time recognized that a good amount of R&D
 efforts is required to establish a reactor and fuel cycle based on metallic fuel, since the experience with respect to metallic
 fuel is also limited.
IGCAR has therefore taken up the planning of necessary R & D to establish the fuel cycle, carry out test irradiations in
 FBTR and gain sufficient experience with respect to the metallic fuel with the long term goal of establishing fast reactors
 with metallic fuel. The core configuration of the later 500 MWe FBRs will be chosen in such a way that the metallic fuel
 can replace some of the oxide fuel bundles.
             Thus, the approach in the Department is to proceed with oxide fuel for the next four 500 MWe FBRs and then
 switch over to metallic fuel to get lower doubling time.  This approach gives continuity in the programme and also adequate
 time to generate necessary data on the utilization of metallic fuel.
During Mid-Term Appraisal (MTA) of Plan Projects, a new Scheme has been introduced for initiating advance action in
 R&D activities to be taken up for development of metallic fuels.  The said project is already sanctioned.  All efforts are
 made to begin with the development of metallic fuel for FBRs, in the X Plan itself, so as to achieve the long-term goals.

The Department has stated that in addition to PFBRs, 4 more FBRs of 500 MWe capacity are planned to be constructed by

Clarification by the Department
The strong correlation between per capita electricity generation and per capita gross domestic product (GDP) is well known. 
 Therefore, to realize the high growth rates envisaged by the country, electricity generation has to increase in tandem.
A group in the Department studied  available information on GDP and population growth forecasts, trends with regard to
 energy-GDP elasticity and electricity intensity of industries and developed a scenario for the growth of electricity. 
 Scenarios have been developed by other agencies as well, though the numbers differ depending on the assumptions made
 for building the scenarios.  The message from all such exercises is the same and that is, India is a poor fuel resource country
 and there is a need to tap every fuel resource to meet India’s energy needs.  The contribution of nuclear energy, therefore,
 has to be increased at the fastest possible pace so that nuclear electricity is able to meet about a quarter of the national
 electricity demand after about five decades and gets poised to make still higher contribution in the subsequent years.
Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) together with other institutions under the DAE framework has a
 mature knowledge of the Pressurized Heavy Water Reactor (PHWR) technology.  The known reserves of uranium in the
 country can support about 10GWe of installed electricity capacity based on PHWRs for a life time of 40 years at 80%
 capacity factor.  With 12 PHWRs under operation and 6 under construction, about half the first stage of the nuclear power

FOOD IRRADIATION
Recommendation
The Committee, therefore, feels that some precautionary measures should be taken by the Department of Atomic Energy
 while irradiating foods so that the possible health risks involved before consumption of irradiated food could be effectively
 dealt with. In this connection, Radiological Safety, Microbiological Safety, Nutritional adequacy and Toxicological Safety
 measures may be kept in view.                                                                                              (Para 35)
Action Taken by the Department
The safety and nutritional adequacy of the irradiated foods have been thoroughly studied for past several decades. Perhaps
 no other method of food processing has been subjected to such a thorough assessment of safety as the radiation processing.
 The various aspects of wholesomeness and safety of radiation- processed foods have been studied in great detail. These
 include investigations on Possibility of induced radioactivity, Microbiological safety, Safety of chemical changes,
 Nutritional adequacy, Animal feeding and Human trials.
Only after studying the results of the above and decades of research, the technology has been approved for commercial use.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
The Committee also feels that long term effects of irradiated food should be studied thoroughly from the point of view of the
 fact that how ionizing radiation alters chemical structure of food material.  This could be managed if a monitored safe label
 of exposure of food to radiation is laid down by the Department of Atomic Energy.                                              (Para 36)
Action Taken by the Department
The changes that take place in food material as a result of processing by radiation have been thoroughly studied. The long-
term effects of consuming radiation-processed foods have been studied in multi-generation feeding trials on animals. Human
 volunteers have eaten irradiated foods for long periods without any side effects. Astronauts and cosmonauts have been
 eating irradiated foods during space flights.  At the energies of the gamma rays from cobalt-60 (1.3 MeV) and those
 recommended for using X-rays (5 MeV) and accelerated electrons                  (10 MeV), there is no induction of
 radioactivity. The microbiological aspects of radiation- processed foods have been studied in detail. None of these studies
 have indicated that foods preserved by radiation pose any special problems in relation to microflora. It has been found that
 there are no unique radiolytic products formed and free radicals in the system disappear depending on the nature of the
 commodity and its post-irradiation storage and treatment. In fact, the chemical differences between radiation processed
 foods and non-irradiated foods are too small to be detected easily. Though rough composition of food remains largely
 unchanged, some losses in vitamins may be encountered. However, these losses are often minor.
In 1980 a joint Expert Committee on Food Irradiation (JECFI) consisting of Food and Agricultural organization
 (FAO)/Internal Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)/World Health organization (WHO) reviewed the extensive data on
 wholesomeness collected up to that time and concluded that irradiation of any commodity up to an over all dose of 10 kGy
 presents no toxicological hazards and introduces no special nutritional or microbiological problems. An Expert Group
 constituted by WHO in 1994 once again reviewed the wholesomeness data available till then and validated the earlier
 conclusion of JECFI. In 1998 another Expert Group constituted by WHO/FAO/IAEA affirmed the safety of food irradiated
 to doses above 10 kGy. Codex Alimentarius Commission that sets standards for food worldwide and the World Trade
 Organization has also recognized the technique.   In addition, a number of scientific bodies and associations have also
 endorsed the safety of radiation-processed foods. These include naming a few:
American Medical Association
The American Gastroentrological Association
American Dietetics Association
American Meat Institute
Institute of Food Technologists
In 1994 Government of India amended Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (1954) Rules and approved irradiation of onion,

Recommendation
The Committee feels that high voltage electron beams generated from linear accelerators which could be a better alternative
 for food irradiation technology than application of Cobalt-60 and cesium 137 because the penetration depth of gama
 irradiation is not there and with shorter exposure time, the food could be safe with this method.  With all other existing
 methods of food irradiation, the Committee feels only low efficiency could be maintained combined with high cost of
 production of irradiated foods.                                                                         (Para 37)
Action Taken by the Department
It is possible to use both machine sources (accelerated electrons and X-rays) as well as radioisotope sources (cobalt-60 and
 cesium-137) emitting gamma rays. Both have their advantages and limitations. The choice of the source would depend upon
 several product and process parameters.  In case of electrons, the depth of penetration is a major problem, that can be solved
 by their conversion to X-rays. However, the conversion of electrons to X-rays is not economical.  On the other hand, cobalt
 sources are very rugged and reliable.

The Committee feels that in order to make the food irradiation a success, the following factors for judging the bactericidal

Kinds and species of organism composing the food.
Numbers of organisms present because the dose of radiation should be proportional to the number of organism present in the
 food.
Composition of the food.
Presence and absence of oxygen
The physical state of the food during irradiation including moisture content and temperature.
Condition of the organism, that is, its age, temperature for growth etc.          (Para 38)

SEISMOLOGY
Recommendation                                                                              
            It is a well-known fact that exact prediction of earthquake is not possible and the science of earthquake prediction
 has not reached a mature stage as yet, though seismologists all over the world are working hard in this area.  It will be a
 great service to humanity if the seismologists succeed one day in their efforts and save the humanity from great devastations

 suitable building laws in the country, especially in the areas which are more sensitive seismologically.  It has to be ensured
 that all construction activities are undertaken with due regard to earthquake.  As regards the existing structures, the
 Department may prepare a plan how to protect them from possible earthquakes in future. The Committee also feels that the

Recommendation
            The Committee feels that thrust of weather forecasting should be on its accuracy and recommends that the

 27)
Action taken by the Department
            The NCMRWF continuously makes efforts to improve accuracy and range of its forecasts and advisories.  This is a
 achieved by improving in various components of its numerical weather prediction system, such as quantity of data that is
 ingested in the forecast system, quality control of various data available for ingesting in the system, maximize use of
 satellite data, develop algorithms for assimilation of new types of data both from Indian satellite and satellite of other
 countries.  The accuracy and range of forecasts based on numerical weather prediction (NWP) model, which are complex
 general circulation models, depends upon the representativeness of initial conditions, proper representation of physical
 processes and most importantly the resolution.  Even though the predication over tropical and Indian Monsoon region still
 remains a formidable challenge for the modeling community of the world, the effort to improve the forecast nevertheless
 continues.  At NCMRWF we have experimented with various physical processed such as boundary layer, radiation, and
 cumulous convection processes to improve the forecasts.  We have also significantly enhanced use of non-conventional data
 from satellite in our assimilation system.  Most importantly, we have increased resolution of our NWP model.
            At NCMRWF the global model is being run at a higher spatial resolution of wave number 170 (equivalent to
 horizontal resolution of 75 km) in experimental mode and the operational model which is of 150 km resolution is running
 regularly up to a time scale of one week.  Also the operational model is run for extended range of 45 days once in month to
 get the accumulated monthly rainfall for the next month. Improvement in the accuracy of forecast is a continued process
 and experiments in insertion of accurate and reliable satellite data and improved techniques of data assimilation are
 continuing.  Also regional model with spatial resolution of about 30 km are being run regularly to supplement the global
 model forecasts.  At NCMRWF, we are also in the process of development collaboration with major global NWP centers,
 notably that of the USA and UK, to improve our mathematical models.
            The number of Agro Advisory Services (AAS) units is being continuously augmented and now stands at 107.
Points raised by the committee
What are the services offered by Agro Advisory Services (AAS)? How effective have they been in helping farmers?
 
Clarification by the Department
Agro-meteorological Advisory Service (AAS) of NCMRWF
Services offered by AAS
         The main objective of NCMRWF is to provide medium range weather forecast based AAS to the farmers of the
 country.The NCMRWF is providing AAS on experimental basis to the farming community, at the scale of agro-climatic
 zone, based on location specific medium range weather forecast. The country is divided into 127 agro climatic zones with
 each zone covering about 3 5 districts. At present NCMRWF has established AAS units in 107 agro climatic zones.  The
 location specific forecasts valid for 4 days comprising of six meteorological variables, viz., total precipitation, average
 cloudiness, average wind speed, predominant wind direction, maximum temperature and minimum temperature are derived

 NWP model outputs. These forecasts of weather elements are subjected to fine tuning through statistical and synoptic
 techniques to obtain final location specific weather forecast. They are disseminated biweekly to AAS units on every
 Tuesday and Friday over Telephone, Fax or Internet system. In addition to these parameters, forecast for weekly cumulative
 rainfall is also sent. Agricultural scientists of AMFUs which are located at SAUs, prepare weather based farm advisory
 bulletins on receipt of MRWF from NCMRWF. These bulletins contain location specific and crop specific farm level
 advisories prepared in local language & incorporate the available knowledge on crop  weather relationships.  Weather
 based agro advisories take into account the prevailing weather, soil & crop condition, and based on the weather prediction
 suggest measures/practices to minimise the losses and also, optimise input  in the form of  irrigation, fertiliser or pesticides. 
 Real time weather and climatic information are essential ingredients for development of agroadvisories. These agro-
advisories are made available to the farming community through print and electronic media and also through direct contact
 by the AAS personnel. The NCMRWF issues forecast  to Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India a week in advance
 for weather condition likely to be experienced in different parts of the country. This is being used to assess the whole
 gambit of agricultural operations viz., crop, seed, fertilizers, insecticide  situations in the country and accordingly forewarn
 concerned State Governments and other agencies with suitable remedial actions.
Usefulness of AAS to the farmers
           A need is felt to continuously monitor and evaluate the usefulness of the agro-advisory service of NCMRWF and
 refine the projections made in the project in terms of benefit from economic view points.  In order to achieve this goal, a
 separate project has been launched in collaboration with National Centre for Agriculture Economic and Policy Research
 (NCAP), New Delhi to evolve and implement an Impact assessment criteria in such a manner that one can very easily
 evaluate that how far a farmer can be benefited to save available natural resources, cost and time by utilising agroadvisories
 in making tactical decisions during his management practices. Therefore, worthiness of AAS can be judged by
 implementing this Impact criteria. The results from the project will be evaluated in due course.
        Some of the units are already assessing economic benefits accrued to the farmers in qualitative terms. For example, the
 farmers of Kovilpatti (Tamilnadu) region adopted weather based advisory of early sowing of Sorgum, Cotton and Pulses as
 good rainfall was predicted during 3
rd week of September 1995 nearly 20 days before the normal date of commencement of
 North-East monsoon rainfall. They reported substantial increase in yield in all the three crops. On the other hand, the
 farmers of Pune region who could not follow the advisory on delayed onset of southwest monsoon faced complete failure of
 crop due to inadequate moisture for germination. Farmers of Ludhiana could save 30% of the total production of Potato and
 Tomato due to frequent and light irrigation of the crop as the NCMRWF predicted occurrence of frost on account of
 considerable fall in the minimum temperature. Minimum temperature had fallen by 6-8 deg. below normal and the frost was
 realised. About 6 thousand hectares of area under potato crop was affected by frost. For Coimbatore, advisories on strong
 winds during July,1995 have helped saving standing Banana crop worth Rs 10,000 per acre. The farmers of Raipur could
 saveupto Rs.5000/- in the case of Chilly and upto Rs 10,000/- in the case of Potato per hectare due to skipping of one
 irrigation after heavy rainfall forecastat crucial phenophase  of the crops. Following the wind speed and direction forecasts,
 they saved at least 20% cost of the insecticides. Based on the cloud and temperature forecasts, they could plan their harvest
 and marketing of vegetables etc. At Madras, Specific instances have shown that by timely forecast of rainfall, farmers could
 prevent spoilage of feed, chick mortality, coccidiosis, lung infection among birds and other bacterial infections. A sudden
 increase of 2-3 deg C in the day temperature during April month in Tamilnadu (particularly in Nammakal region) may lead
 to attack of viral disease to 5-6 weeks old chicks with mortality rate upto 90%. Wide diurnal variations in temperature leads
 to chronic respiratory infection in chicken, which causes 40 to 50% loss in egg production. These results are suggestive of
 success. Clear picture may emerge on completion of systematic study being conducted.

 sophisticated equipments, the System of weather forecasting is still not accurate.  It hopes that constant  efforts will be made

 industries using nanoparticle technology for the purpose of production must be issued a guided publication containing the
 details of safety tests and precautionary measures to be taken by industries before the applications of novel properties of
 nanoparticles.  In view of the increasing research in the field of nanotechnology, the Committee feels  that DST should
 develop a model that would predict the toxicity of certain nanoparticles. The Committee, as a precautionary measure,   
 recommends that   release   of   nanoparticles   towards environment be minimized until its adverse effects are suitably
 understood.  A constant review of the mechanism should also be made, from time to time for ensuring lower exposure
 levels of manufactured nanoparticles in order to provide proper protection to workers engaged in industries and
 laboratories.  The Committee urges upon  the Department to fix a minimum exposure standard of manufactured particles
 after thoroughly examining the international regulatory limit in the field so that properly examined norms of exposure could
 be finalized from the point of view of possible medical hazards of nanoparticles.    (Para
 34)                                                                                                           
 
Recommendation
The Committee is of the opinion that since consequential findings of the application of nanotechnology bring with it a
 number of trade-offs in terms of potential environmental damage and health risk, the primary attention of DST is required in
 the field so that precautionary measures could well be designed before a complete technology base for research in the field
 is finally designed.  The Committee is of the opinion that any commercialization in the field of application of
 nanotechnology should proceed cautiously until scientific toxicological data catch up to the technology.  The scientific
 policy makers, therefore, should move swiftly and responsibly to place a moratorium on the release of new nanoparticles
 into the environment until lab protocols can be established and until toxicology studies can be undertaken and their results
 verified.  It is understood by the Committee that many nanoproponents insist that modifications should be made to the
 particles such as coating them to ensure that they are safely bio-compatible. The Committee feels that at the planning stage
 to test toxicity on several kinds of nanoparticles, a detailed programme should be made and insistence may be placed on
 user industry to reveal precise formulae which they are using to make their novel nano-products.  The Committee also feels
 that the Department of Science and Technology needs to develop an educational programme so that future engineers and
 scientists could understand the adverse health consequences of nanotechnology.                                              (Para 35)         
Recommendation
In India, since nanotechnology research is at its nascent stage, most involving dangerous products could be on a relatively
 manageable scale but the Committee apprehends that in future when relatively larger scale researches would be  undertaken,
 the extreme nanotechnology products can cause even ecological damage, which may become difficult to contain.          
                                                                     (Para 36)
Recommendation                                                            
            In view of the above, the Committee strongly feels that at each step of the product, development from raw-materials
 to the final formula, in vitro
, safety evaluation should be done and further investment in the product development should be
 done only if the previous tests in the nanotechnology development is proved to be negative, in vivo, on human volunteers.
 (Para 37)
 
Recommendation                   
                                                   
            The Committee also feels that an altogether new way of classifying nanoparticles needs to be created that takes into
 account other aspects of the nanoparticles than the toxicity being created by its size.  The full spectrum of toxicities should
 be examined minutely that might arise from nanoparticles of different compositions before its final commercial
 applications.                                                                                       (Para 38)                    
Action taken by the Department-on Recommendations 7 to 12
1.         As Nano technology, on a wide scale, is a new technology, concrete data and studies on its potential health hazards
 and toxicity effects are only slowly emerging even internationally.  Even the physical parameters of nanoparticles, which
 correlate with  health risks, toxicity, etc.  are not completely known, and methods of their measurement outside laboratory
 set-ups not very well established so far.
2.         India may be in an advantageous position to deal with such environmental risks of nanotechnology.  The work in the
 country, at the moment, is mostly limited to small-scale lab investigations on scientific aspects. Large-scale industrial
 applications are expected to take some time.  In view of this national scenario, and the world-situation mentioned above,
 DST, through the existing Nano Science and Technology Initiative (NSTI) (and the proposed Nano Science and Technology
 Mission (NSTM), has adopted the following multi-pronged approach---
At this stage of development in the subject, awareness and education is the best method of prevention. All scientists are
 being educated about the environmental and toxicity aspects of nanotechnology during the peer view of their projects and

REPORT
 
General Background
 
            Remote sensing implies sensing things which are at a distance and detecting and measuring some of their properties without
 actually coming into contact with them. The phrase "remote sensing" is now commonly used to described sensing various aspects of
 the earth system through detectors placed on satellites, aircraft or balloons. Through remote sensing one can know about forest
 cover, vegetation index, soil moisture content, geological aspects, mineralogical conditions of soil, forecast crop yields, detect crol3
 diseases, detect environmental pollution, predict optimal locations for drilling for underground water and so on. It can add to our
 knowledge of changes in climatic conditions, provide accurate and timely information with regard to snow-cover conditions in
 watershed areas and thereby help in making forecasts about the volume of snow-melt run-offs, delineate patterns of urbanisation and
 present a clear picture about the status of environment etc. Through application of remote sensing, and related new mapping
 techniques surveys can be made more accurate and meaningful.
            2. Space-based remote sensing is the process of obtaining information about the earth largely from instruments on board an
 earth observation satellite. Remote sensing satellites have extended the sweep and scope of our observational powers. Detectors
 carried on remote sensing satellites relay an immense amount of data, which must be used wisely and efficiently. Though the data
 generated by these satellites are important, it must be stressed that to get a complete and meaningful picture, this has to be used in
 association with data obtained with aircraft/balloon based remote sensing, data obtained on the ground and other information of an
 economic, sociological, census and statistical nature.
            3. Remote sensing is a very valuable tool for a country like India of vast geographical dimensions and diversity. There is no
 other way in which one can obtain so much relevant information on a rapid, repetitive, real-time basis.
 
            4. The remote sensing programme was initiated in India in the year 1970 when aerial surveys were conducted using a
 Hasselbled camera to obtain IR imagery to study coconut wilt disease in Kerala. Indian space scientists also took advantage of the
 'LANDSAT system’, which was made available by the United States; and developed ground stations and analysis capabilities to
 make full use of data from these satellites. Before venturing on our own operational remote sensing satellite system, like Indian
 Remote Sensing Satellites (IRS), Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) embarked on two experimental remote sensing
 missions viz., Bhaskara-I and II during 1975-1982. Having gained experience from these missions, the satellite-based remote
 sensing system was established in the country with the launch of the first operational Indian Remote Sensing satellite IRS-IA on
 March 17, 1988, which was followed by the successful launch of IRS-IB on August 29, 1991. These satellites are now providing
 unique opportunities to use remote sensing data for monitoring and measurement of our natural, resources and environment. From
 the viewpoint of the functioning of the hardware e.g. satellites, detectors and ground systems, these have been working to absolute
 perfection and to prescribed specifications. At; present remote sensing data are being used for several applications such as:
 agricultural crop acreage and yield estimation; drought monitoring and assessment; flood mapping and damage assessment;
 landuse/landcover mapping for agro-climatic zone planning; wasteland management; water resources management; ocean/maring
 resources survey and management; urban planning; mineral prospecting; forest resources survey and management, etc.
            5. In order to know about the coordination mechanisms which exist between the Department of Space (DOS) and the major
 user Ministries/Departments' at the Centre and in the States and to know whether the remote sensing data are being found useful by
 the user agencies, the Committee took up the examination of the remote sensing operations of the Department of Space, and invited
 user Ministries to present a feedback on the data supplied to them. The examination of the remote sensing activities of the
 Department of Space was undertaken by the Committee on the basis of the Annual Report of the Department of Space for the year
 1993-94.
 
            6. In his presentation, the Secretary, Department of Space informed the Committee about the status of various remote sensing
 application projects and gave his viewpoint as to how the remote sensing data were being utilised by the various agencies. The
 Committee was informed that IRS-IA & IB are today supplying important data which are being utilised under the National Natural
 Resources Management system (NNRMS). This System was set up to facilitate optimal utilisation of the country's natural resources
 by preparing a proper and systematic inventory of the availability of resources. This will help in reducing regional imbalances
 through effective planning and promote long term sustainable development. Data obtained from IRS Satellites are used for several
 applications by various agencies of the Central Government; and of the State Governments, which have set up their Remote Sensing
 Centres. At present there are 22 States which have set up their own, Remote Sensing Centres. There are also a number of
 applications of remote sensing data which are currently being used by private entrepreneurs and voluntary agencies. The Department
 of Space, as the nodal agency for NNRMS, Coordinates the activities between various agencies of the Central and the State
 Governments, NNRMS has become operational to a large extent.
            7. As regards the coordination mechanism which exists between the Department of Space and the other user Departments, the
 Committee was informed by the Secretary of the Department of Space that a Planning Committee of NNRMS (PC-NNRMS),
 chaired by Member (Science), Planning Commission, with Secretaries of the concerned Central Government Departments as
 members., coordinates and guides this effort at the national level. Six Standing Committees in various major areas of application,

MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE AND CO-OPERATION
 
            13. The Ministry of Agriculture is one of the major user Ministries/Departments of the IR data. The Department of Space
 informed the Committee that three important operati6m application projects viz., (i) Crop Acreage and Production Estimation
 (CAPE) (ii) National  Agricultural Drought Assessment and Monitoring System (NADAMS) and (iii) Mapping c Saline/Alkaline
 soils, were being carried out with the assistance and co-operation of the Department of Agriculture and Co-operation in the Ministry
 of Agriculture.
Crop Acreage and Production Estimation
            14. Remote sensing estimates on area under cultivation and production of foodgrains such as wheat, rice, sorghum and oil
 seeds (like groundnut, mustard) for regions/districts identified jointly by the Ministry of Agriculture and the Department of Space
 are generated every season this project is carried out in close cooperation with users from the States and with funding support from
 the Ministry of Agriculture. Production figures are provided one month  in advance of the harvest. They meet the accuracy criterion

National Agricultural Drought Assessment and Monitoring System (NADAMS)
           
            18. The Department of Space informed that, since 1986, Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) information is
 being generated for the entire country at 1 km resolution. This information is being used for assessment and monitoring of
 agricultural drought conditions at district level in 11 States, and it is provided to the Department of Agriculture and Co-operation on
 a regular basis. Currently, sub-district level (tehsil/block mandal) assessment of drought conditions is also being done in Karnataka,
 Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Orissa. It is proposed to extend this programme, in due course, to cover all the drought-prone
 States. The feedback on the information on drought assessment, received from the district collectors/officials has been encouraging;
 and based on the feedback, information on storage levels of reservoirs, fuel/fodder availability, likely impact of drought on
 agricultural production, etc., is being included in the drought assessment reports. Weekly district-wise rainfall summary from the
 India Meteorological Department (IMD) is used in the National Agricultural Drought Assessment and Monitoring System
 (NADAMS). Comparative evaluation Index (VI) based drought assessment with regard to rainfall and aridity anomaly has been
 conducted. IMD issues short-term forecasts (upto 72 hrs.) and long-term seasonal forecasts, which are too general to be used for
 drought monitoring. However, the medium range forecasts of 7-10 days duration issued by the National Centre for Medium Range
 weather Forecasting (NCMRWF) could be used to predict vegetation response. These forecasts are presently experimental. An
 Expert Committee consisting of IMD and National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA/DOS represen­tatives has discussed twice, in
 1993, about the integration of IMD inputs with NADAMS. As part of R&D studies, using the database in Vegetation Index
 generated under this project, biomass estimation and vegetation dynamics at regional scale have been taken up.
           
            19. The Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture told the Committee that the application of remote sensing technology in drought
 monitoring, and assessment based on Vegetation Index (VI) of an area, was also not without its limitations. VI of a particular area
 certainly gave an idea about the extent of greenery, which helps to determine the status of drought in that area. Since such methology
 involved comparison with the data of last year, an accurate assessment become impossible if that year happened to be abnormal. If it
 was either less or more than last year, one really was not able to know about the position in the current year. IMD, no doubt, was
 doing weather forecasting which was of a general nature, and it was not a sub-division level forecast. In view of this, the Secretary,
 Ministry of Agriculture, suggested that there was a need to establish a linkage between the forecast made by IMD, the actual data of
 rainfall and. the VI during a particular period, and by combining all these indicators some kind of model could be developed for the
 future. The Committee feels that the suggestions made by the Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture need to be examined with a view to
 building a more fool-proof model.

Identification of Potential Fishing Zones
 
            21. Information on features such as water colour, turbidity, sea state, jetsam and jetsam, wave size and direction, wind
 patterns and climatic conditions has direct influence on fishing strategies. Timely forecast of potential fishing area can help in
 maximising the gains and optimising the efforts and time put in by the fishing fleets. The advent of remote sensing satellites, with
 their capability to cover large spatial areas over oceans on a repetitive basis, can prove to be of substantial economic benefit,
 particularly for a nation like India having a large coastline and extensive Exclusive Economic Zone. Although direct spotting of fish
 schools is not possible from satellites, indirect methods of identifying potential fishing zones have been found to be feasible. The
 Department of Space has initiated efforts to utilise space borne remote sensing on an operational basis to aid the fishing operations
 on the Indian coast:
 
            22. Presently, the fisheries forecasts are being made on the basis of the Sea Surface Temperature (SST), with the help of
 which zones are delineated where there is temperature gradient. The PFZ information consisting of latitude and longitude positions,
 bearing in degrees, distance in kilometres from the coast, depth in meters and validity period with reference to particular fishing
 centre are disseminated on a near real time basis. The forecasts are normally valid for a period of 3-5 days. Presently, the fisheries
 forecasts are disseminated by FAX/Felex to State Fisheries departments and concerned fishermen associations. It is put up on the
 notice bords in vernacular language for the convenience of fishermen. Local newspapers also publish it. It is also being broadcast
 through the All India Radio. It has been observed that, by and large, the notified grounds, as per the fishery forecast, are found to
 yield better catches of pelagic fishes (increase in catch per unit effort to the extent of 2 to 3 times) compared to unnotified grounds. It
 has also been observed that there is significant increase in catch per unit effort in demersal varieties of fishes in the inshore areas.
 
            23. The Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture agreed that the information of PFZs generated by the Department of Space through
 remote sensing had been found to be useful. The efficiency of the system to bring the information to the fishermen, however, needs
 to be . improved. In actual practice, benefit of this information was being cornered by the fishing trawlers; and small scale fishermen
 remained unaware of it.
 
            24. When the attention of the Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture was drawn to the fact the Department of Space had informed
 the Committee that the information was being broadcast through All India Radio in some States, he replied:
 
"Our feed-back so far is not very encouraging. But technology is there. It is question how we can put the technology to use. It
 is also our shortcoming. The issue is how to use it."
 
            25. The Committee notes that feedback received from the Ministry of Agriculture in this regard was different from the one
 received from the Department of Space. As regards data relating to PFZ not being available to small fishermen the Department of
 Space contended that the question did not arise because the information provided through the PFZ charts was mostly valid beyond
 ten kms. from the coast; these areas are exploited by those with trawlers, whereas traditional fishermen are confined within ten kms.
 On the basis of this information supplied by the Department of Space, the Committee finds that the satellite based PFZ charts
 facilitate mainly the commercial of fishing operations which are being carried out by fisheries departments and fishermen's
 associations who have necessary where withal to fish beyond ten kms. The PFZ maps presently appear to have limited use or no use
 for small fishermen who generally fish within ten kms.
 
            26. The Committee notes the view expressed by the Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture that the Department of Space should
 see to it that satellite based data regarding PFZs should be such as to benefit small fishermen also instead of being utilized largely by
 the fishing trawlers. It also devolves on the State fisheries departments and the local administration to make necessary arrangements
 to disseminate the information in a suitable way. The Committee accordingly recommends that the Ministry of Agriculture should
 coordinate with State fishery departments to take necessary steps to ensure that the satellite based information generated by the
 Department of Space reaches the small fishermen living even in remote villages.
 
            27. In view of the fact that PFZ charts prepared by the Department of                                                   ~Space have limited use
 for the small fishermen, as it is basically valid beyond ten kms., the Committee feels that the Department of Space should make
 efforts to integrate more oceanographic parameters than are being presently made use of, to make fisheries forecast more effective
 for near shore waters.
 
MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT
 
Wasteland Mapping
 
            28. About 16% of India's land area is considered as Wasteland due to various reasons including salinity of soils caused by
 excessive use of fertilisers and improper irrigation procedures, degradation due to the prolonged agricultural usage, deforestation,
 desertic conditions, snow cover, barren rocky and steep slopy areas, etc. The use of remote sensing for mapping wastelands in the
 country was started in 1985. The Department of Space had prepared Wasteland maps for the entire country on 1:1 million scale fin
 that year using Land sat data; and about eight wasteland categories were identified and mapped in that study. From this mapping
