NATIONAL RIVER CONSERVATION PLAN 
Recommendation 
 The Committee is deeply perturbed to note that the Yamuna Water at Delhi continue to be stinking and dirty. It 
notes with concern that the waste is still dumped in the Ya muna river through drains. It also notes with concern about 
the lack of public awareness and public participation in the cleaning of rivers. The Committee is, therefore, of the view 
that the cleansing of Yamuna has to go beyond cosmetic measures like removal of slums along the banks and greening 
of banks. Perhaps, the more concrete solution is to preven t the drainage wastes from entering the river and ensure the 
increase of the flow of the fresh water throughout the year. (Para 48) 
 The Committee is also of the view that  the Ministry, in coordination with the State Government of Uttar Pradesh, 
Haryana & Delhi, should plan a strategy for augmentation of water resources in the upper stretches of the Yamuna and 
for conserving water, both for domestic and irrigation purposes. (Para 49) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
 Cleaning of a river is a mammoth task requiring the involvement of all the stakeholders in the project, viz. Central 
Government, State Government, Local Bodies, Implementing Agencies, NGOs, general public, users, etc. Pollution 
abatement is not a one-time effort and the demands of ri ver cleaning keep on increasing with the increase in the 
population and expansion of townships and the success of the scheme depend on sustained efforts to be made by all 
these agencies. The problem of continuing pollution of Ya muna in Delhi, apart from the normal problem of discharge 
of untreated sewage into the river, can be largely attributed  to large scale extraction of its water upstream of Delhi for 
drinking and irrigation purposes leading to negligible flow in the river beyond Wazirabad at Delhi. 
 A significant development on the issue has been that pursuant to the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court on 
4th August 2004, a High Power Committee was constituted by the Ministry of Urban Development for preparation of 
Integrated Action Plan for the abatement of pollution of River Yamuna in Delhi. The Integrated Action Plan so 
prepared was submitted to the Hon’ble Court in November 2004 with several agencies identified towards 
implementation of the Action Plan for pollution abatement in Yamuna in Delhi. 
 Further, a High Powered Committee under the chairmanship of Member, Planning Commission was constituted 
by the Ministry of Environment & Forests in January, 1998 with representations from ripari an States of river Yamuna 
namely, U.P., Haryana, Delhi, Himachal Pradesh & Rajasthan to consider the issue of maintenance of minimum flow in 
river Yamuna and to suggest remedial measures both short term and long term for maintaining the minimum flow in 
the river. 
 The Committee has already submitted its report on the minimum flow of river Yamuna to Hon’ble Supreme 
Court as per the orders in the Writ Petition No.537 of 1992 (Sureshwar Sinha and others Vs. Union of India). 
 The Committee has recommended on the requirement for maintaining a minimum flow of 10 cumecs (cubic 
metre/sec.) in the river and decided the ratio of shares of a ll the riparian States in order to meet the. minimum flow 
requirement. The report on minimum flow also recommends the need for taking other measures for improving river 
flow, such as timely completion of upstream storages, effective treatment of sewage generated and utilization of treated 
sewage, irrigation/horticulture, improving water use efficiency by the riparian states in irrigation and drinking water 
sectors etc. The issue of augmentation of water resources in the upper stretches of the Yamuna and water conservation 
are within the mandate of the Ministry of Water Resources. 

 Adequate steps are being taken for creating public pa rticipation & awareness towards achieving a clean Yamuna. 
Activities under Yamuna Action Plan Phas e-I (Y API) were taken up in U.P., Ha ryana and Delhi as part of the non-
sewerage interventions during 2000-03 with an objective of generating awareness regarding the pollution in river 
Yamuna, among the beneficiaries in the project area. Several lessons that were learnt from YAP-I and specific value 
added components have been includ ed in YAP-II. The PP&A programme unde r YAP-II shall invo lve public in 
decision-making process by utilizing numerous NGOs. YAP-II also includes public relations/information programme 
in Delhi, to be implemented by Delhi Jal Board. In Delhi PP&A component is to be implemented by Municipal. 
Corporation of Delhi through several grassroots NGOs. This  includes Clean Yamuna Manch at Delhi and other PP&A 
programme (Socio-economic and environmental upgradat ion of CTCs programme, school health and hygiene 
programme, and town specific innovative programme). At present, MCD is in the process of selecting NGOs for 
different components as mentioned above covering all the zones of Delhi. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply and observes that the Ministry should pursu e the Yamuna cleaning 
programme diligently and in a time-b ound manner as the target of cleani ng Yamuna is still far from being 
achieved. The Committee is also not aware about the fate of the report on the Minimum Flow of River Yamuna 
submitted to Hon’ble Supreme Court. A serious and concerted efforts need to be made in this direction. 
Recommendation 
 Cleaning of all major polluted rivers by 2007 is one of the important targets of the Ministry. The Committee, 
however, finds that the Ministry has not been able to meet the proposed target under this programme and with the 
present pace, it would not be possible to achieve the target of cleaning of the polluted rivers by 2007. It’s the final year 
of the Tenth Five Year Plan and the Ministry is not in a position to name a single river where the requisite results have 
been achieved. This reflects that lack adaisical approach and inadequate measur es adopted by the Ministry on such a 
major issue. The Committee expresses serious concern in this regard and recommends that all the phase-wise 
programmes need to be monitored and the Measure of the Performance (MoP) should be introduced to review the 
cleaning activities on urgent basis. (Para 50) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
 Cleaning of major polluted rivers by 2007 is a monitorable target for the Ministry of Environment & Forests in 
the Tenth Plan. The present National River Conservation Plan covers all the major rivers in the country. These rivers 
are a part of the 14 major river basins of the country. Th e Plan envisages execution of works worth Rs.4736 crores 
leading to creation of sewage treatment capacity of 5365 mld out of which 1777 mld capacity has been created till 
March, 2006. Of this, 1051 mld capacity has been created in the first four years of Tenth Plan. The target for the current 
year has been fixed as 253 mld. Since the estimated expenditure for Tenth Plan is Rs. 1427 cr. only, it is obvious that 
the CCEA approved sewage treatment capacity of 5365 ml d under NRCP cannot be created during the Plan. The 
present approved cost of NRCP  is Rs. 4736 crores out of which GOl’s shar e is Rs. 4028 cr. Of this Rs. 928 cr. has 
already been spent during Ninth Plan. This leaves a balance of Rs. 3100 cr. which is required to clean the rivers as per 
the present approvals under NRCP against estimated expenditure of Rs. 1427 cr. for Tenth Plan. 
 The incremental pollution loads of sewage outweigh th e treatment capacity created, due to the exponential 
growth of the big cities on the banks of the major rive rs. Creation of capacity even to the identified pollution 
loads/stretches is not becoming possible due to the resource crunch as detail ed above. Problems in the operational level 
because of lack of infrastructure support by State Governments to the operation and maintenance of assets contribute to 
untreated sewage flowing into the rivers despite capacity being in place for treatment. 
 Inspite of the above constraints there has been a perc eptible improvement in the water quality of river Ganga 
since the launching of GAP-I. A statement of Biochemical Oxygen Demand and Dissolved Oxygen, key indicators of 
water quality during 1986 and 20 05 placed at Annexure-II clear ly shows that there is an  improvement in the water 

quality of river Ganga all along its stretch during this period. This water quality monitoring has been carried out by 
reputed independent agencies like Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur, Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd., Hardwar, 
Indian Toxicological Research Centre, Lucknow, Central Pollution Control Board etc. 
 In order to achieve the target of cleaning of major rive rs by 2007, huge amount of funds  are .required to treat the 
full quantum of identified pollution loads with projections for the project implementation period. Given the position 
that we are in the end of the Plan, the targets need to be inevitably carried to the next five year plan. 
 All the works under the National River Conservation Plan are done on the banks of major rivers in the towns and 
cities/locations in the identified polluted stretches of rivers across the country and identified lakes. Development and 
maintenance of a proper sewerage system inside the towns an d cities is primarily the responsibility of the respective 
State Governments and the prevention and control of industrial pollution is being taken care of by the Pollution Control 
Boards. 
Comments 
 The Committee observes that making  the major rivers of the country pollution free is a mammoth task 
before the Ministry and this can be done only with the cooperation of the concerned State Governments and 
people. For this, people have to be sensitized about th e importance of cleanliness of  these rivers and persuaded 
to extend their full cooperation in this task. Similarly, concerned State Governments h ave also to be impressed 
upon to cooperate in the best possible way. Merely shifting  the responsibility or putting  the blame on them will 
not help in achieving the gigantic go al. Besides this, the need for prudent budgetary planning with fixed time 
frame and will power cannot be over emphasized. 
PREVENTION  OF  AIR  AND  WATER  POLLUTION 
Recommendation 
 The Committee is of the view that Central and State Po llution Control Boards should have a more systematic 
approach to measure ambient air quality with a source-wise inventory and local concentration. The information should 
be collected on a regular basis, standardized for Metros and all urban sectors and should be regularly displayed 
publicly. The Central and State Pollution Control Boards should also monitor local impact of air pollution on health by 
commissioning epidemiological studies and create a comprehe nsive database for toxic effects of each of the emitted 
gases. (Para 52) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
 The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has drawn va rious studies for the year 2006-07 and also includes 
systematic collection of information and monitoring of ambient air. quality. A total of 313 Ambient Air Quality 
Monitoring stations have been established in various cities and towns through concerned State Pollution Control 
Boards. Initiatives have been taken to set up Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) in 
sixteen identified cities namely Hyderabad, Patna, Ahmedabad, Faridabad, Jharia, Bangalore, Pune, Mumbai, Sholapur, 
Jodhpur, Chennai, Agra, Kanpur, Lucknow, Varanasi and  Kolkata. Besides this, CPCB is also setting up twelve 
stations on operational contract basis in four cities which cover Delhi, Chennai, Bangalore and Lucknow. 
 It is further proposed to increase the manual National Air Quality Monitoring Stations as well as introduce 
monitoring of toxic air pollutants at selected locations. Efforts have also been made by CPCB to transmit the air quality 
data on a daily basis to CPCB website through environmental data bank. 
 In order to assess and quantify sources of air pollution, source apportionment studies have been initiated in six 
cities namely Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bangalore and Pune through institutions such as NEERI, Nagpur, The 
Energy Research Institute, Delhi, IITs at Mumbai and De lhi and Automative Research Association of India (ARAI), 
Pune etc. 

 To ascertain the correlation between Pollution and health impacts CPCB has initiated various epidemiological 
studies on the subject. Some of the studies initiated in this regard include : 
 Epidemiological Study to find the Effect of Air Pollutants especially Respirable Suspended Particulate 
Matter (RSPM) and other carcinogens on Human Health in Delhi-CNCI, Kolkata 
 A Study on Ambient Air Quality, Respiratory Symptoms and Lung Function of Children in Delhi-CNCI, 
Kolkata 
 Effects of Environmental Pollution on the Status of Human Health of Delhi Residents - AIIMS, New Delhi 
 Human Risk Assessment Studies in Asbestos Industries in India-ITRC, Lucknow 
 The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) in a ssociation with the State Pollution Control Boards 
(SPCBs)/Pollution Control Committees (PCCs) and institutions is monitoring ambient air quality and is creating a 
database. The results of ongoing source apportionment studies in six cities would indicate the contribution from various 
air polluting sources for evolving a road map for air quality management. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply. 
CONSERVATION PROGRAMME 
Recommendation 
 The Committee feels that the conservation of mangroves an d coral reefs scheme should be reviewed at regular 
intervals and must be accorded priority since mangroves not only protect the coastal communities from the fury of 
cyclones, coastal storms and tsunami, but  also promote sustainable fisheries and prevent sea erosion. In addition, they 
provide medicines and fuel wood. They also serve as the home of a wide range of flora and fauna. Mangroves plants 
survive high salinity, tidal extremes, strong wind velocity, high temperature and muddy anaerobic soil - a combination 
of conditions hostile for other plants. Mangroves  are successfully adapted in colonizing saline intertidal zone at the 
interface between the land and sea along the deltas, shallow la goons, mud flats, bays and backwaters in tropical and 
subtropical shelters coast lines.  (Para 57) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
 The Ministry accords high priority to the conservation a nd management of mangroves in the country and seeks to 
sustain and augment the mangrove forests by both regulatory and promotional measures. The Coastal Regulation Zone 
Notification (1991) under the Environment Protection Ac t (1986) recognizes the ma ngrove areas as ecologically 
sensitive and categorizes them as CRZ-I (i) which implies that these areas are afforded protec tion of the highest order. 
Under the promotional measures, the Government has id entified 38 mangrove areas on a country-wide basis for 
intensive conservation and management.

WETLANDS 
Recommendation 

 The Committee feels that the Ministry should take up the matter with the State Governments as our country’s 
wetlands suffer more than other eco-systems. Many of the wetlands are encroached upon and the remaining are mostly 
polluted with the industrial waste, sewage, pesticides, etc. The Ministry should think of making a suitable law that can 
protect the identified wetlands with a provision for compatible community use. (Para 59) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
 Realizing the importance of fresh water bodies for providing food, fodder, fuel and water for domestic, irrigation 
and industrial purposes; their role in supporting fisheries; number of rare and endangered species of flora and fauna; 
maintenance of natural biodiversity; helping in regulating hydrological regimes, flood control and recharging of 
aquifers etc., Government of India initiated National We tland Conservation Programme in 1987 in close collaboration 
with concerned State Governments. These steps were taken mainly due to degradation and shrinkage of water bodies 
due to encroachment, siltation, weed infestation, catchment erosion, and other resultant problems. 
Promotional measures 
(a) Based on the recommendations of the National Committee on wetlands in different meetings, 71 wetlands 
covering 22 States have been identified so far under National Wetland Conservation Programme under 
which 100 per cent assistance is given to the concerned State Governments. 
(b) Under Management Action Plans various conservation activities are funded which include - data collection 
and survey, identification of problems, mapping of wetlands, landscape planning, hydrology, control of 
encroachments, eutrophication and abatement, aquati c weed control, wildlife  conservation, fisheries 
development and environmental awareness on various aspects of wetlands functioning. 
(c) The management of wetlands is supplemented with research activities under which a Research sub-
Committee has also been constituted to identify more wetlands of national importance and to supplement 
Management Action Plan for intensive conservation on thrust areas of research. 
(d) 25 wetlands covering an area of 667131 hectare in the country have been designated as Ramsar sites of 
international importance so far. 
(e) Ramsar Conservation Award has been given to Chilika Development Authority during 2002 for ecological 
intervention of Chilika wetland. This is for the first time that any Asian country has been given such award. 
(f) Out of 71 identified wetlands, the Management Action Plans (M.A.P.s) for 39 wetlands have been approved 
so far and the process of sanctioning M.A.P.s for other identified wetlands is on. 
Increase in scale 
(a)  Number of wetlands under Wetland Conservation Programme increased from 27 between 1987 to 2002-03 
to 71 in 2004-05, an increase of 44 wetlands in last two years. 
(b) 9 States are new entrants to National Wetland Co nservation Programme. Number of States covered moves 
up from 13 to 22. 
(c) Tenth plan allocation of Rs 30 crores is almost doubl e that of the Ninth plan period at Rs 14.00 crores. 
During Tenth Five Year Plan, an assistance of Rs. 22.43 lakhs has been released till date. 
(d) An allocation of Rs. 90 crore has been sought for the Eleventh Plan Period. 
Regulatory Regime for Wetlands 
(a)  The National Environment Policy (NEP) envisages setting up of a legally enforceable regulatory 
mechanism for identified valuable wetlands to preven t their degradation, and enhance their conservation, 

formulation of conservation and prudent use strategi es with community participation; of eco-tourism 
strategies, integrated wetland conservation including c onservation of village ponds and tanks into sectoral 
development plans for poverty alleviation and livelihood improvement. 
(b)  An exercise is on in the Ministry to set up Regulatory Regime for wetlands on the basis of their 
categorization where regulation could be held at Central/State/local levels. Various parameters are being 
evolved for regulations of various activities at different levels. 
Training 
(a)  A National Training Programme for Integrated Water Resource Management & Wetland Conservation has 
been organized from 7-11 August, 2006 by Chilika Training Authority with the financial support from 
Ministry of Environment & Forests. 
(b)  Other institutes have been identified for organizing the regional training programmes which are : Centre for 
Water Resource Development & Management (CWRDM), Khozikod, , GEER Foundation. Gandhinagar, 
Environment Planning & Coordination Organization (EPCO), Bhopal, Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun, 
Institute of Wetland Management & Ecological Designs, Kolkota/ Department of Science & Technology, 
Govt. of Assam. 
Monitoring 
 A three-tier system at national level, State level and local level is in operation for effective coordination to 
implement the programme. 
- A National Committee on Wetlands was constituted in 1987 for giving advice on policy guidelines for 
wetland conservation in the country. The Committee is headed by Additional Se cretary(Conservation) and 
has members from concerned Ministries dealing with wetland conservation programme and experts in the 
field. The Committee advises Government on appropriate policies and action programmes for conservation 
of Wetlands, research & training, identification of new wetlands for conservation, collaboration with 
international agencies on issues related to these Ecos ystems, and review of progress in the implementation 
of Management Action Plans. 
- The State Steering Committees have been constituted fo r the identified wetlands under the Chairmanship of 
Chief Secretaries in concerned States. 
- At local level, district level committees have been co nstituted under the Chairmanship of District Magistrate 
to monitor the implementation of the scheme. 
Evaluation 
 Ministry is also initiating exercise on evaluation of we tlands conservation activities in those States, which are in 
operation for more than five years. Expert institutions are being identified for evaluation and they will be asked to 
review activities component-wise both from physical & financial point of view. 
Comments 
 The Committee appreciates the activities undertaken by the Ministry in identifying wetlands and pursuing 
this programme with sincerity. 
PROJECTS/SCHEMES FOR NORTH-EAST REGION AND SIKKIM 
Recommendation 
 The gregarious flowering of muli bamboo is a natural ecological phenomenon having high social and economic 
implications. The Committee, therefore, feels that the Ministry of Environment & Forests should collaborate with the 
State Governments to gear up for the impending catastrophe, since the magnitude of the disaster could be very large. 

The Committee recommends that the focus areas in this re gard should be harvesting, regeneration of the area and 
rodent control. (Para 64) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
 The Ministry of Environment and Forests, Government of  India, in consultation with the representatives of the 
North-Eastern State Governments, concerned Ministries and Departments of the Government of India and other 
stakeholders, has prepared an ‘Action Plan’ for management  of gregarious flowering of muli bamboos in the North 
Eastern States to be implemented by the respective Stat e Governments. To supplement the efforts of the State 
Governments, the Ministry of Environment and Forests has initiated a new Centrally sponsored scheme for 
management of gregarious flowering of bamboos in the North-Eastern States. The total outlay for four years, 
commencing from 2005-06, is Rs. 85.00 crores. The major components of the ‘Action Plan’ are harvesting, 
regeneration, rodent control and awareness generation. A Central Monitoring Committee (CMC) has been set up by the 
Government of India under the Chairmanship of Director General of Forests and Special Secretary for periodic review 
of the progress of implementation of the action plan. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply. 
INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION 
Recommendation 
 The Committee feels that the Ministry has not done enough to persuade the international community to adopt 
stringent measures and provide enough cooperation in curbing illegal trade in wildlife parts. The international 
community has not been successful so far to put effective check on illegal trade in wildlife parts, especially tiger parts. 
Therefore, it is very important for the Ministry to take pr oactive and strong measure on this matter. It should take up 
this common issue with the international community through Convention on trade in Endangered Species on Wild 
Fauna and flora (CITES). (Para 66) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
 The Ministry is aware of the illegal trade in wildlife and its derivatives and has raised the issue in various 
international fora / meetings including Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Flora and Fauna 
(CITES). Exchange visits by officers of  CITES - India and CITES - China were held in May-June, 2006 for improved 
understanding and enforcement of conservation issues in the two countries. A meeting within the India-China Protocol 
on Conservation of Tigers is proposed to be held in India later this year. The establishment of the proposed National 
Wildlife Crime Bureau which would include networking with international enforcement agencies, would greatly assist 
in curbing the international illegal trade. 
(A) India is a signatory to many international conventi ons responsible for protection of biodiversity and its  
 habitat. Important conventions include: 
(i) Convention on Biological Diversity, 
(ii) Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, 
(iii) World Heritage Convention, 
(iv) Convention on Migratory Species, and 
(v) Convention on Wetlands (Ramsar Convention). 
 India has played a key role in the CITES in adopting a resolution on conser vation of tiger and other endangered 
wild cats and the need for global support to contain illegal trade in wildlife, their body parts and derivatives are always 

emphasized in the meetings. Further, India has joined the Global Coalition against Wildlife Trafficking, and has a 
bilateral understanding with U.K. in this regard. In addition, India has bilateral arrangements with China and Nepal. 
These include: 
 Indo-Chinese Protocol in tiger  conservation. The protocol, inter-alia, stipulates joint measures to crack down 
illegal activities of poaching of tigers, smuggling and selling of  tiger bones and other parts of the tiger as well as its 
derivatives. 
 Action has been taken for hosting a Chinese delegation in the near future within the ambit of Indo-Chinese 
Protocol on Tiger Conservation. A response has also been received from China in this regard. 
 A bilateral discussion with the Chinese delegation took place at the level of the Minister of State for Environment 
& Forests in November, 2005. The issue of trafficking in tiger skins/body parts as well as body parts of other animals 
into China and Tibet from India, as reported in the media was discussed. 
 India hosted a CITES delegation from China in May, 2006, and issues on illegal trade in tiger and other wild 
animal body parts were discussed. China was also requested to join the global coalition against wildlife trafficking. An 
Indian delegation visited China in June, 2006 for further discussion in this regard. 
 A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) exists with Nepal India to establish a Joint Task Force to check 
trafficking across the borders. 
 Draft Protocols for bilateral cooperation with other neighbouring tiger range countries (Myanmar, Bangladesh 
and Bhutan) have been sent to the Ministry of External Affairs for vetting and concurrence. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply and would like the Mini stry to ensure that its words should also be 
translated into actions and illegal trade in wildlife parts is curbed. The Ministry needs to review its programmes 
and plug the loopholes wherever necessary to implement them more vigorously. 
WILD LIFE PRESERVATION 
Recommendation 
 Keeping in view the aforesaid observat ions made by the Tiger Task Force in its Report. It is observed that the 
basics of the wildlife conservation demand for extremely devoted, trained and high quality performance of existing 
staff alongwith strong law enforcement. (Para 71 ) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
 The States have been addressed in this regard and Central assistance for capacity building towards better 
performance of field personnel is provided to States. Specialized training courses are organized in the Wildlife Institute 
of India for the same. The States are also provided Central assistance under the ongoing schemes, like Project Tiger for 
deployment of ex-army personnel, home guards, CRPF, in addition to other patrolling strategy for complementing the 
initiatives of field staff for enforcement of law in protected areas. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply. 
Recommendation 
 Another factor, which the Committee feels is very important, is to provide special package for staff, amenities 
and incentives like hard area allowance, free rationing etc. for the forest protection guards combined with provision for 
basic infrastructure, such as wi reless sets, cell phones, vehicles etc. so that  these could be effective incentives to boost 

wildlife conservation. Fast track courts  for quick judicial settlements of wildlife crime cases, in the opinion of the 
Committee, can also do great justice towards conservation of endangered species in India like Tigers, Elephants, 
Rhinos, etc. (Para 72) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
 Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Project Tiger, a hardship allowance (project allowance) is provided to 
field staff as an incentive. Further, Central assistance is  also provided for creating basic amenities like hostels for 
children of staff posted in remote tiger reserves, procurem ent of field gear, arms, ammunition, vehicles, wireless sets 
for ensuring protection. The recommendations for providing free ration to field staff, cell phones and fast track Courts 
for quick judicial settlements of wildlife crime cases have been noted for needful action. 
Comments 
 While the Committee appreciates the efforts made by th e Ministry to minimize the hardships of the field 
staff, it must be ensured that field staff in remote tige r reserve should not feel deserted and neglected which can 
reflect in the discharge of their duties. 
Recommendation 
 For mitigation of human-tiger conflict, the minimization of livestock killings is an effective countering method 
towards socio-ecological constraints which may stand in the way of wild life conservation. To minimize the ill-effects 
of livestock killings on people, education and awareness programmes related to ecology and behaviour of tiger, genesis 
of tiger menace, possible mitigation strategies, need to be framed for the villagers in the important areas with a package 
for effective and quick compensation in genuine cases and effective participation of the village populace at the ground 
level which can immensely contribute for wild life conservation of endangered species. (Para 73) 
Action Taken by the Ministry 
 Central assistance under Project Tiger for compensation is provided towards depredation of livestock by wild 
carnivores, belonging to villagers living in the fringe areas of tiger reserves. Likewise, Central assistance is also 
provided for payment of ex-gratia to field personnel killed by wild animals apart from treatment for injury while on 
duty. To elicit the support of local people, Central assi stance for eco-development of fringe / buffer areas, based on 
participatory, village level micro plans, structured with the eco-development committee constituted for the purpose, is 
provided. There is a Memorandum of Understanding with local community while undertaking such initiatives, for 
securing their reciprocal commitment to assist the field staff towards wildlife protection. The site specific eco-
development plan contains a strategy for mitigating the man-animal conflict. Further, assistance is also provided for 
promoting awareness amongst the local people for wildlife conservation. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply and hopes that the steps being taken by the Ministry will help in mitigating 
the human-tiger conflict.

2.  Progress / Achievements during 2005 - 06:  
 PI - Creation of a Bio-cultural repository of Medicinal plants 
 In the year 2005-06, a critical revi ew of the published medical & ethno- botanical literature was undertaken 
to arrive at reliable enumeration of the medicinal plants of India. The review has revealed that 6,200 unique 
species of medicinal plants have thus far been recorded in published literature. This figure has been arrived at 
after carefully eliminating synonymy which inflates the estimate of the species to 8,000 and above. 
Corresponding to this revision the enumeration of the species used by the four codified traditional systems of 
medicine viz., Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, and Gso-rig-pa has also been pegged at 1,590 for Ayurveda, 1,130 for 
Siddha, 504 for Unani, and 253 for Gso-rig-pa. 
 On the basis of market and literature studies, the en umeration of traded species was also updated in the 
current year and enhanced from an earlier estimate of 880 sp ecies to 926 species. This suggests that only around 
15 per-cent of the known medicinal plants of India are in all India trade. The size of India’s medicinal plant 
resources is incidentally of the same order as that of the medicinal plants of China, which also has around 6,000 
ethno-medicinal species of which around 1,000 species are in active trade. 
 The FRLHT botanical team has discovered two sp ecies (Menispermaceae & Eriocaulaceae members) new 
to the botanical world and these have been sent for publication to Rheedea. Furthermore the team has also 
rediscovered in southern India two species viz., Hubbardia heptaneuron Bor  (POACEAE) & Madhuca 
insignis (Radlk.) HJ. Lam (SAPOT TACEAE) that were hitherto reported to be extinct by IUCN. 
 In 2005-06, the total percentage of medicinal plant species used by the different Indian systems of medicine 
captured in the repository has significantly increased and the cumulative picture is given in the tables below. A 
significant feature of the FRLHT herbarium is that it is fully computerized and can be searched both by 
vernacular names of plants as well as by their scientific  names. Another interesting feature is that the herbarium 
records are being digitized and as on December, 2005, 7,300 number of voucher specimens have been digitized.

P2 - Development of Educational Material on the rich  traditional knowledge of the Medicinal Plants of

 At the end of December, 2005, the Centre of Excellence has already completed three major CDs on 
medicinal plants viz., (i) Plants of Charaka Samhita, (ii) Traded Medi cinal Plants of India, (iii) Multidisciplinary

P3 - P4 - Training to Village Botanists in identification and monitoring of Medicinal Plants 
 Another goal of the Centre of Excellence is an experimental project and relates to capacity building in the 
area of basic taxonomy of medicinal plants amongst “village botanists” in peninsular India. The village botanists 
are visualized to be rural persons, who have traditional knowledge about the local medicinal flora and who reside 
in the proximity of the 54 ‘forest gene banks’ that have been established by the state Forest Depts. of Karnataka, 
Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra. 
 The village botanists trained under this program are expected to serv e the Forest Dept. local NGOs, local 
institutions like schools and colleges and tourists in matters like (a) plant identification including the correlation 
between local vernacular names and botanical names, (b) vegetation monitoring, and (c) providing cultural 
information to tourists about local plants. 
 They would generally be expected to function as freelance consultants in the same way as do other locally 
knowledgeable individuals such as folk-healers, traditional birth attendants, local pujaris, water-diviners etc. The 
village botanists are also being informed about the relevant  aspects of the Indian Bio Diversity Act so that their 
services are not misused. 
 A cadre of 100 village botanists from Karnataka, Maharashtra & Tamil Nadu has already been trained over 
the last 3 years. In 2005-2006 this work has been ex tended to Andhra Pradesh wh ere 40 VBs are undergoing 
training. The subjects on which they are being trained are plant morphology, identification, nomenclature, 
classification, herbarium methods, forest types, medicinal plants and their trade, medicinal plants included in Red 
List, CITES and Negative lists, field exposure to biodiversity rich and protected areas, patenting & intellectual 
property rights of Indian medicinal knowledge, national biodiversity act, documentation of medicinal and cultural 
information of plants, seed bank, nursery and propagatio n techniques. A directory of the VBs of Tamil Nadu has 
been published. A formal training manual for VBs has been prepared in Tamil and Telugu. 
P5 - Establishing an ethno-medicinal demonstration garden 
 A 5-acre medicinal plant garden comprising around 600 medicinal plant species has been established on the 
FRLHT campus. In 2005-2006 the following thematic sub-gardens have been established in the main garden viz., 
Garden of Zodiac signs, Garden of Aromatic medicinal plants and Plants used as antidote for poison The garden 

has also developed a nursery to serve households and ins titutions in Bangalore city In 2005-2006 the nursery in 
the garden has distributed 12,000 numbers of plantlets to households and institutions in Bangalore city. 
P6 - Pharmacognostic studies on prioritised medicinal plants 
 The botanical identity of several medicinal plants, can not be ascertained from their “parts” that are used as 
medicine and transacted in trade. The root, sometimes even the small seed, bark, stem pieces, gums, etc , when 
viewed in isolation, cannot be easily linked to a bota nical entity. In several cases there are also specific 
recommendations related to collection procedures related to time and habitats for collection and one does not 
know from the external appearance of the sample if these collection prescriptions were actually carried out. 
 In the Pharmacognosy laboratory a significant study was undertaken to establish the correct botanical 
identity of a plant called Vai-vidang that is very ex tensively used in the Indian systems of medicine. 
Phytochemical analysis (TLC, HPLC) of candidate samples indicated that whereas the literature suggests that 
only Embelia ribes corresponds to Vai-vidang, a field survey revealed that the species E. ribes, E. tsjeriam 
cottam, Maesa indica and Maesa ramenltaceae are being used in practice The study reveals that Embelia ribes 
and E. tsjeriam cottam contained the active ingredient Embellin and therefore can both be accepted as valid 
sources of Vai-vidang However the species Maesa indica, which is also traded as Vai-vidang did not posses this 
compound and should therefore be declared to be an adulterant Molecular (RAPDPCR) and microscopy methods 
have been developed to distinguish the authentic botanicals from the adulterants. In the current year innovative 
and cost-effective field kits for chemical identification and semi-quantification of the active ingredients of two 
important medicinal plants have been developed, tested and validated by users and independent labs. These kits 
represent a creative and useful application of chromatogr aphy for the medicinal plant sector. They will be of 
enormous use to smallscale industry in order for them to implement the good manufacturing practices (GMP) that 
are now mandated by law. 
 In such cases benchmarking of the chemical and ge netic profile of the parts of a properly identified 
botanical entity and collected in the prescribed way, can serve to establish its identity and quality. A substitute or 
adulterant or an improperly collected sample can be detected by matching its chemical and genetic profile with 
the benchmarked profiles of the original botanicals and their prescribed varieties 
 Pharmacognostic studies on ‘prioritised’ species in tr ade wherein adulterants and substitutes are currently 
prevalent are being carried out. 
 Elaborate comparative study of Embellia species mark eted as Vai-vidang has been done using botanical 
trade & Ayurveda information alongside using modern scientific techniques including physico-chemical 
parameters microscopy, assays & chemical fingerprint (TLC, HPLC). The molecular differences (DNA level) 
have also been studied using RAPD-PCR technique. The aim of the study is to resolve issues of controversial 
botanical correlations of Ayurvedic drugs. 
 Molecular studies have been done for candidates used as Vidari and specific PCR products have been 
selected for sequencing from two authentic candidates for Vidari, namely Ipomea mouritiana and Puraria 
tuberosa. Using SCAR technique, specific primers would be made and tested for the purposes of authentication. 
 Field Kits for authentication of identity and semi-quantification of active ingredients in two medicinal 
plants namely, Andrographis paniculata and Withania somnifera were developed. The kits have been tested by 
volunteers and validated by other scientific labs and found to be dependable, simple and scientific. User-friendly 
instructions have been printed for use by small-scale traditional medicine manufacturing units in a non-laboratory 
environment. 
P7 - Medicinal Plants Distribution Maps using GIS 

 Altitude, Rainfall, Soil Type and Forest type maps for India were digitised as base work for mapping. 500 
Geographical Distribution Maps of medicinal plants sp ecies of conservation concern and 80 Eco-Distribution 
maps of Threatened / Endemic Indian Medicinal Plant Sp ecies were prepared. A prototype of Digital atlas of 
prioritized medicinal plants of India is under preparation.

Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this 
One Hundred Sixty-seventh Report on the Action Taken by the Department of Bio-technology on the recommendations 
contained in the One Hundred Fifty-seventh Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants (2006-07) of the 
Department of Bio-technology. 
2. The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Bio-technology on the 
recommendations contained in the One Hundred Fifty-seventh Report of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests on the Demands for Grants (2006-07) of 
the Department of Bio-technology which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 18th May, 2006. 
3. There were fourteen recommendations contained in the One Hundred Fifty-seventh Report of the Committee.

P. G. NARAYANAN 
NEW DELHI ; Chairman, 
December 12, 2006 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

REPORT 
 The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Bio-technology (DBT) on the 
recommendations contained in the One hundred and Fifty-seventh Report of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests on the Demands for Grants (2006-07) of 
the Department of Bio-technology, which was presented to bo th the Houses of Parliament on 18th May, 2006. There 
were 14 recommendations contained in the Report. 
 Action Taken Note on the recommendations of the Committ ee and further clarifications thereon were received 
from the Department of Bio-technology on 14
th August. 2006 and 25th September, 2006, respectively. 
 The Committee’s recommendations, Action Taken thereon by the Department and comments of the Committee 
are set out in the succeeding paragraphs. 
BUDGETARY  ALLOCATION 
Recommendation 
 The Committee notes that the Department has been able to make optimum use of the funds allocation in carrying 
out its various programmes/activities. It also notes the assura nce of the Secretary of the Department that the remaining 
amount of the last quarter of 2005-06 will be fully utilized by March, 2006. (Para 21) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The Department is thankful to the Committee for appreciating the effective and proper management of funds. The 
Department has fully utilized the allocated funds during 2005-06. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply and desires compliance. 
Recommendation 
 The Committee notes the efforts made by the Institute in the areas of stem cell biology, molecular neuroscience 
etc. The Committee is hopeful that the Institute will do its best to develop human embryonic stem cell lines and further 
translational research by transplanting embryonic stem cell lines in animal models of spinal cord and brain injury. The 
knowledge derived from the above is extremely important considering its impact on clinical situations. (Para 25) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 National Brain Research Centre has initiated a major programme with DBT support in Stem Cells, which 
involves both the development of Stem Cells line(s) as well as  their transplantation into animal model with spinal cord 
injury, brain injury and retinal defects. It is held that in the next two years this initiative will provide valuable 
information. The DBT has funded this programme. 
Comments 
 The Committee would like to see that information ge nerated by the National Brain Research Centre 
through development of Stem Cells line(s) as well as th eir transplantation into animal model will go a long way 
in breaking new grounds in the field of therapeutic engineering to cure sp inal cord injury, brain injury and 
retinal defects. 
Recommendation 
 The Committee further notes the importance of research in areas of computational neuroscience, system and 
cognitive neuroscience, developmental neurobiology and basic research towards understanding of neurological and 
psychiatric disorders, as such cases are on the rise in the country owing to the stressful demands of the modern 
civilization which take heavy toll of psychological well-being. (Para 26) 

Action Taken by the Department 
 National Brain Research Centre has initiated a progra mme on neurodegenerative diseases with a view to 
understand both the pathogenesis as well as develop potential therapies for these disorders. The Department has further 
clarified that molecular and cellular neuroscience group is  actively engaged in understanding molecular mechanisms 
involved in the pathogenesis and progression of neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s and 
polyglutamine diseases using cellular and animal models. Several critical partners that mediate break down of 
aggregated proteins have been identified which can be useful as potential drug targets for these diseases. The molecular 
mechanisms underlying the behavioral learning deficit in neurodevelopmental diseases such as Angelman’ s syndrome, 
is also being investigated. Importantly, the neuropharmacological effects of plants that are used in traditional system of 
medicine for improving higher mental function are being examined as potential treatment for senile dementia including 
Alzheimer’s disease. Traditional systems of medicine such as Ayurveda offer a knowledge base that can be utilized for 
development of therapeutic intervention strategies for tr eatment of these disorders. Recent advances in molecular 
biology and neuroscience offer us the tools such as cell lines expressing human neurotransmitter receptors and 
transporters. DNA  microarray technology, transgenic animal  models and rationally defined, validated methods for 
testing higher cognitive functions such as memory are used suitably for assessing the therapeutic potential of the plants 
used in ancient systems of medicine. 
Comments 
 The Committee is of the opinion that  the programme initiated by the National Brain Research Centre on 
neurodegenerative diseases should be  taken in all seriousness keeping in  mind the increasing demand of such 
cures as neurological and psychiatric disorders are on  the rise. The Committee would also like to see the 
optimum use of traditional systems of  medicine, such as Ayurveda and ot her available traditional methods for 
development of therapeutic intervention for treatment of these disorders. 
Recommendation 
 The Committee feels that the development of new vaccines is extremely important. New vaccines and 
immunodiagnostic kits will be required by the country to check  spread of bacterial and viral diseases which either have 
become immune to old vaccines or are still un-tackled. (Para 31) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 National Institute of Immunology, New Delhi is working on newer insights/strategies for developing better 
vaccine as well as diagnostics. Third generation JE vaccine using Adeno virus recombinant has shown promising lead. 
New target has been identified for intervention of the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. New strategies to 
enhance immune response specially TH I type of immunity have been worked out that may work towards paradigm 
shift in overcoming resistance. NII has also shown good leads in the area of cancer based on hCG and SPAG9 that can 
be modulated for cancer therapeutic as well. 
Comments 
 The Committee would like the Department to bring JE vaccine to its logical conclusion so that it can 
benefit the people as soon as possible. Preventing and curing tuberculosis is yet an other area where vigorous 
efforts are required as people suffering from this disease come from poor sections of the society, who in most 
cases are dependent on physical labour for their survival which get hindered as a result of this affliction. 
Recommendation 
 The Committee also feels that in this age of market economics, fundamental high-end research being a high-risk 
venture requires participation from industry for distribution of risks between the research institute and the industry. 
Interaction with industry for manufacture of products deve loped from the research leads is extremely important to 

become commercially viable. The Committee hopes effective participation from the industry, which is also in long-
term interest of quality research, will be encouraged by the Department as far as possible. (Para 32) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 Public-Private partnership is being encouraged by the Department. A new scheme on Small Business Innovation 
Research Initiative (SBIRI) has been launched for supporting Small and Medium Enterprises and Private companies for 
pre-proof of concept Research. Joint partnership resear ch programme for product development have also been 
supported with Industry. The Department through NII has on going collaboration with several industries, namely: 
» Cadila Pharmaceutical Ltd. in tuberculosis and immunity related research 
» NPRL, Mumbai on inhibitor design 
» Panacea Biotech in the area of tissue culture based JEV vaccine 
» Dabur on compounds from traditional system of medicine. Efforts to involve more industries are going on 
for early stage tie up. 
Comments 
 The Committee takes note of the effort made by the Department to make research more and more 
professional and increasingly cost e ffective so that money put in researc h projects not only is recovered but 
surplus is generated which, in turn , can be put in other research project s. Institutions of Public-Private 
partnership should be strengthened further so that research becomes result-oriented and does not remain 
merely academic. 
Recommendation 
 The Committee takes note of Studies that have been initiated to understand the process of differentiation of 
embryonic stem cells into cardomycytes and also into dopaminergic neurons which could be utilized for replacement of 
damaged neurons in neurological disorders such as Parkinson’s. The Committee feels that new discovery about bone 
marrow stem cells is of therapeutic importance and can prove important in finding better cure for diabetes.(Para 36) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 Several programmes have been supported to isolate, propagate and characterize the adult stem cells population 
from various sources; to study the process of differentiation/transdifferentiation of adult stem cell population into 
pancreatic beta cell lineage and to understand the mechanism involved in diabetes reversal in-vivo upon transplantation 
of these stem cells. 
 The programmes supported to study the potential applications of stem cell in the area of diabetes are as follows: 
Project title Implementing Institute 
Islet Neogenesis from Adult Stem/Precursor cells - National Centre for Cell 
A step towards regeneration therapy in Diabetes. Science, Pune 
 Agharkar Research Institute, 
 Pune 
Islet immunoisolation with xenotransplantation and Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for 
stem cell regeneration to islets as strategies for Medical Sciences & 
treatment of diabetes. Technology, 
 Thiruvananthapuram 
 National Centre for Cell 

 Science, Pune 
Characterisation and differentiation of pancreatic National Institute of Nutrition 
progenitor cells / stem cells to insulin secreting Jamia, Osmania, Hyderabad 
cells, from adult mice pancreatic tissue - The role National Centre for Cell 
of specific nutrients Science NCCS Complex, Pune 
  
Comments 
 The Committee would appreciate if the above-mentioned programmes are concluded successfully so that 
the findings can be of use to patients of  diabetes who, of now, have no oth er option but to be fully dependent on 
expensive and constant medication. It would like to be kept informed of the progress made in this area. 
Recommendation 
 The Committee would also like the Institute to make more efforts for understanding the molecular basis of 
.cancer using cell line and animal models as this can help  understand this deadly disease better. The Committee would 
also like to emphasize the importance of studies on sequenc ing of the midgut cDNA library  of Anopheles Stephensii, 
the mosquito responsible for spread of malaria in India as malaria is still prevalent in backward areas of the country and 
still require a lot of effort for total eradication. (Para 37) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The Institute has identified cancer as a thrust area and is already developing several cancer animal models using 
transgenic lines from within the Institute and outside. In the 11th  plan, the Institute proposes to convert its activities into 
Centre of Excellence for cancer biology and application. 
 Further Research efforts on Expressed Tag analysis of Anopheles stephensii are being continued. Further 
emphasis has been laid on sequencing of the library fro m uninfected mosquito midguts and construction of Library 
from Plasmodium infected mosquito midgets and sequencing. 
Comments 
 The Committee is of the opinion that the Institute should continue to focus on cancer biology and should 
make full use of available biotechnologica l research in improving cancer treatmen t. It is also happy to note that 
the Department has a plan to conv ert the Institute into a Centre of Excellence for cancer biology and 
application, in the Eleventh Plan. 
Recommendation 
 The Committee is of the opinion that automated DNA sequ encing, comprehensive in silico modeling studies and 
microarray based approaches, which have already been initiated, should be brought to their logical conclusion. The 
Committee also feels that Data bases of genetic disorders prev alent in India and of the pathogen that causes TB should 
be completed as soon as possible as they can serve as an important referential source for further studies and research. 
  (Para 44) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The super computing facility created at IIT, Delhi was made accessible on biogrid lndia and via Internet to 
scientists and students from different parts of the country.  A website of the supercomputing facility has been launched 
(www.scfbio-iitd.res.in). which summarizes the major R&D and other academic activities at the facility. The 
indigenous suits of programmes have been developed for activ e site directed lead design (Sanjeevini), protein structure 

analysis & prediction (Bhageerath) and Genome analysis (Chemgene). Total 25 modules have been developed under 
this project, which include active site directed lead design, template library, molecule generator, drugs like filters, 
docking, structural analysis, energy analysis, binding affiniti es, protein structure analysis and prediction, generation of 
3 D structure, secondary/tertiary structure generation, sampling protein conformational space. Persistence length, radius 
of gyration, hydrophobicity index. Packing fraction, clash removal, scoring function, Monte Carlo optimizer, 
characterization of structure, free energy evaluation an d chemgene. An Inter Agency programme on Tuberculosis 
Research is contemplated. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply a nd would like a report on the progress made in this connection. 
Recommendation 
 The Committee observes that the research programme of  National Centre for Plant Genome Research (NCPGR) 
aims at contributing to the understanding of the structure, expression and function of genes and arrangement of genes 
on plant genomes and manipulation of plant genes/genomes to breed improved varieties of food and industrial crops for 
high yields of better quality products. The mandate of the Department becomes extremely crucial in the light of the fact 
that India is on the threshold of second Green revolution. The technological advances made  in the field of agriculture 
bio-technology should, in the ultimate analysis, translate into increased farm productions, which can raise per-capita 
income in the farm sector. (Para 49) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 Bio-technological methods including recombinant technology, marker assisted selection methods and molecular 
breeding can supplement our crop breeding efforts. The emphasis of the Agricultural Biotechnology research 
programmes is on improvement of yieid in crops through development of resistance against pest and diseases, tolerance 
to abiotic stresses ( like drought, salinity, etc.) and engineering male sterility in them for hybrid seed. In addition, 
efforts are being made to improve their nutritional quality. 
 The Department is already pursuing programmes on development of transgenic rice tolerant to drought and 
salinity, resistant to tungro virus, brinjal resistant to hit and shoot borer, hybrid mustard through barnase/arstar gene 
technology, pyramiding genes for leaf and strip rust resistance in wheat, development of markers for wheat quality 
improvement, biotechnological interventions improving important millet crops, etc. In addition. recently a programme 
on crop bio-fortification has been taken up for improving iron  and zinc micronutrients in our three major staple food 
crops viz. Wheat, Rice and Maize. These efforts are likely to benefit farmers as well as consumers. 
Comments 
 The Committee is of the view that  bio-technology can play an important role in increasing farm produce 
and thus substantially raise farm income. Agriculture biotechnology can also shoulder the responsibility of 
ensuring food security and the Department has an important task cut out in this respect. 
Recommendation 
 The Committee is of the opinion that the Department has taken steps to carry toxicological evaluation of 
genetically engineered products and development of protocol s/guidelines to evaluate various GM products for its 
toxicological aspects. A state-of-the-art facility for generating toxicological data necessary for the certification and bio-
safety approval of all GM products and to aid research la bs and Industry in evaluating the biotech products in the 
country has been created. The Committee feels issues of genetically modified seeds and their impact on agriculture in 
general and on farmers in particular are profound and have  to be taken seriously. Environmental issues and other 
externalities have to be taken into account before agriculture bio-technology is allowed fully in the field. Besides this, 

the frequency of toxicological evaluation of drugs, vaccin es, and other pharmaceutical and GM products will increase 
in the future and will require optimum utilization of these facilities. (Para 54) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The toxicological evaluation facilities are created in th e country in the public and private sectors and some of 
them meet the global standards. The Department supports these facilities technically by way of designing the relevant 
protocols to address the biosafety concerns as per the regul atory norms depending upon the nature of the product. The 
Department has supported some of the institutions for upgrading their facilities. The Department directs the 
investigators to develop information on the transgenic cr ops which includes impact on Indian agricultural system, 
farming community and environmental safety before they are recommended for cultivation. The Department will 
continue to provide necessary support as and when required for optimum utilization of these facilities for the safety 
evaluation of GM products in Healthcare and Agriculture. The Department has further clarified that the following 
projects and programmes based facilities for GM detection, testing, toxicology etc. have been supported: 
 1. Animal facility at National Institution of Nutrition, Hyderabad 
 2. Animal facility at DRI, Lucknow 
 3. GM detection facility at CFTRI, Mysore 
 4. Toxicological testing centre at ITRC, Lucknow 
 All these facilities serve the public and private sector institutions for GM food testing and evaluation. 
Comments 
 The Committee is of the view th at biosafety concerns are of i mmense importance. Agriculture 
biotechnology should not be contrary to ecological principles. Any such  research should take into account the 
long-term interest of farmers as they  are the ones who should benefit from such research and not greedy 
commercial interests looking for short-term benefits ca using externalities like ecolo gical imbalances and other 
hidden costs, which the poor farmers will have to pay later. 
Recommendation 
 In its interaction with the Secretary of the Departme nt, the Committee expressed concern regarding updating of 
curriculum especially of inter-disciplinary courses like those of biotechnology in various Central Universities. The 
courses have not kept pace with the recent developments in the discipline. The Committee feels that there is a gap 
between the target fixed and goals achieved due to non-availability of qualified scientists. To cope with the 
technological innovation and achieving major break-through, there is a need to develop a new strategy which can meet 
the international standards by way of quality training and education. The Committee is of the opinion that the 
Department should moot an idea of creating a pool of scientists in various fields by encouraging scientists not only 
from various parts of the country but also attracting Indian Scientists working abroad by way of special incentives and 
creating good working environment. It also recommends improvement in syllabi of universities to keep tune with times 
along with improvement in teaching standards. (Para 56) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The Department of Biotechnology has held workshops to consider the curriculum taught in DBT supported M.Sc/ 
M. Tech. teaching programmes and model curricula for M.Sc. (Animal Biotechnology, medical biotechnology, 
agriculture biotechnology, general biotechnology) and M. tech. (Biochemical engineering and biotechnology) have 
been developed and adopted. The Department is formulating an award scheme corresponding to Acharya J.C. Bose 
award and Ramanujam Award instituted by DST to attract NR I scientists working abroad to Indian laboratories for 
specific assignments. 

 The Department has further clarified that that a proposal for National Pool of jobs for scientists has been mooted 
and is under consideration. A proposal for recruiting Resear ch Scientists on a contractual basis under the innovative 
scheme of Centres of Excellence is under preparation. The strategy for the same is being planned in consultation with 
the Planning Commission. 
Comments 
 The Committee is hopeful that th e Department would do the needfu l to bring academic programmes 
relevant to the discipline in tune with the latest developments in the field. It is also hopeful that the schemes 
proposed by the Department would be ab le to attract Indian scientists in the country and abroad to research in 
the country, when implemented. 
Recommendation 
 The problem of inadequate supply of quality researchers for scientific research is dangerously growing to a level 
where it can severely hit scientific progress. Given the fact that metropolitan centres are no longer happy hunting 
grounds to enroll science students as business studies an d information technology provide more lucrative careers, 
potential scientists are to be found in small centres and then appropriately groomed. The Committee strongly 
recommends improved quality of science t eaching in small centres and exposing tale nted students from such centres to 
the bigger world of innovation and discovery. (Para 57) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The Department is awarding DBT -JRF and DBT PDF fello wships every year to enable students to work for 
doctoral and post doctoral work in Indian laboratories. Curriculum revision exercise and replacement of obsolete 
equipment for better Laboratory facilities, visiting faculty programme are being strengthened to Improve quality of 
teaching, in the Universities. M.Sc. Biotechnology Programme is being supported in about 65 universities. which are 
mostly outside the main cities. 
Comments 
 The Committee hopes that the efforts made by the Department will result in availability of quality 
researchers. It also hopes that such efforts will also help in popularizing science as a career option. 
Recommendation 
 The advent of new molecular and cellular techniques of genetic modifications of micro organisms has led to the 
continuing emergence of products including organisms of bio-technology that promises substantial benefits and 
importance to the quality of life. These techniques are available but to be safely and effectively used, they must be 
applied according to a number of priniciples and with th e support of a National Bio-safety Information Network and 
Advisory Service. The Committee is of the opinion that since newly introduced organisms have the potential for trans-
frontier impacts, there is an urgent need to develop national  code of conduct/practice to establish a general frame work 
and guidelines to ensure safety in research, development,  production, trade and use of these Genetically Modified 
Organisms (GMOs). The Committee feels that with the development of Comprehensive Code of Conduct and 
Guidelines for Bio-safety, the safe application of bio-technology in orderly manner would be possible. (Para 58) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The Department of Bio-technology has already prepared guidelines for safe use, application and release of GMOs 
in the environment under the provisions of Rules 1989 of EPA, 1986. These guidelines include “Recombinant DNA 
Safety Guidelines-1990”. “Revised Guidelines for Safety in Bio-technology-1994”. Revised Guidelines for Research in 
Transgenic Plants and Guidelines for T oxicity and Allergen city Evaluation of Transgenic Seeds, Plants and Plant 
Parts-1998" and “Guidelines for Generating preclinical and Clinical data for r-DNA based Vaccines, Diagnostics and 
other Biologicals 1999". All these guidelines provide compre hensive code for conduct fo r safety in research and 

development. production, and use of GMOs and guide the applicants to develop Bio-safety data for assessing safety of 
the biotechnology products in orderly manner before they are approved for use by the society. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply.  
Recommendation 
 Allocation to Public Private Partnership has been increa sed from Rs.20.00 crores in B.E. and Rs.16.54 crores in 
R.E. in 2005-06 to Rs.30.00 crores in B.E. 2006-07. The Committee has been informed that the increased grants are for 
a new Public-Private partnership scheme SBIRI that has been launched during September, 2005. The Committee 
observes that the private companies in different sectors of Biotechnology have shown a good response. Since the 
scheme has been initiated only in the second half of the y ear 2005-06, it hopes a much bett er response during the year 
2006-07. It appreciates the new initiative taken by the Department in this regard and in view of its importance to 
promote innovation for product development, this scheme needs to expand in a big way. (Para 62) 
Action Taken by the Department 
 The scheme “Small Business Innovation Research Initiative (SBIRI) has been launched during September, 2005. 
In view of the good response received, it is proposed to expand the scheme during Eleventh  Plan. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply.
